file: 2007/2007-07-06_golf tournament_contrast_strikes you_contrast in jobs_secretary and boss.gif
title: Boss Golfs, Employee Throws Phone

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm off to the executive golf tournament.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: It just struck me how much contrast there is between your job and mine.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Gotta go.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Let me know if anything else strikes you.

situation: The Boss announces he is leaving for an executive golf tournament while carrying a golf club. His employee at the desk remarks on the contrast between their jobs, and the Boss brushes her off and walks away. In the last panel she angrily hurls an object at him as he leaves.
punchline: The employee's polite-sounding invitation to tell her what else 'strikes' him is a sarcastic setup for her to physically strike the oblivious boss, with the thrown object turning 'strikes you' into a literal threat.
summary: A worker pointedly compares her labor to her boss's leisurely golf outing, then takes revenge with a well-aimed projectile as he departs.

title: Email Judo Against Coworker Requests

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And now for another round of e-mail judo.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Let's see... This guy wants me to attend a meeting.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Eee-yah! I'll tell him I'm booked.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: This guy wants some information.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Eee-yah! I'll tell him my hard drive crashed.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: This idiot wants my input on his document.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Eee-yah! I'll tell him the attachment won't open.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Who's winning today?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Not the people who sent me e-mail. Eee-yah!

situation: Wally sits at his computer and treats his inbox like a martial arts match, karate-chopping each request with an excuse. He dodges a meeting, an information request and a document review by claiming he is booked, his hard drive crashed, and an attachment won't open. Dilbert stops by and asks who is winning.
punchline: Wally's 'victory' is simply avoiding all work by deflecting every colleague's email with a flimsy excuse, so only the senders lose.
summary: A lazy employee gleefully swats away every email request with a made-up excuse as though it were a combat sport.

title: Catbert Hires Mumbler and Deaf Employee

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I hired two people to work on your project.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: One is a mumbler and the other one is hard of hearing but doesn't know it.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Mmmm, afterglow.

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, tells Dilbert he has hired two new people for his project. He reveals that one mumbles and the other is hard of hearing without realizing it. Dilbert sits at his computer, and Catbert is then shown alone, savoring the mischief he has set in motion.
punchline: Catbert deliberately staffed the project with a communication disaster waiting to happen, and he takes sadistic pleasure in the misery it will cause.
summary: The malicious HR director gives an engineer two new teammates whose combined quirks guarantee endless miscommunication, then gloats over the chaos to come.

title: Dilbert Resigns With Insulting Drawing

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My side job as a cartoonist is doing well, so this is my resignation.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My new career involves sitting around in my pajamas and thinking of ways to ridicule you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Actually, it's not so much a letter of resignation as it is a drawing of your body with a manure head.

situation: Dilbert walks into the Boss's office holding a piece of paper and announces he is quitting because his side job as a cartoonist is successful. He explains that his new career is to sit at home in pajamas thinking up ways to mock the Boss. He then reveals the 'resignation letter' is actually a cartoon of the Boss's body with a manure head.
punchline: Dilbert's resignation is literally an insulting cartoon of the Boss, showing he is now free to ridicule management for a living.
summary: A newly successful cartoonist hands in his notice in the form of a rude caricature of his superior.

file: 2007/2007-06-24_run by attorney_hi with hammer_attention_painful process_final result_hammer is quicker.gif
title: Hammer Beats Legal Review

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Run this by our attorney.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: May I vigorously hit myself with a hammer instead?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You have my attention.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Either way, it's a painful process that won't change the final result.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But the hammer is quicker and it will still make you feel as if you made me do something.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay. Try the hammer thing.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Bam! Ouch! Bam! Ouch! Bam! Ouch!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now run it by our attorney so it feels as if I did two things.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert to run a document past the company attorney. Dilbert argues that legal review is a painful process that won't change the outcome, and offers to hit himself with a hammer instead as a quicker alternative. The Boss agrees, Dilbert injures himself, and the Boss then demands the attorney review anyway.
punchline: The Boss accepts the self-inflicted injury as a way to feel productive, then insists on the legal review too, so he can feel he accomplished two things and Dilbert's pain bought him nothing.
summary: Offered a quicker way to feel in control, a manager takes the painful shortcut and still demands the original pointless step.

title: Boss Blames Dilbert for Button

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why did you add this button to the user interface?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You told me to.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why would I tell you that?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You always suggest random changes to create the illusion of adding value.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, remove that button.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's only on your copy.

situation: Dilbert confronts the Boss about an unwanted button that was added to the user interface. The Boss claims Dilbert asked for it, since Dilbert always suggests random changes to look useful. When Dilbert demands the button's removal, the Boss reveals it only exists on Dilbert's copy.
punchline: The Boss has deliberately added a pointless change to Dilbert's own copy, turning Dilbert's habit of making meaningless suggestions back on him.
summary: A designer who pads his work with needless tweaks finds his manager has turned the tables with a pointless change of his own.

file: 2007/2007-07-28_eliminated budget_automated test software_new code_automated test_end any converstaion_calling person big baby.gif
title: Big Baby Ends Every Conversation

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You eliminated the budget for automated test software. How are we going to test our new code?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Go write some automated test software, you big baby. I already pay you, so it's free.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Today I learned you can end any conversation by calling the other person a big baby.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Waa-waa! Do you want your bottle?

setting: The Boss's office, then Dilbert's home
situation: Dilbert confronts his boss about cutting the budget for automated test software and asks how the new code will be tested. The boss tells him to write the test software himself, since he's already paid and it costs nothing, and insults him as a big baby. Later Dilbert tells Dogbert about his new conversation-ending trick, and Dogbert immediately uses it on him.
punchline: Dilbert proudly adopts the boss's tactic of ending a conversation with an insult, and Dogbert promptly ends the conversation by mocking him with the same tactic.
summary: After his boss dodges a budget complaint by calling him a baby, Dilbert tries the same cheap trick at home and gets mocked in return by his dog.

title: Outsourced Employee Returns as Contractor

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ted, I'm going to eliminate your function and outsource it to the Dogbert outsourcing company.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: I need a job.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You're hired.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: I'm baaack!

setting: Office and Dogbert's outsourcing company office
situation: The Boss tells Ted that his function is being eliminated and outsourced to the Dogbert outsourcing company. Ted then asks Dogbert for a job and is immediately hired. Ted returns to his old office, now working for the outsourcing firm and doing the same job as before.
punchline: Outsourcing just moves the same employee onto another company's payroll, so Ted ends up back at his own desk doing the same work, presumably at greater cost to the company.
summary: A laid-off worker is rehired by the outsourcing vendor and promptly walks back into his old job.

title: Concept Product Press Conference Fiasco

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're going to take a page from the automakers' playbooks.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Automakers prove their design skills by creating concept cars that will never go into production.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then they prove their management skills by producing cars that are less attractive than corrective under-pants.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tomorrow we're holding a press conference to show the world our own concept product.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our concept product can stop global warming and wax your back at the same time.

transcript.speaker: Reporter
transcript.text: Can it actually do those things?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why do you care?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So... actually it's just a huge waste of our time.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You have a mighty low opinion of news.

setting: Conference room, then a press conference outside an office building
situation: The Boss tells his team the company will copy automakers by unveiling a concept product that will never be built. At the press conference he claims the product can stop global warming and wax your back. When the reporter asks if it really works, the Boss deflects, then admits the whole event is a waste of the reporter's time.
punchline: The Boss implies that journalists will report on anything, however absurd or meaningless, which is a sarcastic insult to the news media.
summary: A manager copies car makers by announcing a ridiculous vaporware product to the press and then scoffs at the reporter for bothering to cover it.

title: Software Yells At Employees Instead

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, I bought Dogbert's management software to yell at you so I don't have to.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I recommend track 3, titled "You're my least valuable asset."

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Who wants to buy Dogbert's noise cancellation headphones for bad employees?

transcript.speaker: Computer
transcript.text: I need you less than my mousepad.

situation: The Boss holds a gadget loaded with Dogbert's management software and tells Wally it will do his yelling for him, recommending a track that insults him. In the last panel Wally sits drinking coffee while the device keeps insulting him, and Ratbert wanders by offering noise cancellation headphones for bad employees.
punchline: Dogbert profits from both sides of the problem by selling the boss automated insults and then selling the insulted employee headphones to block them out.
summary: A manager outsources his scolding to a purchased gadget while a scheming pet markets earphones to the employee on the receiving end.

file: 2007/2007-09-11_end of buisness_corpse flotaed_ocean floor_seven hours_come back_anticipation_killing alice.gif
title: Alice's Seven-Hour Dread, Boss Postpones

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, see me at the end of business today.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Ohmygod, ohmygod, what corpse floated up from the ocean floor? I can't wait seven hours. Gah!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Seven hours later

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What?! What?! What?!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can you come back tomorrow?

setting: Office cubicle and the Boss's office
situation: The Boss tells Alice to see him at the end of the business day, and she spends the whole day in a panic imagining what old mistake has resurfaced. When she finally arrives seven hours later, frazzled and shouting, the Boss casually asks her to come back tomorrow.
punchline: The Boss's vague summons caused Alice a full day of needless anxiety, and he then blithely reschedules, prolonging her torment without any awareness of what he put her through.
summary: A manager's cryptic request for an end-of-day meeting leaves an employee frantic all afternoon, only for him to casually postpone it.

title: Green Consultant Hates Earth A Little

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Green Consultant

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Stop eating, breathing, driving, defecating, and procreating.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Sit in the dark and decompose on some garden seeds.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Or do you admit you hate Earth?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: A little.

situation: Dogbert, working as a green consultant, advises the Boss to stop all basic human activities like eating, breathing and driving to help the environment. He then tells him to sit in the dark and decompose on garden seeds. Dogbert asks whether the Boss would rather admit he hates Earth, and the Boss admits he does, a little.
punchline: Dogbert's absurdly extreme environmental advice is framed as the only alternative to hating the planet, and the Boss shrugs and admits that he does, a little.
summary: A consultant demands such extreme eco-sacrifices from a client that admitting to disliking the planet starts to seem like the reasonable choice.

file: 2007/2007-01-28_meeting staff_chain of command_fake hone calls_hanging around office_waiting to get off phone_weirdo_go away.gif
title: Mutual Avoidance Up the Chain

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: I enjoyed meeting your staff. Keep up the good work.

transcript.speaker: Middle Manager
transcript.text: This isn't my staff. I report to the guy who reports to you.

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: Really? Which one of you reports to me?

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: Well, that explains why you keep hanging around outside my office.

transcript.speaker: Senior Manager
transcript.text: I've been going to your office for years, waiting for you to get off the phone so I could talk to you.

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: I've been making fake phone calls for years, hoping the weirdo outside my office would go away.

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: Keep up the good work.

situation: A senior executive meets a group of employees and compliments the staff, only to learn that the man he is addressing is not his direct report. The two men realize that one has been waiting outside the other's office for years, while the other has been faking phone calls to avoid him.
punchline: An executive has spent years pretending to be on the phone to dodge his own direct report, showing how out of touch and avoidant management can be, and then simply tells him to keep up the good work.
summary: Two managers discover that years of awkward hallway lingering and fake phone calls were each trying to avoid the other.

title: Put In Charge, Not Really

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You'll be in charge of this project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's my budget?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll need to approve all expenses.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Who will report to me?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your team will report to me and I'll tell them what to do.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll start on the project plan.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Um. . .

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Skip that part. I already have a plan in my head.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hypothetically, who would take the blame if this project failed?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, you're in charge. . .

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he will be in charge of a project, but then keeps control of the budget, the team, and the planning. When Dilbert asks who takes the blame if the project fails, the Boss walks away and says Dilbert is the one in charge.
punchline: The Boss gives Dilbert all of the responsibility and blame for the project while keeping every bit of the actual authority.
summary: A manager hands over a project in name only, retaining all decision-making power while making sure his subordinate absorbs any failure.

title: Simulating a Pandemic's Productivity Loss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Run a simulation of our productivity if we lost half our workforce to a pandemic.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Should I assume we lose the productive people or the people who ask other people to run pandemic simulations?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Try both ways.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay. I'm done.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert to simulate how productivity would suffer if half the workforce were lost to a pandemic. Dilbert asks whether the lost half would be the productive workers or the managers who request such simulations. The Boss tells him to try both, and Dilbert immediately announces he is finished, implying the results are obvious.
punchline: Dilbert's instant 'I'm done' implies that losing the people who request pandemic simulations would cost the company nothing, so no actual simulation is needed.
summary: A manager's request for a workforce-loss model gets a swift answer that suggests management contributes nothing to output.

file: 2007/2007-08-03_use open source_emergency_trade publication_no one gets hurt.gif
title: Boss Discovers Open Source, Staff Intervene

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: From now on, I want you to use open source software for everything we do. It's free.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll be right back.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's an emergency. I think he's been reading.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: We know you have a trade publication in here. Hand it over and no one has to get hurt.

situation: The Boss orders Dilbert to switch the company to open source software because it's free. Dilbert rushes to Alice, alarmed, saying the boss has been reading. Alice then storms into the boss's office and demands he hand over his trade publication, like a hostage negotiator.
punchline: The boss only gets dangerous ideas from trade publications, so his employees treat his reading material like a weapon that must be confiscated before anyone gets hurt.
summary: When the boss gets a costly-sounding tech idea from his reading, his employees react as if disarming a dangerous man.

file: 2007/2007-09-08_new circuit design_worse_everyone says so_not familiar_spoke with people_rumprs_innuendo_made up staory.gif
title: Everyone Says: One Person's Rumor

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Everyone says your new circuit design is worse than the old one.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: By "everyone," do you mean you heard it from one person who doesn't like me, and isn't familiar with either design?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I also spoke to the people who heard it from that one person.

setting: Office, in front of Dilbert's workspace
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that everyone says his new circuit design is worse than the old one. Dilbert challenges the claim, suggesting it traces back to a single person who dislikes him and knows nothing about either design. The Boss replies that he also consulted people who merely heard the criticism from that same person.
punchline: The Boss treats secondhand repetition of one person's baseless opinion as independent confirmation, so the 'everyone' consensus is really just one biased source echoed.
summary: A manager passes along a damning verdict on an engineer's work that turns out to be a single grudge-holder's gossip repeated by others.

title: Dilbert Sprays Whistleblower, Keeps Cheap Shoes

transcript.speaker: Escaped Worker
transcript.text: Please help me. Your dog has enslaved my people in your basement and forced us to make running shoes!

transcript.speaker: Escaped Worker
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! My eyes!!!

transcript.speaker: Sound Effect
transcript.text: Pssst

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I like to help people, but I also like inexpensive footwear.

situation: A hooded figure bursts into Dilbert's kitchen and begs for help, claiming Dogbert has enslaved his people in the basement to manufacture running shoes. Dilbert, sitting at the table with his coffee, responds by spraying the intruder in the face with a spray bottle. He then muses that he likes cheap shoes too much to intervene.
punchline: Dilbert knowingly tolerates slave labor because it keeps his footwear cheap, a jab at consumers who ignore sweatshop conditions behind inexpensive goods.
summary: A pleading escapee reports forced labor beneath the house, but the homeowner would rather keep his bargain sneakers than get involved.

title: Dogbert's Career Advice: Love Not Working

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert, Career Counselor

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Do something you love.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I love not working.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Do you have any loves that are less loserish?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I love to watch bowling!

situation: Dogbert, acting as a career counselor, advises Dilbert to do something he loves. Dilbert says he loves not working, so Dogbert asks for a less loserish passion. Dilbert replies that he loves to watch bowling, which is no better.
punchline: Dilbert's second-choice passion, watching bowling, is just as loserish as his first, showing his answers are equally unhelpful for finding a career.
summary: A dog counselor tells a client to pursue his passion, and the man's two answers are laziness and spectator sports.

title: Customer Waits for New Model

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When do you expect to come out with a new model?

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: In about two months.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll wait and buy the new model.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Did I say two months? I meant never.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Never? That must mean your company is going out of business and won't support this product.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's a length of time between two months and never that would cause you to buy now?

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: One year.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Our new model comes out in a year.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll wait until then.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: You're the worst customer ever.

setting: A sales office, with Dilbert speaking to a vendor's salesman over the phone
situation: Dilbert phones a vendor and asks when the next model of a product will be released. Every time the salesman gives a date, Dilbert says he will wait for it, so the salesman keeps changing his answer, first to never and finally to one year. Dilbert simply says he will wait anyway.
punchline: The salesman is outmaneuvered because Dilbert refuses to buy until the new model appears, and the salesman, who wanted a sale now, ends up complaining that Dilbert is the worst customer ever.
summary: A buyer calmly turns every release-date answer from a salesman into a reason to postpone his purchase.

title: Raises Based On Looks

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Every company needs goals.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We have division goals, department goals, district goals, personal goals and affiliate goals.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You will all attend a four-hour training session on how to write goals.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Every week you will report on how you are doing compared to your goals.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Those reports will be entered into a giant database.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Won't the size and complexity of the database make it impossible to know what's really happening?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yes. That's why your raises will be based on what you look like.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Bummer for you.

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: The Boss announces an elaborate goal-setting system with many layers of goals, mandatory training, and weekly reports fed into a giant database. Dilbert points out that the database will be too big and complex to reveal anything useful. The Boss agrees and reveals that raises will instead be based on appearance.
punchline: After building a huge goal-tracking bureaucracy, management admits the data is useless and decides raises on looks, and the final jab suggests the unattractive employees are out of luck.
summary: A manager piles on goals, training and reporting, then concedes the data is meaningless and ties pay to physical appearance.

title: Vendor Dodges Every Price Question

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What would your system cost?

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: We can deliver in two weeks.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But what would it cost?

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: A lot of vendors deliver in four weeks, but we can do it in two.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm asking about price, not delivery schedules.

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: Do you want it shipped by ground or air? Air is even faster.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What does it cost?

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: Ground costs less than air.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: GAAA!!! What does the system cost?!!

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: For ground?

situation: Dilbert repeatedly asks a vendor's sales rep how much her system costs. She answers every time with delivery times and shipping options, never giving a price. Dilbert finally snaps in frustration, and she responds by asking whether he means the price for ground shipping.
punchline: The vendor's evasive non-answers drive Dilbert to a breakdown, and she still doesn't give a price, implying the system cost is something she is deliberately avoiding.
summary: A salesperson answers every request for a price with talk of delivery speed and shipping methods until her customer loses it.

title: Fired Over Budget Typo

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ted, I have to let you go, but there's a good reason.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: There's no money to pay your salary because I made a typo in my budget request.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Until then, I was totally planning to reward your hard work.

setting: The Boss's office, with an exterior shot of the office building in the middle panel
situation: The Boss tells Ted he is being laid off and claims there is a good reason. He explains that his own typo in a budget request left no money to pay Ted's salary. He adds that he had been planning to reward Ted's hard work, and Ted reacts with angry, clenched-fist disbelief.
punchline: The Boss's own clerical mistake costs an employee his job, and his insincere claim that he was about to reward Ted makes the firing even more insulting.
summary: A manager sacks a loyal employee because of his own budgeting blunder, then claims a reward was on the way.

file: 2007/2007-06-13_passion for job_ceo's visit_meeting_condescending_rented mules_intimidate_corproartions_afford luxury items_ping pong table_no raise_offend_belitte_pay dosparity_slavery_business.gif
title: CEO Buys Ping-Pong Table

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: CEO visit

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: It's important that you have a passion for your job.

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: For example, my passion involves working you like rented mules so I can afford to purchase luxury items.

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: I bought a ping-pong table with the raise you didn't get.

setting: Conference room during a CEO visit
situation: The CEO visits and lectures employees about having a passion for their jobs. He then cheerfully admits his own passion is overworking them to fund his luxury purchases. He caps it off by saying he bought a ping-pong table with the raise the employees were denied, while Dilbert and the Boss sit silently at the table.
punchline: The CEO's "passion" is exploiting his workers, and he openly brags that their denied raises paid for his own frivolous perk.
summary: An executive preaching job passion casually reveals he profits by squeezing his staff and spending their withheld pay on recreation.

file: 2007/2007-01-30_analyzed dna_most qualified applicant_willing to work_has three ears_snout_life expectancy of thursday_new guy.gif
title: DNA-Selected Hire Dies Thursday

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I analyzed the DNA of all of your applicants to find the best fit for the job.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The most qualified applicant who is willing to work for you has three ears, a snout, and a life expectancy of Thursday.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, meet the new guy. And do it quickly.

transcript.speaker: New Guy
transcript.text: Cough cough

setting: The Boss's office and a nearby hallway
situation: Dogbert, acting as a hiring consultant, tells the Boss he used DNA analysis to find the best-fit applicant. The only qualified person willing to work for the Boss turns out to be a sickly, mutated man with three ears and a snout, who is coughing and has only days to live. The Boss then introduces him to Dilbert and tells Dilbert to hurry.
punchline: The Boss's pay and working conditions are so bad that the only willing candidate is a dying mutant, so Dilbert has to rush through the introduction before the new hire expires.
summary: A consultant's genetic screening turns up a coughing, snouted, three-eared hire who will be dead by week's end, and the boss urges haste.

title: Wally's Facial Expression Avoids Action Items

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wally, you have attended thousands of meetings and never gotten an action item. What is your secret?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: When the action items are handed out, I use a certain facial expression to ward them off.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: ...And I'll need some-one to...

setting: Office cubicle and a conference room
situation: Dilbert asks Wally how he has managed to avoid ever being assigned an action item in thousands of meetings. Wally, holding his coffee mug, explains that he uses a special facial expression to ward them off. In the meeting, the Boss starts asking for someone to take a task while Wally sits with a blank, vacant stare.
punchline: Wally's secret to dodging work is simply looking so vacant and unhelpful that nobody dares assign him anything, and the meeting proves it works.
summary: A lazy employee reveals that he evades meeting assignments by pulling a particular face, and a scene in a conference room shows the trick in action.

title: Dogbert's Absurd Dwarf PR Campaign

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert does public relations

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Our products are made by asthmatic dwarves. You should do a story on that.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Not enough? Okay, what if the dwarves are also polygamous serial killers?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: When you talk to the reporter, try to slouch, wheeze, and act henpecked to the point of homicide.

setting: Dogbert's office, then the Boss's office
situation: Dogbert, acting as a PR consultant, phones a reporter to pitch a story about his client's products being made by asthmatic dwarves. When that seems insufficiently newsworthy, he escalates the pitch to polygamous serial killers. He then coaches the Boss to act like one of these dwarves for the reporter interview.
punchline: Dogbert's PR strategy is to fabricate an increasingly lurid story and then have the Boss pose as the sickly, henpecked dwarf to sell it to the media.
summary: A PR-minded Dogbert keeps embellishing a ridiculous press pitch, then instructs his clueless client to play along in costume.

file: 2007/2007-06-08_happy birthday_50 years old_entire life_delusional thing_old man_office_computer_aging_dementia_life changes_technology.gif
title: Turning 50 Is Pleasantly Delusional

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Happy birthday. What's it like to be 50?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It's great! I've never felt better in my entire life!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So it's sort of a delusional thing?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Yes, luckily.

situation: Dilbert stands holding a coffee mug and wishes a seated coworker a happy birthday, asking what turning 50 feels like. The coworker, sitting at his computer, enthusiastically claims he has never felt better. Dilbert asks if that's a delusion, and the coworker cheerfully agrees.
punchline: The coworker admits his claim of feeling great at 50 is a delusion, and is relieved that the delusion is what's getting him through aging.
summary: A man turning fifty confesses that his sense of feeling wonderful is a fortunate illusion helping him cope with getting older.

title: Catbert Detects False Hope

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Stop right there. I'm detecting a glimmer of hope.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I was hoping I would be appreciated for my hard work.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: False hope is okay. Carry on.

situation: Catbert, holding a handheld detector, stops Dilbert after sensing a glimmer of hope in him. Dilbert admits he was hoping to be appreciated for his hard work. Catbert checks the reading and decides it is only false hope, so Dilbert is allowed to carry on.
punchline: Catbert, the evil HR character, polices employee optimism, and only lets hope slide when it is false, implying appreciation for hard work will never actually come.
summary: A gadget-wielding feline HR officer scans an employee for optimism and waves him on once he confirms that the hope is unfounded.

file: 2007/2007-07-25_punching people_high rates_ridiculous combpver_punch face in_regain element_surprise_therapy session_couch_expressing.gif
title: Therapist Becomes Punching Target

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I can't stop punching people who deserve to be punched.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: For example, your high rates and ridiculous combover make me want to punch your face in.

transcript.speaker: Therapist
transcript.text: But you won't, right?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Let's see what happens when I regain the element of surprise.

setting: A therapist's office with a couch and armchair
situation: Alice lies on a therapist's couch and confesses she can't stop punching people who deserve it. She then offers the therapist himself as an example, citing his high fees and ridiculous combover. When he nervously asks if she won't actually do it, she ominously says she'll wait until she has the element of surprise back.
punchline: Alice's therapy session turns into a thinly veiled threat against the therapist, who has just unwittingly given her a target by overcharging her and sporting a silly combover.
summary: A woman describing her violent urges to her therapist helpfully demonstrates them on him, then promises to strike once he's off guard.

title: Redundant Messages Across Every Channel

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Did you get the note I left on your monitor?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Did you get my voicemail?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Did you get my e-mail?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Should I tell you what the note and voicemail and e-mail said?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There's something wrong with you.

situation: A coworker keeps checking whether Dilbert received her note, voicemail and e-mail, and he answers yes each time. She then offers to tell him what the three messages said, as if he might not have read them, and he tells her there is something wrong with her.
punchline: She sent the same message through every possible channel and then asked if she should repeat it, so Dilbert bluntly points out her obsessive, redundant behavior.
summary: A persistent colleague confirms delivery of a message sent three different ways, then offers to recite it aloud, earning a blunt insult.

file: 2007/2007-07-16_elbonian branch_in  my own country_see you inperson_mud_work long hours_wear dockers.gif
title: Elbonian Manager Sinks in Mud

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: What is he doing?

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Sometimes we use mud to muffle laughter.

situation: The Boss stands waist-deep in mud among a group of Elbonians and announces that he will manage their branch office remotely from his own country. He demands long hours and Dockers-style business casual from people who will never meet him. By the last panel he has sunk completely into the mud, with only his shoes visible, while the Elbonians explain they use mud to muffle laughter.
punchline: The Elbonians have quietly buried the condescending boss in mud to hide their laughter at his absurd demands, so his remote management of them ends literally underground.
summary: A manager dictating terms to a foreign workforce he will never meet gets quietly swallowed by the mud as the locals stifle their laughter.

title: Fired Employee Must Train Replacement

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carl, I have to fire you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're totally incompetent at everything you do.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Before you go, I'd like you to teach Dilbert how to do your job.

setting: Conference room table in the office
situation: The Boss fires an employee named Carl in front of Dilbert, telling him he is totally incompetent at everything he does. Then, in the final panel, the Boss asks the same fired employee to train Dilbert to take over his job.
punchline: The Boss's own logic contradicts itself: he declares Carl incompetent at everything, yet wants him to teach someone else how to do the job.
summary: A manager dismisses a worker as hopelessly inept and then, in the same breath, asks him to pass his skills on to a coworker.

title: Boss Threatens Dilbert Over Comic Strip

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You can't have a side job of drawing a comic strip about the workplace.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I should fire you for mocking the management of this company in newspapers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Because then I'd mock you less?

situation: The Boss stands over Dilbert's desk holding a printed comic strip and complains that Dilbert can't moonlight as a cartoonist drawing strips about the workplace. He says he should fire Dilbert for mocking the company's management in newspapers. Dilbert calmly responds by questioning whether firing him would actually reduce the mockery.
punchline: Dilbert points out that firing him would free him to mock management even more, so the boss's threat is self-defeating.
summary: A manager threatens to dismiss an employee for lampooning management in a newspaper comic, only to be reminded that dismissal would not silence the satire.

title: Pre-Meeting Scheduled After the Meeting

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you set up my pre-meeting for Wednesday?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Yes. It's on Thursday.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You scheduled my pre-meeting for the day after the meeting?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That was the only day that everyone could make it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There's no point in having a pre-meeting after the actual meeting.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Sure there is. You can talk about how much better the meeting would have been if you had been prepared.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Here comes the Pointy-Haired Boss. You'd better scurry away before he gives you more work.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: There's a fine line between evil and underpaid.

situation: Dilbert asks Alice, who handles scheduling, whether his pre-meeting is set for Wednesday, and learns she booked it for Thursday, the day after the real meeting. Alice insists it was the only day everyone was available, and mockingly suggests the pre-meeting can be used to discuss how much better the meeting would have gone with preparation. She then warns him to flee before the boss arrives with more work, privately reflecting on her own behavior.
punchline: Alice's thought that there's a fine line between evil and underpaid suggests her petty, obstructive behavior is the product of being underpaid rather than genuinely malicious.
summary: A pre-meeting booked after the meeting it was meant to prepare for leaves Dilbert baffled while his scheduler coolly rationalizes it and admits her sinister streak comes from low pay.

title: Dilbert Estimates Time Until Boss Forgets

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When you're done researching new technology, I want you to inventory our furniture.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When do you think you'll be done?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When will you forget you asked me, and assign the furniture project to someone else?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Two weeks.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll be done in 15 days.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert to inventory the office furniture once he finishes researching new technology. Dilbert asks the boss for a time estimate on the technology research, and the boss, caught off guard, replies with a number of weeks. Dilbert then pads his answer by a day, matching the boss's estimate plus one.
punchline: Dilbert asks the boss to estimate how long it will take until the boss forgets the request, then gives an answer just past that, so he can keep delaying the furniture task until it is reassigned or forgotten.
summary: Dilbert dodges an unwanted assignment by timing his deadline to outlast his boss's short memory.

title: Redesigned Headquarters Has Horse's Rump Entrance

transcript.text: I redesigned your headquarters building.

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: What's this part that looks like a horse's rump?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That's the entrance to the executive suite.

setting: Executive office with a large desk and armchair
situation: Dogbert, having bought a company's goodwill, tells the bald executive across the desk that he plans to make changes. He shows off his redesign of the headquarters building, and the executive, reading the plans, points to a part that resembles a horse's rump. Dogbert says it is the entrance to the executive suite.
punchline: Dogbert is insulting the executives by making the doorway to their suite look like a horse's rear end, implying that's how he views management.
summary: After buying out a firm's goodwill, Dogbert redraws its headquarters so the executive wing is reached through something shaped like the back end of a horse.

title: Alien Fired Before Mentioning Linux

transcript.speaker: Alien

transcript.speaker: Alien
transcript.text: I am a superior being, you moron! Listen to what I tell you and then do it!

transcript.text: I fired him before he started yammering about Linux.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Easy come, easy go.

situation: A small teal alien stands on the Boss's desk, complaining that no one on Earth will listen to his advanced technology, then insults the Boss and demands obedience. The Boss later tells Catbert, the evil HR director, that he fired the alien before it could start talking about Linux.
punchline: The Boss dismisses a superior alien being, whose advanced technology turns out to be just Linux evangelism, a dig at how tech zealots lecture people nobody wants to hear from.
summary: An arrogant extraterrestrial hawking world-changing technology gets sacked by a boss who spotted the Linux sales pitch coming.

title: Dogbert's Lawsuit Threat Over Cursors

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I represent the law firm of Dogbert, Dogbert, and more Dogbert.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your company's web page steals people's cursors and puts them in your own search field.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And my suit is too tight. When you put it all together, I might have to kill you.

situation: Dogbert, dressed in a suit and standing on a desk, introduces himself as a lawyer to a man seated in a leather chair. He accuses the man's company website of a technical grievance about stealing cursors, then adds an unrelated complaint about his own ill-fitting suit.
punchline: Dogbert piles a trivial web-design complaint and his uncomfortable suit onto his legal grievance, then escalates absurdly into a death threat, mocking frivolous litigation and lawyers' intimidation tactics.
summary: A tiny canine attorney lists petty grievances against a company and casually threatens murder because his clothes pinch.

title: Dilbert Flees, Boss Hears Teamwork

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Aayi-yi-yi-yi!

transcript.text: I hope that was the sound of teamwork.

situation: Dilbert peeks around a corner, hoping to reach his cubicle without running into anyone. In the next panel he sprints down the hall screaming, carrying his briefcase. The Boss, sitting in his office, hears the scream and hopes it was the sound of employees working together.
punchline: The Boss is so out of touch that he interprets an employee's panicked scream of fear as a sign of teamwork.
summary: A coworker bolts through the halls shrieking in terror while his oblivious manager optimistically mistakes the noise for collaboration.

situation: Dilbert, acting as the sales engineer, is asked by a customer whether the product really heals itself, as the sales rep claimed. When the customer tries to rephrase the question to get a straight answer, Dilbert panics and insists on only one way per question.
punchline: Dilbert dodges admitting the sales rep's claim is false by confirming only that it was said, and desperately blocks any rephrased question that might force him to tell the truth.

title: Budget Typo Bans Hardware and Software

He explains that only two things can't be bought for the lab this year. Those two things turn out to be hardware and software, the very things a test lab needs.
punchline: The supposedly minor budget typo effectively forbids purchasing the only things a test lab actually requires, showing management's casual incompetence.
summary: A manager downplays a budgeting slip-up that leaves a technical lab unable to buy any of its essential equipment.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert whether all department heads have approved their business plan. Dilbert explains that the other departments want the project to fail so they look better and win more budget. The Boss, missing the point, asks how to speed up the process, and Dilbert replies that he is already failing as fast as he can.
punchline: The Boss is so oblivious that he asks how to accelerate failure, and Dilbert sarcastically answers that he's already failing as fast as possible.
summary: A manager wonders how to hasten a project's doomed approval after learning rival departments are rooting against it for their own budgetary gain.

situation: The Boss explains to Dilbert that he hired Nancy specifically because she has had so many personal problems recently, reasoning that bad luck is unlikely to continue. Nancy stands nearby and then blurts out that she is in love with a medical school cadaver, undermining his theory.

summary: A manager bets that his new hire's streak of misfortune is nearly over, only for her to announce an absurd new personal crisis on the spot.

punchline: Alice's brutally creative threats make her the obvious source of comic-strip material, so Dilbert's question about where she gets her ideas is really a wry nod to the strip's own writing.

title: Software That Yells For You

transcript.text: There's the kind you can solve by yelling and the kind you can solve by buying some sort of software.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That's why I created "Some Sort of Software That Yells."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ooo!!!

situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, explains to the Boss that management problems fall into two categories: those solved by yelling and those solved by buying software. He then presents his own product, a boxed program called "Some Sort of Software That Yells," which combines both. The Boss is delighted and eager to buy it.
punchline: Dogbert exploits the Boss's two favorite management tools by selling him a software product that merges them, mocking how managers grab vague software purchases as a cure-all.
summary: A canine consultant packages a manager's two go-to problem-solving habits into a single boxed product and watches his gullible client swoon.

title: Wallpapering Fog at Work

situation: A senior executive dismisses a presenter because he didn't understand the pitch. The Boss then tells Dilbert the CEO rejected his idea without giving any reason. Dilbert, holding a coffee mug, complains to Wally that his work feels futile, and Wally says he doesn't care enough to feel that way.
punchline: Wally avoids the frustration of pointless, unappreciated work by simply never caring about it in the first place.
summary: After his idea is shot down for unexplained reasons, Dilbert laments the futility of his efforts while Wally explains that he protects himself by staying emotionally detached.

title: Carol Excluded From Key Employees Dinner

transcript.text: Carol, set up a dinner for all key employees.

transcript.speaker: The Boss

situation: The Boss tells his assistant Carol to organize a dinner for all key employees. When she asks who counts as key, he tactlessly tells her it's everyone except her. She angrily curses the dinner, and he offers to bring her mints from the restaurant if there are extras.
punchline: The Boss makes Carol arrange an event she is not important enough to attend, then offers her a restaurant mint as a pathetic consolation prize.
summary: A boss casually informs his assistant that she is the one person not worthy of attending the dinner she is being asked to plan.

title: Punching Her Sane

transcript.text: Dilbert totally flipped out when I showed him the cost estimates.

transcript.text: Really? Or is this one of those cases where someone acts normally and you inexplicably tell the world that they totally flipped out?

transcript.speaker: Carol

situation: Alice tells Carol that Dilbert totally flipped out when she showed him the cost estimates. Carol skeptically suggests Alice is exaggerating a normal reaction, which provokes Alice. Alice tells Carol not to flip out, and Carol privately thinks about punching her sane.
punchline: Carol's calm skepticism sets Alice off, and Carol's thought of punching her sane shows the irony that Alice is the one actually flipping out.
summary: A coworker questions whether a colleague's claim of someone else's meltdown is just exaggeration, and the accuser then comes close to a meltdown herself.

title: Boss Delegates His Own Blog

transcript.text: I'm starting my own blog!

transcript.text: Dear God, no!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Every day I will record my personal thoughts about our business.

situation: The Boss announces to Tina, the tech writer, that he is starting a blog to share his personal thoughts on the business. Tina reacts with horror, and he then assigns her to write the first post for him by noon. She ends up with her head in her hands.
punchline: The Boss wants a blog of his own personal thoughts but has someone else write it, and is eager to find out what he is thinking, which implies he has no thoughts of his own.
summary: A manager launches a blog of his supposedly personal thoughts and hands the writing to an employee, curious to learn what his own opinions are.

title: Brain Monitor Reveals Employee's Blinding Thoughts

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: All of your brain activity is in the zones that control love of coffee, digestive functions and... uh-oh.

transcript.text: I'm blind!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oh, that one.

situation: Catbert, the HR director, reads out the results of an employee brain monitor to Dilbert, who is wearing a monitoring device on his head. The readout shows no work thoughts, only coffee and digestion, until Catbert spots something else in the data and is suddenly struck blind. Dilbert calmly acknowledges it.
punchline: Whatever disturbing thought Dilbert's brain is processing is so horrifying that merely reading about it blinds the HR director, and Dilbert is unfazed because he's used to it.
summary: A cat in charge of personnel analyzes a worker's mental scan and loses his sight upon discovering the last item it reveals.

title: Your Success Diminishes Me

setting: Office desk or conference table against a plain blue background
situation: Dilbert sits quietly next to a coworker with a black bob haircut and a red sweater. She calmly announces that his success diminishes her, then goes back to sitting serenely while Dilbert awkwardly glances at her.
punchline: She openly and deadpan admits to envy, treating a coworker's achievements as a personal loss instead of hiding her jealousy.
summary: A calm colleague deadpans an honest confession of professional jealousy and leaves her bewildered neighbor to react.

title: Funding Rebels Through Stock Swap

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I reached an agreement with the rebels so they won't attack our factory in Elbonia.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's a stock swap. Every time they collect a ransom, the value of our company will increase.

transcript.speaker: Woman in audience
transcript.text: Doesn't that make us terrorists?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Very indirectly.

situation: Dilbert presents to colleagues, pointing at a picture of the company's factory in Elbonia, and explains he made a deal with local rebels not to attack it. The deal is a stock swap in which the company's value rises whenever the rebels collect ransoms. A coworker asks if this makes the company terrorists.
punchline: Dilbert admits the company is financially tied to terrorism, but hedges with 'very indirectly' to dodge responsibility.
summary: To protect a remote factory, an engineer strikes a deal that makes the company profit from the rebels' extortion, and shrugs off the ethical implications.

title: Dogbert the Quantifier's Eight Fans

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I have the ability to quantify the unquantifiable.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That is why they call me Dogbert the Quantifier.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Who calls you that?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Eight people.

situation: Dogbert, wearing a blue hat, boasts to Dilbert that he can quantify the unquantifiable and says that's why he is known as Dogbert the Quantifier. Dilbert asks who actually calls him that. Dogbert answers with a precise, tiny number.
punchline: Dogbert, who prides himself on quantifying things, undercuts his own grand reputation by revealing it amounts to a precise but tiny figure of just eight people.
summary: A self-promoting consultant brags about a flattering nickname, only for its pitifully small following to be revealed in exact numbers.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Bid low. We'll make it up with change orders and unexpected essential upgrades.

transcript.text: In other words, I've been randomly assigned to create lies for a proposal we can't win for a service we can't perform.

Dilbert protests that the company lacks the products and expertise and is too expensive, but the Boss tells him to lie, bid low, and recoup the money through change orders and surprise upgrades. Dilbert sums up the absurdity of the assignment.
punchline: The Boss's cheerful reply that Dilbert makes competing sound bad shows he sees deceptive lowball bidding as normal business, not as something wrong.
summary: A manager randomly hands off a doomed sales bid and instructs the engineer to fabricate capabilities and underbid, planning to claw the money back later with add-on charges.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Luckily I have developed a fool-proof DNA test for identifying losers.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Well, I'm afraid your DNA doesn't match mine, loser.

setting: Conference room during a consulting session
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, tells a meeting full of managers and Dilbert that their company has too many losers on the payroll. He announces he has a foolproof DNA test for identifying losers. He then sits across from an executive and delivers the result of the test.
punchline: Dogbert's 'test' simply checks whether someone's DNA matches his own, so anyone who is not Dogbert is declared a loser, a self-serving and meaningless consulting method.
summary: A consultant dog claims a scientific genetic test can spot useless employees, then fails a client simply for not sharing his DNA.

title: 300 Man-Days, One Afternoon, Everyone Fired

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired all of you because the project will take 300 man days to complete.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: There are 300 of you, so I want you to finish by five o'clock and clean out your desks. You're all fired.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If it takes more than one meeting to manage a project, I lose interest.

setting: Office meeting room, then the Boss's office
situation: The Boss addresses a group of 300 hired workers, explaining that the project needs 300 man-days. He then tells them to finish all of it in a single day and fire them at five o'clock. Afterward, he explains to Catbert, the HR director, that he loses interest in projects needing more than one meeting.
punchline: The Boss's absurd arithmetic treats 300 people as able to compress 300 man-days into one day, then he fires them all because his attention span can't handle managing a project beyond a single meeting.
summary: A manager hires a crowd of workers for a big job, orders them to finish it in one afternoon, and dismisses them all because he can't be bothered to manage anything longer.

title: Dieting Boss Watches Doughnut Eating

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Mm-guwung-mm-guh-muh

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's hard to pick the one best doughnut I've ever had, but this one is in my top five.

situation: The Boss, sitting at his desk looking unhappy, asks Wally how his diet is going. Wally stands holding a coffee mug and cheerfully eats a doughnut in front of him, mumbling through a full mouth, then comments on how it ranks among the best doughnuts he has ever had.
punchline: Wally answers a question about his diet by gleefully eating a doughnut in front of his boss, rubbing in the temptation while the Boss visibly suffers.
summary: A boss quizzing his employee about dieting is answered by the employee savoring a doughnut right in front of him.

title: Boss Defends Asbestos While Wearing Hazmat

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The employees are getting all whiney about the asbestos in the ceiling.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I told them it wasn't dangerous, but apparently I'm not credible in this hazmat suit.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't think it's fair that they judge me by my clothes.

situation: The Boss, dressed head to toe in a hazmat suit, complains to a coworker that employees are whining about asbestos in the ceiling. He says he assured them it was safe but that they don't believe him because of his protective suit. He then protests that it's unfair to be judged by his clothes.
punchline: The Boss wears full protective gear while insisting the asbestos is harmless, and is oblivious that his own outfit is exactly what undermines his credibility.
summary: A manager in a full protective suit can't understand why his staff doubt his claim that the toxic ceiling material is perfectly safe.

title: Everything Marked Urgent Means Nothing

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: So I spent the entire week working on the first one.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Next week I plan to continue not feeding the squirrels by the east entrance.

situation: At a meeting table, Wally tells the Boss that every e-mail he sent was flagged as highest priority. Wally explains he therefore devoted the whole week to only the first one. He then adds he'll keep ignoring an unrelated squirrel-feeding task next week.
punchline: When everything is marked top priority, nothing is prioritized, so Wally uses it as an excuse to do one task slowly and ignore the rest.
summary: A lazy employee turns his manager's habit of flagging every message as urgent into a justification for getting almost nothing done.

transcript.text: Alive?

setting: Outdoor path during a walk, then Dilbert's home
situation: Dilbert is walking with a woman and boasts that he designed a product so enjoyable that its users starve to death while using it. She says that makes him like a serial killer, and he replies that he keeps no souvenirs. Later, at home, Dilbert says she isn't his type, and Dogbert asks the dark question of whether he means alive.
punchline: Dilbert's offhand remarks about his date make him sound like a killer, and Dogbert's one-word reply implies his only type is dead women.
summary: A man's bragging about an irresistibly addictive invention gets him compared to a murderer, and his dog caps it with a morbid quip about his romantic tastes.

title: Financial Advisor Fleeces Gullible Client

punchline: The advisor candidly admits he is steering the client into bad investments, and the client is so oblivious that he approves anyway.
summary: An investment counselor cheerfully describes how he will skim a fee and park the rest in shady products, and his unquestioning customer signs on.

punchline: Dogbert's tech support does no real troubleshooting; it blames a random product and ignores the customer's knowledge, mocking how arbitrary and dismissive real help desks can be.

punchline: Dilbert's calm reassurance that despair will lift 'any minute now' is sarcastic, implying the new guy's hope for job satisfaction is hopelessly naive and the misery is permanent.
