She warns him that the drinks won't buy a favorable article, and he replies that he only expects her to publish his press release as if she wrote it. He then points out that she gets paid the same whether she does real work or just gets drunk.
punchline: Dogbert cynically suggests that journalists lazily republish press releases as their own reporting, so the drinks cost him nothing and her effort makes no difference to her pay.
summary: A pooch publicist plies a reporter with cocktails and reveals his real plan is to have her pass off his canned announcement as her own story.

title: Boss Replaces Meetings With Spreadsheets

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Cancel all of my meetings. I'm going to manage by making spreadsheets and sending e-mails.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: With any luck, I'll never again need to speak with unimportant subordinates such as yourself.

transcript.speaker: Employee (thought)
transcript.text: C23 is in a bad mood today.

situation: The Boss tells his assistant to cancel all his meetings because he plans to manage only through spreadsheets and e-mails. He then insults the assistant by calling subordinates unimportant and hoping never to speak with them again. In the last panel the assistant leaves, thinking in spreadsheet terms about the boss's mood.
punchline: The assistant has been so reduced to spreadsheet thinking that he refers to the boss by a cell reference, 'C23', as if the boss were just another data point, mirroring the boss's dehumanizing attitude.
summary: After announcing he'll rule by spreadsheet and never speak to underlings again, a manager gets mentally filed away as a mere cell in a grid.

title: Quantifying the Unquantifiable by Lying

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, I need you to create a PowerPoint presentation that will save our department from being eliminated.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You must quantify the unquantifiable. And that can only be done by a process that I call lying.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Lying is a process?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It can be, if you use enough slides.

situation: The Boss tells Asok to build a PowerPoint presentation that will keep their department from being eliminated. He explains that the value of the department can't be measured honestly, so Asok must quantify it by lying. When Asok questions whether lying is a process, the Boss says it counts if the deck has enough slides.
punchline: The Boss openly admits that justifying the department requires fabricating numbers, and treats the sheer volume of slides as what turns lying into a legitimate business process.
summary: Facing the axe, a manager orders a young engineer to fabricate a slide deck that makes his department's worth look measurable.

file: 2007/2007-06-29_career counselor_no marketable talent_keep positive_not going to change_unemployable.gif
title: Dogbert's Brutally Honest Career Counseling

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert, Career Counselor

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You have no marketable talent.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You're totally unemployable and that's not going to change.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The important thing is to keep a positive attitude.

situation: Dogbert, working as a career counselor, sits behind his desk facing a bald client. He bluntly tells the client they have no marketable talent and are permanently unemployable. He then wraps up with the standard advice to keep a positive attitude.
punchline: Dogbert delivers a devastating, hopeless assessment and then tacks on generic cheerful career advice, as if staying positive could offset being unemployable.
summary: A career counselor dog crushes his client's job prospects completely, then offers a hollow pep talk as the only remaining guidance.

title: Green Consultant Harvests Coworker Methane

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Green Consultant

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your coworkers have identified you as a source of methane.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If we capture this free source of energy we can power a small office building.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I give and I give.

situation: Dogbert, working as a green consultant, tells a balding coworker that his colleagues have identified him as a source of methane. He proposes capturing the gas as free energy to power a small office building. In the last panel the man walks the hallway with a hose attached to his pants, chatting with a coworker while holding a coffee mug.
punchline: The man is thrilled to be recognised as a contributor, framing his flatulence as selfless generosity to the company, while the hose in his pants makes the green-energy scheme literal.
summary: A consultant talks an employee into having his bodily gas harvested as an eco-friendly power source for the office.

title: Company Funds Terrorists, Rationalized Away

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I heard your company is funding terrorists.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Very indirectly.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And they aren't the bad kind of terrorists. They're more like rebels who sometimes do terrorist things.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: How did they brainwash you so fast?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Iran supplied them with PowerPoint.

setting: Dilbert's living room, beside the couch
situation: Ratbert, perched on the couch, tells Dilbert he has heard that Dilbert's company is funding terrorists. Dilbert downplays it, saying the funding is indirect and that the recipients are more like rebels than real terrorists. When Ratbert asks how he was brainwashed so quickly, Dilbert explains that the group was given PowerPoint.
punchline: Dilbert's easy acceptance of a morally dubious rationalization is blamed on the persuasive power of PowerPoint presentations, implying that corporate slideware can brainwash anyone.
summary: A coworker's pet confronts him about his employer bankrolling militants, and his smooth excuses turn out to be the product of a slide deck.

file: 2007/2007-02-23_pr campaign_stock price_grossly inflated_buy companies_make money_manage companies.gif
title: Inflated Stock Buys Doomed Companies

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Thanks to my P.R. campaign, your stock price is grossly over-inflated.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Now you can use your stock to buy companies that actually make money.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: After you manage those companies into the toilet, give me a jingle.

situation: Dogbert, standing on the Boss's desk, explains that his PR campaign has artificially inflated the company's stock price. He suggests the Boss use the overvalued stock to acquire profitable companies. Dogbert then predicts the Boss will run them into the ground and asks to be called when that happens.
punchline: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, knows the Boss's poor management will ruin any healthy company he acquires, and he's already lining up the next paid job for the cleanup.
summary: A canine consultant helps a clueless executive buy successful businesses with hype-fueled stock, fully expecting him to wreck them and need rescuing.

title: Learning to Enjoy Disappointing People

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I disappoint people, but I'm learning to enjoy it.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The key to happiness is to love who you are, not who others want you to be.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Doesn't that make you a sociopath?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Yeah. I love that about me.

setting: Conference room table during a meeting
situation: Wally, eating a sandwich at a meeting table, announces that he disappoints people but is learning to enjoy it. He then offers a self-help style line about loving who you are rather than who others want you to be. Dilbert points out that this makes him a sociopath, and Wally happily agrees.
punchline: Wally twists a feel-good self-acceptance platitude into a justification for not caring about others, and cheerfully embraces being called a sociopath.
summary: A cheerfully lazy coworker turns a motivational happiness slogan into an excuse for being antisocial and proudly owns the label.

title: Consultant Consults the Consultant

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You should hire me as your management consultant.

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: We're a management consulting firm. We don't need a management consultant to consult us.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Are you saying that management consulting is worthless?

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: No, I'm saying we already know everything about management consulting.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: How can you be so sure I can't help you when you don't know what my advice will be?

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: Okay, you're hired. What's your advice?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Beats me. I'll have to ask my management consultant.

setting: Conference room at a management consulting firm
situation: Dogbert pitches himself as a management consultant to the head of a management consulting firm, who says they don't need outside advice. Dogbert turns the objections around until the executive gives in and hires him. When asked for advice, Dogbert admits he has none and says he will consult his own management consultant.
punchline: Consultants get hired on circular logic and then have no actual advice, simply passing the question along to yet another consultant.
summary: A canine salesman talks a consulting company into hiring him, then reveals his only plan is to outsource the thinking to another consultant.

title: Human Ashtray Mistakes Ash for Hole

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Jeff, the human ashtray

transcript.speaker: Jeff
transcript.text: Watch out for that hole in the ground!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's not a hole. It's just a dark spot on the floor from some of your ash falling there.

transcript.speaker: Jeff
transcript.text: Oh.

transcript.speaker: Jeff
transcript.text: I can't tell the difference between my ash and a hole in the ground.

transcript.speaker: Unknown
transcript.text: Dilbert, did you meet your new boss?

situation: Jeff, a coworker whose head is a smoking ashtray, warns Dilbert about a hole in the ground. Dilbert explains it is just a dark spot of ash that fell from Jeff. Jeff admits he cannot tell his ash from a hole, and a new boss with devil-like hair then appears and is introduced to Dilbert.
punchline: The gloomy, ash-covered Jeff is apparently the more pleasant workplace presence, since Dilbert's new boss arrives looking like a devil.
summary: A walking ashtray co-worker confuses his own fallen ash for a pit, and the scene ends with the arrival of a horned new supervisor.

file: 2007/2007-02-04_assigning balme_eventual failure_wrong vendor_alienate the client_rendered mott_by noncompoops.gif
title: Assigning Blame Before the Project Starts

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'd like to kick off the project by assigning blame for its eventual failure.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Shouldn't we do that after the project is over?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I see no reason to wait.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well... okay.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our boss will make us use the wrong vendor.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wally won't do any work. Alice will alienate the client, and Ted is generally worthless.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In summary, my excellent work will be rendered moot by nincompoops.

transcript.speaker: Man in suit
transcript.text: Do you even work here?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No, I was just in the neighborhood.

situation: Dogbert, chairing a project kickoff meeting, proposes assigning blame for the project's inevitable failure right at the start. Dilbert initially objects but then goes along, blaming the boss, Wally, Alice and Ted while praising his own work. In the last panel, a stranger asks Dogbert whether he even works at the company.
punchline: Dogbert isn't an employee at all and just wandered into the meeting, which explains his absurd approach, while Dilbert happily seizes the chance to preemptively blame everyone else.
summary: A pre-emptive blame session kicks off a doomed project, with Dilbert cheerfully pinning the coming failure on his colleagues, until someone realizes the meeting's leader is a random dog.

title: Stretch Goals Beyond Reach

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I wrote out my goals for the coming year.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I set them higher than I can achieve because our boss said it's good to have stretch goals.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Well, more for us.

situation: Asok, holding a sheet of paper, tells Dilbert and Alice that he wrote his yearly goals. He explains he deliberately set them higher than he can achieve because the boss said stretch goals are good. Alice responds by noting that his shortfall will benefit everyone else.
punchline: Alice sarcastically points out that if Asok's goals are unachievable, his failure leaves more rewards and bonuses for his coworkers.
summary: A young employee proudly admits his yearly targets are impossible to hit, and a colleague cheerfully notes that his failure will be everyone else's gain.

title: Sweatshop Workers in the Basement

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You might hear some noise from the basement tonight.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I got a big order for running shoes, so I'm making the Elbonians work around the clock.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Here's some pepper spray in case any of them escape.

situation: Dilbert is reading in bed when Dogbert casually warns him about noise from the basement. Dogbert explains he has a big running shoe order and is forcing captive Elbonians to work around the clock. He then hands Dilbert pepper spray in case any of them escape.
punchline: Dogbert treats a forced-labor sweatshop in the basement as a routine business matter and offers only pepper spray as a precaution for the host.
summary: Dogbert calmly reveals he is running an illegal shoe-making operation staffed by captive workers beneath Dilbert's house.

file: 2007/2007-02-08_goals for th eyear_replace my soul_become immortal_coffee.gif
title: Wally's Goal: Coffee Immortality

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, what are your goals for the coming year?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My goal is to replace my soul with coffee and become immortal.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I mean something about work.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Oh, I thought you said my goals.

setting: Office meeting table during an annual goals review
situation: The Boss asks Wally about his goals for the coming year during a one-on-one meeting. Wally, with his coffee mug in front of him, answers with an absurd personal goal of replacing his soul with coffee to become immortal. The Boss clarifies he meant work goals, and Wally explains he assumed the question was about his own goals.
punchline: Wally's deadpan answer shows he has no work ambitions and treats the boss's goal-setting question as a request about his personal life, implying work goals are not really his goals.
summary: Asked about his objectives for the year, a coffee-addicted employee describes a bizarre personal quest and then implies company goals aren't really his own.

title: Plain Doughnuts Delivered Every Week

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Every week I order sugared doughnuts online and every week they deliver plain doughnuts.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Those aren't plain. Ratbert licks the sugar off of them when they arrive.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I work in a cubicle. I can get used to this too.

situation: Dilbert complains that the sugared doughnuts he orders online always arrive plain. An offscreen voice explains that Ratbert licks the sugar off them when they arrive. Dilbert thinks to himself that he can get used to this, just as he has gotten used to working in a cubicle.
punchline: Dilbert shrugs off the unsanitary, sugar-licked doughnuts as just another unpleasant thing he has learned to tolerate, like his cubicle job.
summary: A man learns why his online doughnut orders never come sugared and resigns himself to it the way he has to his drab office life.

file: 2007/2007-01-11_sales engineer_making sale_install_few extra features_massage table_sprawl_get naked.gif
title: Salesman Promises Extras, Client Expects Massage

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Sales engineer

transcript.speaker: Sales Engineer
transcript.text: I did the hard part of making the sale. All you have to do is install it.

transcript.speaker: Sales Engineer
transcript.text: I might have promised them a few extra features.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Did you bring your own massage table or should I just get naked and sprawl on a desk?

setting: Office hallway and a customer's office
situation: A sales engineer tells Dilbert that the sale is done and he only has to install the product, then admits he may have promised a few extra features. Dilbert arrives at the customer's office, where the customer asks whether he brought his own massage table or should just strip and sprawl on a desk.
punchline: The 'extra features' the salesman casually promised turn out to be absurd, apparently including a massage, leaving the engineer to deliver on an embarrassing overpromise.
summary: A salesman hands off a closed deal to the engineer after quietly promising the client unspecified bonuses, which the client interprets in a very awkward way.

title: Hands Stuck in Coffee Mugs

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You have a pattern of raising no objections to plans and later acting as if you opposed them from the start.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hope to thwart you by asking you to sign off on this plan in writing.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ooh, if only you had asked me before my hands got stuck in these coffee mugs.

setting: Office desk, a meeting between Dilbert and his boss
situation: Dilbert confronts his boss about a habit of staying silent about plans and then later claiming he always opposed them. Dilbert pulls out a document and asks the boss to sign off on the plan in writing. The boss, who has conveniently got both hands stuck in coffee mugs, says it's too bad Dilbert didn't ask earlier.
punchline: The boss dodges accountability yet again by inventing an absurd physical excuse that prevents him from signing anything.
summary: A worker tries to trap his evasive manager into signing his approval on paper, but the manager slips away with a ridiculous excuse.

title: Negotiating With Elbonian Extortionist Rebels

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Rebels have threatened to attack our Elbonian factory unless we give them a million dollars.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's outrageous! Tell them their competition offered to not attack us for half that price.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Negotiations begin

transcript.speaker: Elbonian Rebel
transcript.text: That wouldn't even cover our costs of not attacking!

setting: The Boss's office, then a muddy field in Elbonia
situation: Dilbert tells the Boss that rebels will attack the company's Elbonian factory unless they are paid a million dollars. Instead of refusing, the Boss treats it like a procurement deal and tells Dilbert to haggle by citing a competitor's cheaper offer. Dilbert meets the rebels in the Elbonian mud, where they complain that the lower price wouldn't cover their costs.
punchline: The Boss treats extortion as a routine vendor negotiation, and the rebels respond as if they were a service provider whose margins are being squeezed by a lowball bid.
summary: Faced with a protection racket, management haggles over the price like it's an ordinary supplier contract.

title: Share a Computer, Go to Hell

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I need this software to do my job.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The software budget is spent. Just share a computer with someone who has this software.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Why don't you take your tiny mittens and a thermometer to hell and wait for a sign that it's your turn.

setting: Office, the boss's desk and a coworker's cubicle
situation: An employee asks his boss for software he needs to do his job. The boss says the software budget is spent and tells him to share a computer with someone who already has it. The employee approaches the coworker with the software, who angrily tells him to go to hell and wait for a sign that it's his turn.
punchline: The boss's cheap fix of sharing a computer predictably produces a hostile coworker who has no intention of sharing, and her sarcastic insult about tiny mittens and a thermometer paints the employee as a pathetic supplicant.
summary: Denied software funding, a worker is told to borrow someone else's machine, only to be met with a scathing and sarcastic brush-off.

title: Wally's Priority Advice: Send Them Away

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wally, too many people are asking me for things. How can I set priorities?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Wait until everyone is yelling at you and then help whoever makes the scariest threat on any given day.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is that what you do?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No, I tell people to go ask you.

setting: Office break room by the coffee machine
situation: Dilbert asks Wally for advice on prioritizing the many requests he receives. Wally, pouring coffee, recommends helping whoever makes the scariest threat each day. When Dilbert asks if that's Wally's own method, Wally reveals he simply redirects people to Dilbert.
punchline: Wally's own strategy for avoiding work is to dump all the requests on Dilbert, which is exactly why Dilbert has too many people asking him for things.
summary: A coworker seeking help managing his overloaded workload learns that the real source of his burden is the very person advising him.

title: Dogbert's Absurd Value Claims Consulting

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Quantifier

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How can I quantify the benefits of my department?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Try making absurd claims of value while hoping that no one asks questions.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Does that work?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I hope so. Here's my invoice.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant called the Quantifier, is asked by the Boss how to quantify the benefits of his department. Dogbert advises making absurd claims of value and hoping nobody asks questions. When the Boss asks if that works, Dogbert admits he only hopes so and hands over his invoice.
punchline: Dogbert's advice is to bluff, and he is bluffing himself: he has no idea whether it works but still bills for the consultation.
summary: A consultant dog tells a manager to justify his department with baseless boasts, then confesses he is merely hoping it works while charging for the tip.

file: 2007/2007-07-19_employee orientation_no time_exercise_long hours_trans fat_positive note_payroll dedcution_service_save money_dirt_cubicle_burial site_health.gif

file: 2007/2007-01-05_amortize the depreciation_energency hoagie_quality of decions_too hungry_quality of decisons_hunger pangs_effect thinking.gif

transcript.text: Don't ask him for anything today.

situation: The Boss sits at his desk and muses that his diet has made him too hungry to listen well, hoping it won't hurt his decisions. Dilbert warns a coworker not to ask the Boss for anything, and she replies that she has brought an emergency hoagie to deal with the situation.

summary: A famished manager garbles financial buzzwords into gibberish, so his staff respond by arming themselves with a sandwich.

title: Toxic Sandwich Catches Lunch Thief

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I cleaned it up, but there was no place to put all of the hazardous waste.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I couldn't put it in the regular trash or the recycling bin.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It's not legal to pour it down the drain or flush it.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: So I put it between two pieces of bread and left it in the break room refrigerator.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Gaaa!!!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Not really. I just wanted to find out who's been eating my lunch.

She says she put it in a sandwich and left it in the break room fridge, and Wally panics after realising he ate it. Alice reveals she was only trying to catch whoever has been stealing her lunch.
punchline: Wally, the lunch thief, exposes himself by panicking, and Alice's reassurance that he won't die 'instantly' implies the sandwich may still be harmful.
summary: A coworker sets a trap for a lunch thief by hinting she hid toxic waste in a sandwich, and the culprit gives himself away.

title: Strategic Assets Dislike Accountability

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Strategic assets don't like accountability.

setting: Office, Catbert's desk in the HR department
situation: The Boss tells Catbert, the head of Human Resources, that HR is the company's most important strategic asset. He then reasons that this makes Catbert responsible for the loss of market share and suggests he fire himself. In the last panel the Boss is left with torn, clawed clothes and scratches, thinking about how strategic assets resist accountability.
punchline: The Boss blames Catbert for the company's decline and is mauled for it, learning that the HR 'asset' he praised will not accept blame.
summary: After flattering the HR director as a key asset, a manager pins the company's slump on him and pays for it with a shredded suit.

title: Literal All Hands Meeting Is Creepy

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Creepy.

punchline: The 'all hands' meeting was taken literally, attended by nothing but creepy floating hands, so Dilbert's one-word review of 'creepy' is the only fitting response.
summary: A company meeting made up of nothing but wiggling, disembodied hands leaves one employee unsettled.

file: 2007/2007-06-16_charge your time_appropriate code_unfunded_time codes_falsify report_no projects funded_meeting_business.gif

file: 2007/2007-01-04_diet_eating disorder_first 20 pounds_diet with buddy_lose weight_weight issues_health.gif

title: Catbert Cauterizes Reincarnated Soul

transcript.text: Because I can.

situation: Catbert, using a gadget he calls a soul-o-meter, tells an employee sitting across the desk that he has had several previous lives. He then zaps the man's head with a glowing ring, claiming it will keep his soul from reincarnating again. The man recoils in pain while Catbert explains he did it simply because he has the power to.
punchline: Catbert, the evil human resources director, inflicts a pointless and painful procedure on an employee with a flimsy pretext, admitting he does it purely because he can abuse his authority.
summary: A sadistic HR cat burns an employee's head with a gadget under a made-up spiritual excuse, then shrugs that he just felt like it.

file: 2007/2007-08-10_tall pants_old fashioned_hairpiece_glove on tail_money to treasury_first primary.gif
title: Dogbert Campaigns for President

transcript.text: I'm wearing my tall pants and my old-fashioned hairpiece because I'm running for president.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I put a glove on my tail so I can shake 50% more hands.

situation: Dogbert, wearing absurdly tall pants and a hairpiece, announces to Dilbert that he is running for president. He explains his campaign gimmicks, including a glove on his tail to shake more hands, and then states a policy of giving all the treasury money to Iowans. He admits he may reverse that position after the first primary.
punchline: Dogbert's campaign mimics real politicians by pandering shamelessly to early primary voters in Iowa and openly planning to flip-flop once he no longer needs their votes.
summary: A costumed Dogbert launches a presidential bid built on handshake tricks and a cash giveaway to one state that he already plans to abandon.

title: Boss Brushes Off Employees Without Awards

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Managing is a lot easier now that we've given up on winning one of those "best places to work" awards.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you have a minute?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Not for losers.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: There was a time when I wouldn't have known how to handle that situation.

situation: The Boss, holding a coffee mug, says management has become easier since the company stopped trying to win a 'best places to work' award. Dilbert pops his head in the door to ask for a minute, and the Boss curtly dismisses him as a loser. The Boss then congratulates himself on how well he now handles such situations.
punchline: Without the pressure of a 'best places to work' award, the Boss feels free to treat employees with open contempt and considers that a management improvement.
summary: Having abandoned any hope of a workplace award, a manager finds it much simpler to wave off his staff with insults.

title: Dilbert's List of Evasive Answers

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We're planning to outsource half of the department.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You can't tell anyone.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it true that half of the department will be outsourced?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Before you answer, I should tell you that I've made a list...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...of all the responses that mean the same as yes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: For example, if you say, "Ignore the rumors," that means yes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Also on the list are, "Why do you ask?" and, "Who told you that?"

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That list is stupid.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! That's number 8 on my list!!!

situation: Catbert, the human resources director, tells the Boss that half the department will be outsourced but that he can't tell anyone. When Dilbert asks the Boss if the rumor is true, he first announces a list of evasive answers that all secretly mean yes. The Boss, trying to deflect, says the list is stupid, which is itself one of the answers on the list.
punchline: The Boss's attempt to dodge the question by dismissing Dilbert's list ends up being item number 8 on that very list, confirming that outsourcing is happening.
summary: A manager sworn to secrecy about layoffs gets caught out by an employee who has pre-listed every dodge that gives the game away.

title: Pay Segment for the Unimportant

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I decided to segment the compensation of different classes of employees.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You'll be in the segment that gets paid the same no matter what you do.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I call your segment the "relatively unimportant" segment.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Catchy.

situation: Catbert, the HR director, tells Alice he has divided employee compensation into segments. He assigns her to the group whose pay never changes regardless of performance, then labels it the 'relatively unimportant' segment. Alice responds with a sarcastic one-word reply.
punchline: The company's compensation scheme openly brands some employees as unimportant and pays them a flat rate no matter their effort, and Alice sarcastically praises the label as 'catchy'.
summary: An HR cat sorts workers into pay tiers and cheerfully files one employee under a flat-pay group he names for its lack of importance.

file: 2007/2007-02-06_boss gives pen_20 years at job_could be old.gif
title: Anniversary Pen From The Ear

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Congratulations on 20 years of service. Here's a pen with the company's logo.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I have one just like it. At least I think this one is mine. I might have gotten them mixed up.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Which one looks like it spent the least time in my ear?

situation: The Boss presents a long-serving employee with a company-logo pen as a 20-year service award. He then admits he may have mixed it up with his own identical pen. He asks the employee to pick whichever one looks like it spent the least time in his ear.
punchline: The token gift for two decades of loyalty is so cheap and unthoughtful that it may be the boss's own used pen, one he keeps in his ear.
summary: A manager marks a worker's two-decade career with a logo pen, then confesses it might be his own ear-stored one and lets the worker pick the cleaner option.

title: Buzzword Report Disguised as Work

transcript.text: ...to maximize synergy capture and optimize our resource utilization.

situation: At a meeting table, a bald coworker gives his weekly status report using a stream of corporate jargon about mapping requirements and optimizing resources. The middle panel shows an office building exterior while his buzzwords continue. He then admits that if any of it sounded like real work, he will do more of it next week.
punchline: His status report is so full of meaningless buzzwords that he cheerfully admits it may not describe any actual work, and he has no real plans to do any.
summary: A worker pads his weekly update with empty jargon, then jokes that he will gladly do more of anything that sounded productive.

punchline: Even a nonsense noise the boss makes is already trademarked, and the lawyer insults it by saying it sounds like a monkey passing a kidney stone.
summary: A lawyer finds that every conceivable product name, from brilliant to dreadful, is already trademarked, leaving the boss to improvise a noise that earns a gross insult.

situation: Wally checks the vacation schedule to find out when Ted is away, then uses Ted's absence as an excuse to dodge the boss's requests for cost estimates and a revised timeline. He then slips into Ted's empty cubicle and takes the office supplies, offers to fetch pens for Dilbert, and finally quizzes Dilbert about his own upcoming vacation.
punchline: Wally is exploiting coworkers' vacations as an excuse to avoid work and to help himself to their desk supplies, and he is already planning to do the same to Dilbert.
summary: A lazy engineer turns a colleague's time off into an alibi for skipping assignments and a chance to raid the abandoned desk.

title: Dilbert Demands Lawn Mowing Reciprocity

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Dilbert, do you have some time to help me with this technical analysis?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sure, if you'll go to my house and mow my lawn so this doesn't become a lopsided relationship.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Why must you be so difficult to abuse?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Go spit in your socks.

situation: A coworker stands at the edge of Dilbert's cubicle and asks for help with a technical analysis. Dilbert agrees only if the coworker will mow his lawn in return, so the favor goes both ways. The coworker complains that Dilbert is hard to take advantage of, and Dilbert replies with a crude insult.
punchline: The coworker openly admits he expects to exploit Dilbert, and is annoyed that Dilbert insists on a fair exchange instead of being a pushover.
summary: A colleague hoping for free expertise is frustrated when Dilbert demands a favor in return and refuses to be taken advantage of.

title: Ignored Coworker Fears Being Unimportant

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Alice, may I ask you a question?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Alice?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Alice?

transcript.text: Am I totally unimportant?

situation: Asok repeatedly tries to get Alice's attention to ask a question, but she keeps typing at her computer and ignores him. He becomes upset and wonders aloud if he is totally unimportant. A small red cat on a desk then remarks that he is looking at a bunch of talking clothes.
punchline: The cat's remark implies Asok is so insignificant that he isn't even perceived as a person, only as a set of clothes that talks.
summary: A junior employee agonizes over being brushed off by a colleague, and a nearby cat makes his sense of insignificance even worse.

punchline: The Elbonian is evidently planning to microwave something alarming (such as a live or inappropriate item, possibly a brain or animal), which tests Dilbert's tolerance for other cultures' customs.
summary: A foreign coworker's odd microwave plans leave Dilbert struggling to stay tolerant.

In the last panel an apparently unclothed Dilbert, holding only a briefcase, tells Dogbert about the company's attitude toward workplace awards.
punchline: Management's absurd, dehumanizing policies (oil instead of clothes, twenty people per cubicle) make it obvious the company has abandoned any hope of ever being named a best place to work.
summary: Absurd new rules about wearing oil and packing staff into cubicles lead to a wry remark that the company has stopped chasing workplace awards.

title: Golfing Retreat Vision Not Recorded

situation: The Boss tells his staff about a management retreat that he considers productive. The managers golfed until they supposedly came up with a new company vision. Since nobody wrote the vision down, they plan to go on another retreat next month while Dilbert, Wally and Alice listen.
punchline: The managers treat a golf outing as serious strategic work, and because they recorded nothing they will happily repeat the pointless exercise, showing that the retreat produced no real result.
summary: After a golf-filled executive getaway yields a supposed breakthrough that nobody documented, the boss announces another outing to rediscover it.

punchline: Dilbert summons Alice, presumably to handle the confrontation for him, but ends up yelling at the whistler himself, dismissing his own fear of confrontation as a mere 'work-around'.

setting: Boss's office and a hallway at the office
situation: The Boss denies ever reviewing a design, so Alice presents a printed copy of his own e-mail proving he did. He dismisses it as inconclusive and asks whether she has any DNA evidence. Afterward Dilbert hears screaming and asks about it, and Alice, carrying a bag, says she had to collect some DNA.
punchline: Alice takes the Boss's absurd demand for DNA evidence literally and violently obtains it, with the screaming implying she hurt him in the process.
summary: Faced with a boss who refuses to accept written proof, a fed-up engineer goes to painful lengths to supply the forensic evidence he asked for.

title: Alien Genius Meets Corporate Quagmire

transcript.text: It's a quagmire.

setting: Office desk during an interview or meeting
situation: A small green alien with antennae sits across a desk from Dilbert and announces that it has come to share its advanced intelligence with the company. Dilbert replies that he is also highly intelligent, but the company does not welcome that sort of thing. The alien then walks away, summing up the workplace as a quagmire.
punchline: Even an alien with superior intelligence recognizes that this company punishes or ignores intelligence, making it an unwinnable swamp.
summary: A visiting extraterrestrial genius quickly learns from an employee that brilliance is unwelcome at this workplace and leaves unimpressed.

title: Boss's Made-Up Words Need Editing

situation: The Boss asks Tina, the technical writer, to edit a memo before he sends it out. She reads it and finds it full of invented jargon like 'incentiment' and 'leadershipping', and she is left with little after removing them. She bursts into laughter at the 'underboard' line, and the Boss walks away complaining that he is trying to 'moralify' his staff.
punchline: The Boss is oblivious that his motivational memo is nonsense, and he even invents another fake word ('moralify') while complaining that his employees don't appreciate his efforts.
summary: A manager's memo packed with invented buzzwords sends his editor into hysterics, yet he blames her for not being motivated.

summary: A manager touts action-oriented thinking but dodges the first question about actually changing anything, earning a sarcastic reply.

summary: A manager facing the axe offers to explain his department's value, but his boss dismisses the idea as being against decisive leadership.

punchline: Catbert twists the Boss's remark about a 'firm grip' into a crude innuendo, implying the drawing depicts something quite different from the Boss losing control.
summary: A relaxed employee doodles embarrassing sketches of his manager, and the manager's worry about his leadership gets a cheeky double-meaning reply.

file: 2007/2007-09-10_tall pants_traditional hair_unholy allaince_military industrial  complex_attack allies.gif
title: Presidential Candidate Seeks Best ROI

transcript.text: I'll need more than tall pants and traditional looking hair to get elected president.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Friend
transcript.text: I'm hoping to form an unholy alliance with the military industrial complex.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're willing to attack allies?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Friend
transcript.text: It's the highest R.O.I.

setting: Dilbert's workplace, in the office and at a desk
situation: A man with neat hair tells Dilbert that looking presidential won't be enough to win the presidency, and says he plans to ally himself with the military industrial complex. In the last panel, he sits across a desk from the Boss, who reads from a long scroll and asks whether he would really attack allies. He replies that doing so gives the highest return on investment.
punchline: The would-be president justifies attacking allies purely as a business calculation, treating war like an investment with the best R.O.I.
summary: A politician-in-waiting coolly admits he will cozy up to arms interests and even turn on friendly nations, because the numbers say it pays best.

title: Human Ashtray Jeff Gets Kicked

transcript.speaker: Jeff
transcript.text: Hi, I'm Jeff, the human ashtray.

transcript.speaker: Jeff
transcript.text: I like to lean in real close to people so they can enjoy my aroma!

transcript.speaker: Coworker (offscreen)
transcript.text: Ow! Ow! Ow!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sounds like someone is getting his ash kicked.

situation: A coworker named Jeff introduces himself as the human ashtray to a woman at her computer. He then leans in very close to her face so she can smell the stale smoke on him. She reacts with pain, and Dilbert and a coworker listen from behind a cubicle wall.
punchline: Dilbert puns that Jeff is 'getting his ash kicked' (a twist on 'ass kicked') because his smoky, invasive habit earns him a beating from the offended coworker.
summary: A cigarette-smelling colleague crowds a woman's personal space to share his odor, and the sounds of her retaliation prompt a pun from the neighbouring cubicle.

title: Planning Instead Of Doing Work

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I spent my entire day planning and scheduling future work, and no time doing work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Tomorrow I plan to spend the entire day explaining why I didn't have time to do work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It hurts less if I call it a plan.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What happens if you call it your purpose?

situation: Dilbert sits at his computer and thinks about how he spent the whole day planning and scheduling future work without doing any actual work. He then thinks tomorrow will be spent explaining why no work got done. At home he says it hurts less to call this a plan, and Dogbert asks what happens if he calls it his purpose.
punchline: Dogbert sarcastically suggests Dilbert's life purpose is to plan and explain rather than accomplish anything, which makes the futility hurt even more.
summary: A worker admits his days vanish into scheduling and excuse-making, and his dog points out that this endless cycle might be his true calling.

title: Dogbert's Free Publicity Advice

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert does public relations

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You can't get free publicity simply by doing something better.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You have to do something in a way that has never been done.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's a Sir Richard Branson sort of thing. You wouldn't understand.

setting: Office meeting room and conference table
situation: Dogbert, acting as a PR consultant, advises the Boss that doing something better won't earn free publicity; it has to be done in a way that's never been done. In the last panel the Boss, now sitting at a meeting table with Alice, Dilbert and Wally, parrots the advice as a 'Sir Richard Branson sort of thing' and dismisses them as unable to understand.
punchline: The Boss absorbs Dogbert's consulting advice and immediately passes it off as his own visionary insight, condescendingly telling his staff they wouldn't understand.
summary: After a consultant explains that attention comes from novelty rather than quality, the boss repeats it to his team as if it were his own superior wisdom.

title: Boring Keynote Speaker Makes CEO Look Good

transcript.text: Dogbert's Speakers Bureau

transcript.text: I booked you to do the keynote speech for a big company.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: How large is the audience?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: 1,500 victims.

situation: Dogbert, running a speakers bureau, tells a bald, bespectacled speaker that he has booked him for a corporate keynote. The reason given is that the speaker is so dull that the CEO's own comedy skit will look less painful by comparison. When the speaker asks about the audience size, Dogbert calls the 1,500 attendees 'victims'.
punchline: The speaker is hired purely as a dreadful warm-up act, and Dogbert cheerfully admits the audience of 1,500 will be suffering victims.
summary: A talent agent hires a tedious speaker as a foil so a company's cringeworthy executive skit seems tolerable, and calls the crowd victims.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Grrrr!!!

setting: Political campaign scene, then Dilbert's office cubicle
situation: A suited candidate asks Ratbert to be his vice presidential running mate, explaining that Ratbert's job is to be so unpopular that nobody would want to assassinate the candidate and put Ratbert in office. Ratbert eagerly agrees, and in the last panel he is seen biting Dilbert's shoe while Dilbert tells him to stop campaigning on it.
punchline: Ratbert is so annoying that he is the perfect unpopular running mate, and he proves it by gnawing on Dilbert's shoe and irritating him.
summary: A politician picks Ratbert as his deputy purely because the little rodent is so detestable that killing the boss would be unthinkable, and Ratbert immediately demonstrates his talent on Dilbert's footwear.

summary: An openly malicious HR chief takes offense when his open malice is praised as admirable candor.

title: Asbestos Ceiling To Be Disturbed Today

transcript.speaker: Bear-suited coworker

transcript.speaker: Bear-suited coworker
transcript.text: They say you don't need to worry about it unless it gets disturbed.

transcript.speaker: Bear-suited coworker
transcript.text: They plan to disturb it today.

situation: A coworker wearing a bear costume warns a man at his desk that facilities has found asbestos in the ceiling. He reassures him that it is only dangerous if disturbed, then reveals that facilities plans to disturb it that day. In the last panel, ceiling tiles and debris rain down on the seated man.
punchline: The reassurance that asbestos is harmless unless disturbed is undercut by the revelation that facilities intends to disturb it today, showing the company's careless disregard for employee safety.
summary: A warning about hazardous ceiling material turns ominous when it emerges that maintenance is about to stir it up, with debris falling on a bewildered worker.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Is that all you did?

setting: Customer's server room or lab, with a table and server racks
situation: Dilbert, working as a sales engineer, tells a customer he has integrated their product with her network. punchline: Dilbert openly admits the 'integration' is a sham, a fake product made of a shoebox of twigs, and treats using a fancier cable as the only thing he'd be wasting effort on.
summary: A sales engineer cheerfully admits his product integration is nothing more than a cable plugged into a box of garden debris.

file: 2007/2007-07-05_executive golf tournamnet_cigar smokers_foursome_golf cart_gas leak_baked lunch_beans_flint.gif

punchline: Carol politely presents what is clearly a plot to blow up her boss as ordinary event planning, and he is too oblivious to notice.
summary: An assistant calmly describes a golf outing arranged so that every detail could ignite her unsuspecting boss.

title: Boss Answers Before Hearing Question

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Just because my head is an ashtray, that doesn't mean I can't be a good manager.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ask me any question and I will show you my managerial talent.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The answer is six bags of potatoes!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: May I ask the question first?

situation: The Boss, whose head is a smoking ashtray, insists he can still be a good manager and invites Dilbert to ask him any question. Before Dilbert can say anything, the Boss blurts out a nonsensical answer about bags of potatoes. Dilbert politely asks if he can pose the question first.
punchline: The Boss's idea of managerial talent is giving confident answers before knowing the question, which shows he has none.
summary: A boss with an ashtray for a head boasts of his management skills, then proves otherwise by announcing an answer before any question is asked.

title: Technical Writer Insults Backfire

transcript.speaker: Technical Writer

situation: A technical writer stands before Catbert, the evil HR director, and wonders aloud why technical writers earn less than engineers. Catbert answers with a cutting insult about her intelligence. When she complains that the conversation has turned nasty, he piles on with an insult about her dress.
punchline: Asking Catbert a self-pitying question gets her told she is too dim to be an engineer, and then insulted again about her clothing for good measure.
summary: A complaining writer asks an innocent question about pay and gets savaged twice by a spiteful red cat.

file: 2007/2007-07-21_all motivation_temporary_lead engineer_buzz kil_right back at you.gif

situation: Dilbert proudly announces his promotion to lead engineer, only for a coworker to say he got the same promotion. Both are deflated and trade complaints about killing each other's buzz. In the last panel the Boss, with Catbert beside him, philosophizes that motivation never lasts.
punchline: The company hands out the same promotion to everyone so it feels meaningless, and the Boss cynically admits that employee motivation is fleeting anyway.
summary: Two engineers discover they received identical promotions, and the boss shrugs that any motivational boost is bound to fade.

title: Coworker Enjoys Pointing Out Mistakes

transcript.text: I wrote this last year.

transcript.speaker: Coworker

situation: A female coworker mocks Dilbert for putting last year's date on a report. She openly admits she likes pointing out his mistakes to feel better about herself. When Dilbert points out that he did write the report last year, she tells him the conversation will go faster if he just says he didn't.
punchline: The coworker cares only about being right and feeling superior, so she demands Dilbert deny the truth rather than let facts get in the way of her criticism.
summary: A smug colleague gloats over a supposed dating error, then insists the exchange would be quicker if the accused simply denied the facts.

summary: An HR villain introduces brain monitors to catch employees enjoying pleasant thoughts, and the constant alarms show the Boss that ignorance was better.

situation: The Boss tells a meeting that he has given Disgruntled Doug the critical job of building the company's pricing model. He then reveals that he gave Doug's cubicle to an intern and offers a cardboard box from a laser printer as a temporary workspace. punchline: By mistreating the employee responsible for the pricing model, the Boss has given him a motive to sabotage it by lowballing the costs, which would hurt the company.

punchline: The HR director, supposed to enforce workplace conduct, treats Alice's violence as a useful remedy and recruits her to punch more of the company's crazy employees.

summary: A manager enforces a baffling rule he can't explain, and the reveal is that an evil cat's random rule-making machine invented it.

Dilbert and a coworker peek over the cubicle wall and comment that it was too fast as the employee reels in his chair.
punchline: Catbert grants the request exactly as asked, knowing that someone kept away from sunlight for 25 years will be painfully harmed by an abrupt move to the window.
summary: A man who spent decades without natural light gets his wish for a window seat and is promptly blinded by the sun.

title: Meetings About Meetings About Deciding

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, set up a meeting with the Technology Review Board to decide how we'll decide on new technologies.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Do you also need a meeting to decide how you will put together a meeting to decide how to decide things?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe I should get some people together to help you answer that question.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Maybe.

situation: The Boss tells his assistant Carol to schedule a meeting with the Technology Review Board to decide how new technologies will be chosen. Carol sarcastically asks whether he also needs a meeting to plan that meeting. The Boss misses the sarcasm and suggests gathering people to help answer her question, which would mean yet another meeting.
punchline: The Boss takes Carol's sarcastic question about endless meetings literally and proposes another meeting to answer it, proving the recursion she mocked.
summary: A boss orders up a meeting about how to decide things, and when his assistant mocks the infinite regress, he responds by planning yet another meeting.

title: Boss Sells Soul for Doughnut

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: According to my soul-o-meter, you still have 1% of your soul.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I'll give you a doughnut for it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sold.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's funny how quickly a good day can become a great day.

situation: Catbert, holding a handheld soul-measuring device, tells the Boss he has only 1% of his soul left. Catbert offers a doughnut in exchange for it, and the Boss immediately agrees. The Boss then happily eats the doughnut at his desk, thinking about how his good day just got better.
punchline: The Boss has so little soul left, and so little principle, that he trades the last of it for a doughnut without hesitation and feels happier for it.
summary: A malicious cat from HR buys the final scrap of his manager's soul for a pastry, and the manager is delighted with the deal.

title: Punch Me So I Feel Something

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My job is an endless series of mind-numbingly unimportant tasks.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My central nervous system is starting to atrophy.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm kind of busy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Punch me in the head so I can feel something.

setting: The Boss's office, with Dilbert standing in front of his desk
situation: Dilbert stands before his seated boss and complains that his work consists of endless trivial tasks. He says the monotony is causing his nervous system to atrophy. The boss brushes him off as busy, so Dilbert bows his head and asks to be punched in it just to feel something.
punchline: Dilbert's job is so numbing that he would rather be physically hurt than feel nothing, and the boss ignores this cry for help because he is busy.
summary: A worker numbed by trivial assignments begs his indifferent manager for a blow to the head just to feel alive.

title: Ratbert Sings Without Needing Reason

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: (No dialogue. Ratbert sits quietly on the desk beside Dilbert, who types at his computer.)

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Tra-la-la la-la-la-la!!!

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Why do I need a reason?

situation: Dilbert works quietly at his computer while Ratbert sits on the desk beside him. Ratbert suddenly bursts into loud, cheerful singing, and Dilbert glances over at him. When Dilbert apparently questions it, Ratbert responds that he doesn't need a reason to sing.
punchline: Ratbert cheerfully sings for no reason at all, which stands out as absurd in a workplace where everyone is expected to justify everything they do.
summary: A small pet rat interrupts his keyboard-tapping owner with exuberant singing and refuses to explain himself.

punchline: Dilbert takes the Boss's absurd order to kill the intern after three questions literally and immediately starts counting, since the intern's first innocent question is already one.
summary: A manager enlists an employee to stonewall the executive's son so the department's flawed methods stay hidden, and the employee starts tallying the newcomer's questions right away.

transcript.text: You can still live a normal life.

situation: Alice, a woman with big curly hair, visits a doctor in a white coat with a stethoscope. He diagnoses her with a 'bad case of chair buttocks' from sitting too long. He first reassures her that she can live normally, then undercuts it by saying that only holds if she doesn't mind being pointed at and laughed at.
punchline: The doctor's reassurance turns out to be a deadpan insult, since the condition is so embarrassing that people will mock her for it.
summary: A physician delivers an absurd medical verdict about a sedentary desk worker, then casually admits the social cost of the condition.

title: Selling Goodwill Off the Balance Sheet

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: A mysterious buyer offered a million dollars for the right to decrease our goodwill.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You might have a bit less job satisfaction next week.

setting: The Boss's office, then a grassy hillside outdoors
situation: The Boss tells Dogbert, who sits across his desk, that he sold off some of the company's excess goodwill to a mysterious buyer for a million dollars. In the last panel Dogbert and Dilbert sit on rocks overlooking a hillside, and Dogbert reveals that he is the buyer and that employees' job satisfaction is about to suffer.
punchline: The Boss treats goodwill as an accounting asset to be sold, but Dogbert buys the right to reduce it, which means he will literally make employees' goodwill and job satisfaction worse.
summary: A manager cheerfully cashes in on surplus accounting goodwill, not realizing the buyer plans to spoil the actual goodwill of his workforce.

situation: The Boss hands Carol a wad of fake 'morale dollars' as a reward for almost perfect attendance. He explains they are not real money and can only be redeemed for things she doesn't want or need. He then adds that he entered her in a raffle she didn't win, and Carol responds by loudly blowing her nose.
punchline: The company's 'rewards' are worthless and insulting, and the boss's sheer lack of appreciation leaves Carol so exasperated that all she can do is honk her nose into a tissue.
summary: A manager rewards an employee's attendance with useless play money and a rigged-feeling raffle loss, and she can only respond with a loud honk.

summary: Faced with remote workers who slack off unobserved, the Boss takes Catbert's malicious advice to bluff about spying and fire people at random, and he loves every wicked bit of it.

summary: A presenter jokes that audience questions only pile on more work, and the very next question proves him right by proposing he handle everything alone.

summary: At a meeting full of attendees with no expertise or power, the only honest contribution is a promise to misunderstand, and the group settles for building on it.

summary: A manager gives his engineer a new role of dressing up salespeople's falsehoods and cheerfully recommends staying away from anything factual.

punchline: The coworker projects her own agitation onto Dilbert, accusing him of losing his cool when she is the one visibly flustered by a simple question.

situation: The Boss asks a coworker at the meeting table whether he is wearing noise cancellation headphones. The coworker, who is wearing them, can't hear and keeps saying "What?" while The Boss repeats the question louder each time, eventually shouting. Alice remarks that this won't end well.
punchline: The Boss keeps escalating his shouting to ask a question whose answer is obvious from the fact that the coworker can't hear him, so he's wasting effort on an unanswerable question.
summary: A manager yells ever louder at a colleague who cannot hear him because of the very headphones he is asking about.

title: No-Email Fridays Sound Ridiculous

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In order to boost productivity, the company has decided that employees can not use e-mail on Fridays.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What if my highest priorities require e-mail? Should I waste my day doing worthless stuff?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Geez, somehow you made a great idea seem ridiculous.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Yeah, that's all me.

situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces a policy banning e-mail on Fridays to boost productivity. Alice objects that her top priorities require e-mail and asks whether she should spend the day on worthless tasks. The Boss complains that she made his great idea seem ridiculous, and she sarcastically takes credit.
punchline: The policy is obviously absurd on its own, but the Boss blames Alice for making it look ridiculous, and she sarcastically accepts the blame.
summary: A manager's productivity-boosting email ban is challenged by a sensible objection, and he blames the objector for the idea's silliness.

title: Boss Wants Mark Twain Blog Post

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This blog post you wrote for me isn't witty enough.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Try it again, but make me sound like Mark Twain.

transcript.speaker: Writer
transcript.text: "I reckon you'd be hankerin' for some quality. 'Taint happenin' but it orter."

setting: Office, in the Boss's office and at the writer's desk
situation: The Boss complains to a young woman with a black bob haircut that the blog post she ghostwrote for him isn't witty enough. He then asks her to rewrite it so he sounds like Mark Twain. Annoyed, she goes back to her computer and types a sarcastic reply in a folksy dialect, which effectively insults his demand for quality.
punchline: The writer disguises her sarcastic jab at the Boss's unrealistic expectations as Mark Twain-style folksy prose, saying quality isn't going to happen even though it ought to.
summary: A frustrated ghostwriter answers her boss's request for a literary-style rewrite by slipping a backhanded insult into a mock frontier dialect.

title: Boss Can't Resist Reading Email

transcript.text: I called this meeting to discuss the changes to the pension plan.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: We already saw the company-wide e-mail about the changes.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: And we're all engineers, so we understand the details better than you do.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'll bet you intend to waste our time by reading the e-mail to us.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You can't stop yourself. It's some sort of compulsion.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: If you read that e-mail, it's proof that something is wrong with your brain.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can't... resist... reading... e-mail.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Gaaa!!!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Best meeting ever.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Best meeting ever.

situation: The Boss calls a meeting to discuss pension plan changes, but Alice points out that everyone has already read the company-wide email. She predicts he will waste their time by reading it aloud and declares that doing so would prove something is wrong with his brain. The Boss, unable to resist, reads the email anyway while Alice and Dilbert enjoy watching him fail.
punchline: Alice uses reverse psychology to taunt the Boss into reading the email aloud, and his compulsion makes him fall for it, giving the team a gleeful victory.
summary: A taunting employee dares her boss not to read an email aloud, and his helpless urge to do it makes the meeting a triumph for everyone else.

title: Employment Turns Your Backside Boxy

transcript.text: This is the posterior of a healthy, unemployed woman.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Prolonged exposure to employment will create more of a box shape.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: I'd offer you a lollipop, but it would only make things worse.

situation: A doctor points to an X-ray-style chart of a rounded posterior and explains it belongs to a healthy, unemployed woman. He then shows a boxy one, saying that long-term employment squares off the shape. Alice, seen from behind in the first two panels and grimacing in the last, is told he'd give her a lollipop but it would only worsen her condition.
punchline: Sitting at a desk all day flattens and squares your rear end, and the doctor delivers the insult with a deadpan refusal of a lollipop.
summary: A doctor uses medical charts to tell a frazzled office worker that her job is literally reshaping her backside.

title: Boss's Trapdoor Lever Fails Him

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Snap

situation: The Boss scolds an employee for writing a blog that embarrasses the company, then pulls a lever on his desk to punish him. The lever snaps off in his hand, so the planned punishment fails and he has to ask the employee to call the facilities department and return the next day.
punchline: The Boss's dramatic, villain-style punishment is ruined because his trapdoor lever is broken, leaving him dependent on the very employee he tried to punish.
summary: A manager's theatrical attempt to dispose of a blogging subordinate collapses when the mechanism he built for it breaks.

title: Ratbert Feasts on Dilbert's Cables

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Have fun working while I'm home chewing on your computer cables.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I'll probably start with a USB cable appetizer, then do the Ethernet cable with blue cheese dressing.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Then I'm going to wrap my colon around some coax.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I envy you, and it's disturbing.

setting: Dilbert's bedroom, on top of a dresser as he gets dressed for work
situation: As Dilbert gets ready for work and puts on his tie, Ratbert announces that he will stay home and gnaw on Dilbert's computer cables. He describes a multi-course meal of USB and Ethernet cables, finishing with a gross coax cable joke. Dilbert admits he envies Ratbert's day, and that he finds the envy disturbing.
punchline: Dilbert's job is so miserable that he envies a rat's plan to eat computer cables all day, and he's disturbed by his own envy.
summary: A pet rodent happily plans a gourmet meal of computer cabling while his owner heads off to work and wistfully wishes he could trade places.

transcript.text: What would you like to do with your degree in... flower arranging?

transcript.text: I'd like to be a billionaire.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Are you willing to work hard?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That would sort of defeat the purpose.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a career counselor, asks Dilbert what he wants to do with his flower arranging degree. Dilbert says he wants to become a billionaire. When Dogbert asks whether he is willing to work hard, Dilbert says that would defeat the purpose.
punchline: Dilbert wants to be a billionaire but sees effort as the very thing wealth is supposed to let him avoid, showing absurdly lazy ambition.
summary: A career counselor discovers his client dreams of enormous wealth but considers labor an unacceptable part of the plan.

title: Boss Applies for Dilbert's Dream Job

setting: Office cubicle and the boss's office
situation: Dilbert sees an engineering opening in research and development on his computer and daydreams about escaping his badly managed, futile current job. In the last panel his boss, at his own desk, spots an opening for a manager in the same department and has the same idea.
punchline: Dilbert wants to flee the mismanagement his boss creates, but the boss is also eager to move into research and development, suggesting everyone sees that department as the way out of a bad job, and implying the mismanagement could follow Dilbert there.
summary: While Dilbert hopes a new R&D engineering post will free him from a dysfunctional workplace, his boss eyes the matching management vacancy in that same department.

punchline: Dilbert tells his peers the unvarnished truth about his failing project but reports everything as fine to his boss, showing how employees hide bad news from management.
summary: A candid colleague hears the grim truth about a doomed project, while the boss who asks the same question gets a breezy reassurance.

situation: Tina stands beside a coworker's cubicle and complains that his crunchy snacks are too loud. punchline: The snacker turns her complaint about etiquette into a challenge, implying she is less appealing to him than salty snacks, so he has no reason to stop.
summary: A woman scolds a noisy snacker in the next cubicle, and he coolly replies that she would have to outcompete his devotion to salt.

title: Dogbert's Password Recovery for Morons

transcript.text: Dogbert's Password Recovery Service for Morons

setting: Dogbert's desk at his password recovery service
situation: A bald, tie-wearing man comes to Dogbert's password recovery service for morons because he forgot his password. Dogbert asks his name, and the man says it is Ned, though he is not even sure. Dogbert guesses that his password is "Ned", and the man is so amazed he calls Dogbert a mystical seer.
punchline: Dogbert looks like a psychic genius only because his customer is so dim that his password is simply his own name, which Dogbert then exploits by recruiting him into a cult.
summary: A forgetful customer is awed by a dog who guesses his password on the first try, and the dog seizes the chance to recruit him.

title: Blame Another Vendor's Faulty Integration

transcript.text: Make it look like another vendor's fault.

setting: A meeting room, then Dilbert's cubicle
situation: A customer points out that the salesman's network product looks like a shoebox of twigs and leaves, so it clearly doesn't work. The salesman cheerfully claims his engineer will make it work through integration. He then goes to Dilbert, the engineer, and tells him to make any failure look like another vendor's fault.
punchline: The salesman knows the product is worthless and plans to cover for it by pinning the inevitable integration failures on someone else.
summary: A vendor sells a junk product to a skeptical buyer, then orders his engineer to shift the blame onto competitors when it fails.

punchline: Dogbert's PR stunt is a disastrous lie, and when challenged he deflects with a fat joke, arguing that the Boss shouldn't question a professional's methods.
summary: A boss hires a canine consultant for publicity, only to learn he has publicly declared the company's goods lethal and recalled them, then gets mocked for his weight when he complains.

A bald, bespectacled coworker suggests simply pretending to be good at something and calling that the strategy. He then sips his coffee and apologizes for jumping ahead, as if he had just shared the next step of the plan.
punchline: The coworker's cynical shortcut is how many companies actually 'align' strategy with capability, and his apology implies it was the planned next agenda item.
summary: A manager wants strategy and capabilities to match, and a colleague offers the cheat of declaring whatever you can already do to be the strategy.

In the last panel the artist storms off in a rage, with cursing symbols flying out the door, and Dogbert muses that nobody likes being quantified.
punchline: Dogbert assigns a laughably low dollar value to an artist's worth and is unsurprised that the insulted artist is furious, since reducing creative value to a number offends people.
summary: A self-appointed measurer of the immeasurable puts a tiny price tag on a designer's value and watches the angry fallout.

situation: An interviewer in a red jacket asks Dogbert, a presidential candidate, what he would do in his first hundred days in office. Dogbert answers that he would spend that time carving his name into all the furniture, then turn his attention to attacking Switzerland.

title: Investor Wants Customers Injured

setting: Conference room during a business meeting
situation: The Boss explains to colleagues that the company funded its expansion by selling its balance-sheet goodwill to a wealthy investor. The investor then reveals a list of customers he wants the company's products to injure. When he says the company's lawyer botched the contract, the boss notes that the lawyer is now on the investor's list.

title: Coworker's Head Stuck in Ear
