transcript.text: He was violating my personal space and his head got stuck in my ear.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: You need a huge yawn to open the ear canal so he can get out.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Yes, I do have lots of pictures of my porcelain frog collection. Why do you ask?

setting: Doctor's examination room and an office cubicle
situation: Dilbert sits on an exam table explaining to a doctor that a coworker invaded his personal space and now has his head stuck in Dilbert's ear. The doctor advises a huge yawn to open the ear canal. In the last panel, Tina, with the same coworker's head stuck in Dilbert's ear, calmly mentions her porcelain frog photos, apparently the coworker's reason for lingering too close.
punchline: The coworker got his head stuck in Dilbert's ear after inching too close to look at Tina's boring pictures of her porcelain frog collection, so the absurd medical emergency stems from an ordinary workplace small-talk intrusion.
summary: A man's head ends up lodged in a colleague's ear after he crowds in too close, and the cure involves yawning.

file: 2007/2007-02-18_arc welder_barrel of kerosene_growth on neck_health plan_laid eggs_pregnant termite_quick search_to diagnose_use google.gif
title: Google Is The Health Plan

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The new company health plan is Google.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: From now on, employees must use Google to diagnose their own illnesses.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: For example, this guy has a growth on his neck.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I do?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: A quick search on my BlackBerry tells me it's...

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: What is it?!!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Ooh. Wow.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: A pregnant termite crawled into your mouth and built a hive in your esophagus.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: GAAA!!!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Stop being a baby. The treatment for that is...

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Do you have an arc welder and a barrel of kerosene?

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, announces that the company health plan is now Google and that employees must diagnose their own illnesses online. He demonstrates on an employee with a growth on his neck, and his BlackBerry search yields a horrifying diagnosis involving a termite hive. The recommended treatment is absurdly dangerous.
punchline: Self-diagnosing with a search engine produces terrifying, absurd results, and the cheap 'health plan' recommends a lethal treatment, showing HR's indifference to employee wellbeing.
summary: An HR cat replaces medical coverage with internet searches and cheerfully offers a ghastly diagnosis and an even worse cure.

title: Senior Discount Insult in Rebel Negotiations

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Rebel negotiations

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your price to not attack our Elbonian factory is too high.

transcript.speaker: Rebel
transcript.text: We can give you the senior citizen discount.

transcript.speaker: Other Rebel
transcript.text: Snort

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's just mean.

transcript.speaker: Rebel
transcript.text: Sorry. I'll switch to more observational humor.

setting: A stone room in Elbonia with a round table and a puddle of water on the floor
situation: Dilbert negotiates with two tall-hatted Elbonian rebels who are demanding payment not to attack his company's Elbonian factory. When he says their price is too high, one rebel offers him the senior citizen discount, which makes the other snort. Dilbert objects that this is mean, and the rebel apologizes and says he will switch to observational humor.
punchline: The rebel's offer of a senior citizen discount is really a joke about Dilbert's age, and his apology simply swaps it for a different style of comedy rather than stopping the insults.
summary: A tense protection-money haggle with Elbonian rebels turns into a stand-up routine when one of them mocks the negotiator's age.

file: 2007/2007-08-17_too much work_solution_coffee swilling squirrel_work faster_time stands still_slow_too lsow_hyper.gif
title: Hyper Beaver Teaches Carol Speed

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, I give you far too much work. There's only one solution.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired a coffee swilling beaver to show you how to work faster.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: When I watch you, it's as if time stands still.

setting: Conference room, then Carol's desk in the office
situation: The Boss admits he gives Carol too much work, and his solution is to hire a caffeinated beaver to teach her to work faster instead of reducing her workload. In the last panel the jittery beaver sits at Carol's desk holding a coffee cup while Carol, working at her computer, remarks that watching the beaver makes time feel like it has stopped.
punchline: Carol sarcastically implies the beaver is painfully slow and irritating to watch, so the manager's supposed productivity fix only makes her work worse.
summary: Rather than cutting an overloaded employee's workload, her manager brings in a jittery caffeinated animal to coach her, and she responds with a dry insult.

title: Wally's Noisy Furniture Keynote Advice

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Wally's keynote speech

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The source of all unhappiness is other people.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The sooner you learn to think of other people as noisy furniture, the sooner you will be happy.

transcript.speaker: Audience Member
transcript.text: That's the stupidest advice I've ever heard!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Hey, it's a talking ottoman! Hee-hee!

setting: Auditorium stage during a keynote speech
situation: Wally gives a keynote speech claiming that other people are the source of all unhappiness and advising the audience to think of people as noisy furniture. An audience member shouts that this is the stupidest advice ever heard. Wally responds by treating the heckler as a talking ottoman.
punchline: Wally immediately demonstrates his own advice by dismissing a critic as a piece of talking furniture, amusing himself while proving his cynical philosophy.
summary: A speaker who tells his audience to treat others as chattering furniture applies the idea to the first person who objects.

title: Deadly Product Outperforms Eating

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This product will leapfrog the iPod and provide pleasure to all five of your senses.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The user can download pictures, smells, tastes, and celebrity tickling patterns.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The test group preferred it over eating. They're all dead.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It has the coolness factor.

setting: Conference room during a product pitch
situation: Dilbert presents a new gadget to the Boss and a colleague, with a slide showing a man wired up to the device. He lists its sensory features, then admits that the test group preferred it to eating and are now all dead. The Boss is unfazed and approves because of its coolness factor.
punchline: The product was so addictive that test users stopped eating and died, yet the Boss only cares that it is cool.
summary: A gadget pitch reveals that its testers starved to death, and management shrugs it off because the thing seems trendy.

title: Department Explains Things to Morons

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our CEO wants to eliminate our department because he doesn't know what we do.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need someone to tell me what we do so I can tell him.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We explain things to morons.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Should I be writing this down?

setting: Conference room during a department meeting
situation: The Boss tells his team that the CEO wants to cut their department because he doesn't understand what it does. He asks someone to explain their function so he can relay it upward. Dilbert bluntly says they explain things to morons, and the Boss asks if he should write that down.
punchline: Dilbert's description of the department's job is an insult that perfectly fits the clueless Boss, who is too dim to notice and earnestly wants to record it to pass up to the CEO.
summary: Facing the axe because nobody understands their role, a department gets a brutally honest job description that its oblivious manager takes at face value.

title: Ashtray-Headed Manager Researches Management

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: There's more to being a manager than just having an ashtray for a head.

transcript.speaker: Ashtray-Headed Manager
transcript.text: There is?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Yes, and I am doing a lot of research to find out what those other things are.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Later, at the library

transcript.speaker: Ashtray-Headed Manager
transcript.text: This is good stuff.

setting: Office hallway, then a library restroom or stall
situation: A coworker tells an ashtray-headed manager that management involves more than having an ashtray for a head. The manager says he is researching what those other things are. Later, at the library, he sits on a toilet reading a magazine called Cat Fancy and thinks it is good stuff.
punchline: His idea of research into management is reading a cat magazine on the toilet, showing he has no clue what managing actually requires.
summary: A clueless manager vows to study up on his job but spends his research time with a cat magazine in a bathroom stall.

file: 2007/2007-01-01_beef_cake_diet_drink kool aid_eat it too_just derts_meat and potatoes_pie hole_vendores_play on words_food metphors_health.gif
title: Food Metaphors Provoke Diet Insult

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our meat and potatoes is knowing how to sandwich in our product without causing the other vendors to beef.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'll get our just desserts when they drink the Kool-Aid. Then we can have our cake and eat it too.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Are you on a diet?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Shut your pie hole.

situation: The Boss explains his vendor strategy to Carol, his assistant, using an unbroken string of food idioms. Carol finally asks whether he is on a diet, since he cannot stop talking about food, and he snaps at her with yet another food idiom.
punchline: Carol points out his obsession with food phrases, and the Boss answers by telling her to shut her 'pie hole', proving her point with yet another food expression.
summary: A manager's strategy talk is so packed with food idioms that his assistant wonders if he is hungry, and he replies with one more.
keywords: have your cake and eat it too

title: Winner's Mentality Needs Dumb Optimism

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Asok, you need to have more of a winner's mentality.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: If I had that sort of thing, why would I work here?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Ideally, we want you to be dumb and optimistic at the same time.

situation: Catbert, acting as the evil human resources director, tells Asok he needs a more winner-like mentality. Asok points out that a real winner wouldn't be working at this company. Catbert replies that the company actually wants employees who are both dumb and optimistic.
punchline: Asok's logic that winners wouldn't work there is confirmed by Catbert, who admits the company prefers naive, hopeful employees who don't know any better.
summary: A corporate HR cat demands a winning attitude from an employee, then reveals the company's real wish is for cheerful foolishness.

file: 2007/2007-04-01_busy_make appointment_always busy_in between_no time_make no time_unpredictable_secretary_shouts.gif
title: Boss Is Never Not Busy

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you have a minute?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No. I'm busy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When would be a good time for me to come back?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Come back when I'm not busy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Aren't you always busy?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Heck, no.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sometimes I'm in between doing one thing and doing another thing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When will that happen?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's unpredictable.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ask Carol to call you when I'm not busy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Carol, would you...

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I'm busy!

setting: Office, the Boss's desk and Carol's desk
situation: Dilbert tries to get a minute of the Boss's time and is told to come back when the Boss isn't busy. The Boss admits he is only free in unpredictable gaps between tasks, then tells Dilbert to have his assistant Carol call him when he's free. When Dilbert asks Carol, she also shouts that she is busy.
punchline: Busyness is so contagious that even the assistant meant to schedule the Boss's free moments is too busy to help, so Dilbert can never get any time with him.
summary: An employee is stonewalled by a manager who is perpetually occupied and an assistant who is equally unavailable.

title: Boss's Useless Research Progress Report

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I narrowed down the options to an alternative that costs too much and another that won't work.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I didn't do any research. It's more of an experience sort of thing.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Next week I plan to think about the option of using technology that isn't yet available.

situation: The Boss reports to a meeting about his progress on choosing a solution. He says he has only narrowed the options to one that costs too much and one that won't work, did no research, and plans to consider technology that doesn't exist yet. Dilbert sits silently beside him while an executive at the head of the table ends up with his head in his hand.
punchline: The Boss presents a complete lack of useful work as a decision process, with his plan for next week being to consider technology that doesn't exist, which drives his superior to despair.
summary: A manager proudly updates a meeting on a selection process that has produced nothing but two bad choices and a plan to consider imaginary technology.

title: Boss Contradicts His Own Instructions

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You said to tell you if marketing wasn't cooperating.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You can't come running to me with every little problem. Go fix it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then why did you tell me to tell you?!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's just something I say.

situation: Dilbert reports that marketing isn't cooperating, just as his boss previously instructed him to do. The boss scolds him for bringing him every little problem and tells him to fix it himself. When Dilbert points out the contradiction, the boss shrugs it off as a meaningless habitual phrase.
punchline: The boss's instruction to report problems was never sincere; it's just an empty thing he says, so employees are punished for following his directions.
summary: A manager reprimands his employee for doing exactly what he'd asked, then admits the original request was only a throwaway line.

title: Telekinesis Versus Ceiling Asbestos

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: They found asbestos in our ceiling. We're all in danger.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I must use my telekinesis to remove the asbestos.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gaaa!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The threat has been neutralized. You must never ask me how it was done.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm not even curious.

situation: A coworker in a face mask holding a mug tells Dilbert that asbestos was found in the ceiling. Dilbert imagines using telekinesis to remove it, clutching his head in strain, then announces the threat is gone and warns the coworker never to ask how. The coworker flatly says he isn't curious.
punchline: Dilbert's dramatic claim of secret superpowers is met with total indifference, since the coworker obviously doesn't believe him and doesn't care.
summary: A man who claims to have secretly dispatched a workplace hazard with mind powers gets a deadpan brush-off from his unimpressed coworker.

file: 2007/2007-06-27_personal problems_doctors_opeation_serial problems_steady diet_licorice_diet soda_spleen_c4 explosive_support group_alqueda.gif
title: Nancy's Spleen Becomes Explosive Support Group

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Nancy, the employee with serial personal problems

transcript.speaker: Nancy
transcript.text: The doctors say I need an operation.

transcript.speaker: Nancy
transcript.text: They think my steady diet of licorice and diet soda turned my spleen into a C-4 explosive.

transcript.speaker: Nancy
transcript.text: So I joined a support group. Have you heard of Al Qaeda?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gotta go...

situation: Nancy, introduced as the employee with serial personal problems, tells Dilbert she needs an operation because her diet of licorice and diet soda supposedly turned her spleen into plastic explosive. She then says she joined a support group and asks if he has heard of Al Qaeda. Dilbert hurriedly excuses himself and leaves.
punchline: Nancy has joined a terrorist organization as her 'support group' for being a walking explosive, so Dilbert flees.
summary: A coworker with endless troubles reveals her bizarre medical condition and her alarming choice of support group, sending a colleague running.

file: 2007/2007-07-30_automated sytem_arbitrary deadline_work smarter_not harder_sense of urgency_get work done.gif
title: Work Smarter, Boss Should Change Too

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't develop an automated testing system by the arbitrary deadline you set.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Try working smarter, not harder, with a sense of urgency, and a bias for action.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or maybe you could do something differently.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm not the one who can't get his work done.

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss at a meeting table that he can't build an automated testing system by the arbitrary deadline the Boss set. The Boss replies with a string of management buzzwords about working smarter. When Dilbert suggests the Boss could change his own approach, the Boss deflects by pointing out that Dilbert is the one failing to finish his work.
punchline: The Boss dodges all accountability for his unrealistic deadline by recasting the problem as Dilbert's personal failure, ignoring that the deadline itself is the cause.
summary: A manager answers an employee's objection to an impossible deadline with empty slogans, then refuses to consider that his own demands might be the problem.

title: Everyone Points at Someone Else

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Who needs a little management help on their project?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You could almost feel the teamwork in the air.

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: The Boss asks the meeting attendees who needs management help on their project. Every person at the table immediately points at a colleague instead of volunteering. Catbert, watching from the side with a coffee mug, sarcastically remarks on the teamwork.
punchline: Nobody will admit to needing help, so everyone blames someone else, and Catbert sarcastically calls this 'teamwork.'
summary: When management offers assistance, the whole room reflexively directs the spotlight onto their neighbours.

file: 2007/2007-02-12_bearded guy_too close_dilbert_bugged out_touching brain with nose.gif
title: Bearded Coworker Invades Dilbert's Space

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Then I said...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: (thought) He is totally violating my personal space with his non-standard facial hair.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Ha! Ha! Ha! Ha!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: (thought) Gaaa!!! His warm, moist breath is all over me!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Please stop touching my brain with your nose.

situation: During a meeting, a bearded coworker leans in extremely close to Dilbert while telling a story and laughing. Dilbert silently suffers through the invasion of his personal space, thinking about the beard and the warm breath. Finally he speaks up with an oddly worded request for the man to back off.
punchline: Dilbert's request to stop 'touching my brain with your nose' is a deadpan, absurd way of saying the coworker is leaning so close that it feels like he is poking his head.
summary: A close-talking bearded colleague crowds Dilbert at a meeting until Dilbert politely asks him to stop poking his brain with his nose.

title: Get Well Card Too Late

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Have you signed Ted's get well card yet?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Don't leave that here. Ted passed away two weeks ago. How long have you had the card on your desk?

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Have you signed Ted's get well card yet?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Put it on the pile.

situation: A coworker carrying a coffee mug and a card asks Alice whether she has signed Ted's get well card. Alice points out that Ted died two weeks ago and asks how long the card has been sitting on her desk. The coworker then asks Dilbert the same question, and Dilbert tells him to put it on the pile.
punchline: Office paperwork is ignored so long that nobody noticed the get well card became pointless, and Dilbert's pile of neglected items shows the problem is routine.
summary: A circulating card for a sick colleague goes unsigned for so long that the colleague dies before anyone gets to it.

file: 2007/2007-01-24_alien_bring technology_handle oa agavel_new guy_order in the court_simpletons_snout_working out_health.gif

summary: A condescending alien newcomer gets mocked for his gavel-shaped snout, and the noise from his work soon sounds like a courtroom.

title: Boss's Diet Warning Gets Laughs

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Ha ha ha ha ha ha ha ha

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I thought of something funny totally on my own.

situation: The Boss tells his meeting attendees that his diet may leave him less mentally sharp than usual. A coworker bursts into loud, uncontrollable laughter. He then explains that the laughter came from a funny thought of his own, not from the Boss's remark.
punchline: The laughter seems to mock the idea that the Boss ever had sharp focus, but the coworker claims it was unrelated, which makes the insult even more pointed.
summary: A manager apologizes in advance for dieting-related dullness, and an attendee's explosive laughter is passed off as a private joke.

file: 2007/2007-08-24_future product features_3 priorities_essential_critical_must have_pretend to add value.gif
title: Three Identical Priority Groups Prioritized

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: As you requested, I sorted the future product features into three priorities.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let me know which group I should stop working on.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is the part where you pretend to add value.

setting: Office meeting with the boss at his desk
situation: Dilbert reports to his boss that he sorted future product features into three priorities, pointing to a board labeled essential, critical, and must-have. He asks the boss to choose which group to stop working on. He then tells the boss this is the point where he pretends to add value.
punchline: All three priority labels mean the same thing, so the boss cannot meaningfully pick one to drop, and Dilbert sarcastically points out that the boss's input is just for show.
summary: An engineer hands his manager a priority list whose categories all mean the same thing and invites him to cut one, knowing the manager has nothing useful to contribute.

title: Everyone Has the Highest Salary

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, you have the highest salary in the department. But don't tell anyone what it is.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, you have the highest salary in the department. But don't tell anyone what it is.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't believe I never thought of that before.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Yeah, especially since you're the highest paid manager.

situation: The Boss privately tells Alice that she has the highest salary in the department and asks her to keep it secret. He then tells Dilbert exactly the same thing. Afterward he marvels at how clever this trick is, while Catbert, the evil HR director, points out that the Boss himself is the highest paid manager.
punchline: The Boss gleefully gives every employee the same flattering lie, without recognizing that Catbert's remark about him being the highest paid manager shows how well-practiced he is at ruining others' morale while pocketing the best pay.
summary: A manager tells each worker in turn that they are the top earner, swearing them to secrecy, and congratulates himself on the cheap motivational ploy.

file: 2007/2007-02-14_25 each_cheap hot dogs_cover charge_employee appreciation day_evil director_harder to appreciate_pocket money.gif
title: Paying for Your Own Appreciation

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Employee Appreciation Day is next Tuesday. The cover charge is $25 apiece.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: How do we know you won't buy cheap hot dogs and pocket the rest of our money?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Every day it gets harder to appreciate you.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Gulp. Gulp. Gulp.

setting: Conference room table in the office
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, tells the employees at a meeting that Employee Appreciation Day will cost them $25 each to attend. A bald coworker asks how they can be sure he won't buy cheap hot dogs and keep the leftover money. Catbert responds with a pointed insult while the coworker nervously gulps his coffee.

summary: The cat in charge of HR charges staff admission to their own appreciation party and answers suspicion about skimming with an insult.

title: Hosing Our Own Company First

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We have a squatter problem.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We must make our empty cubicles appear occupied or else we'll lose them to other departments.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When we're done hosing our own company, can we start hosing the competition?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our customers are next.

setting: Conference room during a management meeting
situation: The Boss tells the meeting that other departments are taking over his department's empty cubicles, so he wants the vacant spaces made to look occupied. Dilbert sarcastically asks whether, once they finish damaging their own company with this scheme, they can move on to damaging the competition. The Boss cheerfully replies that their customers are next.
punchline: The Boss treats Dilbert's sarcastic remark about harming the company as a to-do list, revealing that his turf-protecting deception will eventually extend to cheating customers too.
summary: A manager's plan to fake occupied cubicles in order to hold onto office space draws a sarcastic jab that he happily takes as a roadmap for deceiving customers.

title: Speaker Refuses To Meet Expectations

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's Speakers Bureau

transcript.text: What topic would you be speaking about?

transcript.speaker: Applicant
transcript.text: I would speak about the folly of trying to satisfy other people's unreasonable expectations.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Would you show up on time?

transcript.speaker: Applicant
transcript.text: No. I doubt I would even prepare a speech.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a speakers bureau agent, interviews a bald man in glasses and a tie who wants to be a paid speaker. The man says his topic would be the folly of satisfying other people's unreasonable expectations. Dogbert asks if he would show up on time, and he says no and that he probably wouldn't even prepare a speech.
punchline: The speaker takes his own talk topic so literally that he will not meet even the most basic expectations, turning his lecture into a practical demonstration of his philosophy.
summary: A would-be motivational speaker pitches a talk against meeting expectations, then proves his commitment by promising to be late and unprepared.

file: 2007/2007-06-26_serial personal problems_in love_medical school cadaver_bad decisons_acting cold_boyfriend acting cold.gif
title: Dating a Cadaver, Blaming Others

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Nancy, the employee with serial personal problems

transcript.speaker: Nancy
transcript.text: I'm in love with a medical school cadaver.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Do you ever think that maybe your personal problems are caused by your own bad decisions?

transcript.speaker: Nancy
transcript.text: How's it my fault that my boyfriend is acting cold?

situation: Nancy, introduced as the employee with serial personal problems, tells a coworker she is in love with a medical school cadaver. The coworker suggests her troubles might stem from her own bad decisions. Nancy responds by asking how it's her fault that her boyfriend, the cadaver, is acting cold.
punchline: Nancy is oblivious to her own poor judgment, complaining that her boyfriend is cold when he is literally a dead body.
summary: A woman prone to romantic disasters falls for a corpse and then protests that she is blameless when he turns chilly.

title: Ethicist Approves Hating Bad Emailers

transcript.speaker: Computer
transcript.text: "Yes, do that right away."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do what?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can I ignore e-mail from people who don't include my original message in their reply?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yes, and you can hate them, too.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: 90% of happiness is picking the right ethicist.

situation: Dilbert receives an email reply that gives an instruction with no context, so he has no idea what it refers to. He asks Dogbert, acting as his ethicist, whether he may ignore people who don't quote the original message, and Dogbert says yes and he may hate them too. Dilbert walks away cheerfully, delighted with the permission.
punchline: Dilbert has found that picking an ethicist who tells you what you want to hear, including that your grudges are justified, is the secret to happiness.
summary: After an unclear email reply leaves him confused, Dilbert gets his dog advisor to bless ignoring and resenting careless emailers.

title: Dogbert's Death-Threat Diet Advice

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert: Diet Guru

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Try stuffing fewer groceries down your maw.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I was hoping you'd give me motivation.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Stop eating or I'll kill you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Would I get a last meal?

situation: Dogbert, working as a diet guru, gives the Pointy-Haired Boss the blunt advice to eat less. The Boss says he wanted motivation instead, so Dogbert threatens to kill him if he doesn't stop eating. The Boss responds by asking whether he would get a last meal.
punchline: The Boss is so fixated on food that even a death threat prompts him to ask about his final meal, showing he has no intention of changing his eating habits.
summary: A canine dieting consultant offers a lethal incentive to a overweight executive, who can only think about dinner.

title: Automated Replacement Skips Incompetent Parts

transcript.speaker: Fired Employee
transcript.text: Although I've been fired for gross incompetence, I'm professional enough to train you before I leave.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Don't bother. I already coded a Java app to do everything you do.

transcript.speaker: Fired Employee
transcript.text: Everything?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Except for the incompetent parts.

situation: A coworker who has been fired for gross incompetence offers to train Dilbert, his replacement, before leaving. Dilbert says training is unnecessary because he has already written a Java application that does everything the man does. When asked if it does everything, Dilbert adds that it leaves out the incompetent parts.
punchline: Dilbert's program replicates only the useful work, which implies the fired man's incompetent output was all that distinguished him from a simple script, and that his job was easily automated.
summary: A dismissed employee kindly offers to hand over his duties, only to learn his successor has already automated his job minus the mistakes.

title: Managing By Spreadsheet, Hoping For Magic

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've decided to manage by spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll track things until all of our problems fix themselves.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Your optimism is cute.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Thanks. You're pretty fuzzy yourself.

setting: Office, in front of Catbert's desk
situation: The Boss, holding a coffee mug, announces to Catbert that he will manage by spreadsheet. He explains his plan is simply to track things until all the problems solve themselves. Catbert calls his optimism cute, and the oblivious Boss takes it as a compliment and returns it.
punchline: The Boss's management strategy is to passively record problems and hope they vanish, and he is too clueless to realize Catbert's 'cute' is a patronizing insult.
summary: A manager's plan to simply watch a spreadsheet until his troubles disappear earns a condescending remark from the HR cat, which he mistakes for flattery.

file: 2007/2007-06-20_green consultant_rm your suv_hybrid cars_stop using fuel_save earth_other people sacrifice.gif
title: Dogbert's Green Plan: Ram Hybrids

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Green Consultant

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Try ramming your SUV into hybrid cars.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That should stop them from using fuel altogether.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You can't save the Earth unless you're willing to make other people sacrifice.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm in.

setting: Dogbert's consulting office, across a desk
situation: Dogbert, working as a green consultant, advises the Boss to ram his SUV into hybrid cars so they stop using fuel. He explains that saving the Earth requires making other people sacrifice, and the Boss eagerly agrees to the plan.
punchline: Dogbert's 'environmentalism' is really a license to harm others, and the Boss happily signs on because the sacrifice isn't his own.
summary: A consultant pitches an absurdly destructive eco-strategy that conveniently lets his client keep his gas guzzler while punishing everyone else.

title: Ratbert's Grim Morning Forecast

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Today you will wear clothes you don't want to wear.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: You'll drive somewhere you don't want to be, and do things you don't want to do.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Have a nice day.

situation: Ratbert stands on Dilbert's bed in the morning while Dilbert gets dressed and ties his tie. Ratbert gives a deadpan preview of the day: unwanted clothes, an unwanted commute, and unwanted tasks. He finishes with a cheerful 'Have a nice day' as Dilbert stares back.
punchline: Ratbert's accurate but bleak description of a typical workday makes the closing 'Have a nice day' a sarcastic contradiction.
summary: A small pet delivers a gloomy rundown of the day's obligations before wishing his owner well.

title: Dogbert's Absurd Presidential Campaign Speech

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert for President

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Vote for me or the terrorists will use your skulls for salad bowls.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I promise to take money from the people who don't vote for me and give it to the people who do.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Pollution has vitamins!

transcript.speaker: Audience member
transcript.text: I like how he makes me feel.

setting: Political rally stage with a podium in front of a crowd
situation: Dogbert campaigns for president from a podium. He opens with a ridiculous scare tactic about terrorists, then promises to take money from non-supporters and give it to his voters, and finally makes a baseless claim that pollution has vitamins. A voter in the crowd cheerfully says he likes how Dogbert makes him feel.
punchline: Voters ignore fear-mongering, bribery and nonsense claims and support the candidate simply because he makes them feel good, satirizing how emotion beats substance in politics.
summary: A candidate dog wins over a crowd with scare tactics, bribes and blatant nonsense, and the audience loves the feeling more than the facts.

file: 2007/2007-01-26_meeting right now_lunch time_12 hours_misery_envy_dead don't eat lucnch.gif
title: Missing Lunch Means Envying the Dead

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can you come to a meeting right now?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, it's almost lunch time.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If I miss lunch, my day will be 12 hours of uninterrupted misery. I will envy the dead.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's stupid. The dead don't eat lunch either.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert to attend a meeting immediately, but Dilbert refuses because lunch is near. He dramatically claims that skipping lunch would lead to twelve hours of misery so bad he would envy the dead. The Boss responds with a literal-minded rebuttal that the dead don't eat lunch either.
punchline: The Boss misses the hyperbole entirely and 'refutes' Dilbert's exaggeration with absurd literal logic, implying the dead are no better off for missing lunch.
summary: A manager dismisses an employee's dramatic complaint about skipping lunch by pointing out, with bizarre literalism, that corpses go without meals too.

title: Worthless Employee of the Month Prizes

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The best choice for employee of the month is...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Congratulations to Alice for being our employee of the month!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You get to use my parking spot near the entrance for the rest of the month.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I take public transit to work.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You also get to take the rest of today off.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It's already five o'clock, and you said I need to finish my project by tomorrow morning.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And you get to have pizza with me.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm on a #!@*% low carb diet!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I nailed it.

setting: Office meeting area and The Boss's office
situation: The Boss announces Alice as employee of the month and lists the rewards, but each one is useless to her. She doesn't drive to work, the time off is already over and she has a deadline, and she is on a low carb diet. In the final panel The Boss, eating pizza alone, congratulates himself on the job he did.
punchline: The Boss thinks he nailed the recognition when every perk he offered is useless or insulting to Alice, showing how clueless and self-serving management rewards are.
summary: A manager hands out an award with perks that are all irrelevant to the winner, yet he is thoroughly pleased with himself.

title: Boss Checks Dashboard, Falsifies Data

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can monitor the company's key metrics from my executive dashboard.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh. I need to do a better job of falsifying my data.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Allow me to set the stage for your next assignment by reminding you that stockholders have never done anything for you.

setting: Office cubicle and the Boss's office
situation: In the first two panels, Dilbert thinks about how an executive dashboard could let a manager watch the company's key metrics, and then realizes that means he must falsify his own data more convincingly. In the final panel, the Boss tells Dilbert that stockholders have never done anything for him, as a lead-in to an unethical assignment.
punchline: Dilbert recognizes that dashboard monitoring will expose fudged numbers, while the Boss casually justifies cheating shareholders by saying they've never done anything for Dilbert.
summary: A worker realizes that management dashboards mean his doctored numbers must get better, while his boss primes him to deceive investors.

file: 2007/2007-11-26_agile programming_cpmplain_training_write code_no more planning_no more documentation_just start writing.gif
title: Agile Means Code and Complain

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're going to try something called agile programming.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That means no more planning and no more documentation. Just start writing code and complaining.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm glad it has a name.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That was your training.

situation: The Boss gathers Dilbert and Wally at the conference table to announce the company is adopting agile programming. He explains it as dropping all planning and documentation and simply starting to write code and complain. Wally remarks that he is glad the approach has a name, and the Boss says that remark was the entire training.
punchline: The Boss reduces agile methodology to a sloppy free-for-all and treats a one-sentence explanation as complete employee training, while Wally's quip reveals that this is how they already work.
summary: A manager rolls out a software methodology by describing it as skipping the paperwork and griping, then counts that explanation as the staff's training.

title: Bring Solutions, Not Problems

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't bring me problems, bring me solutions.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When I bring you solutions, you tell me they won't work and treat me like a moron.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What's the problem with that?

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert to stop bringing him problems and to bring solutions instead. Dilbert points out that whenever he does offer solutions, the Boss rejects them and insults his intelligence. The Boss then asks, with no apparent self-awareness, what is wrong with that.
punchline: The Boss cannot see that his own dismissive behavior is the problem, and he treats Dilbert's complaint as if it were not an issue at all.
summary: A manager demands solutions from his employee, then fails to notice that he shoots down every one and belittles the person who offers it.

file: 2007/2007-11-08_bar code scanner_lab tests_capital budget_varainace_three bids_form a team_purchase order_quitters.gif
title: Bar Code Scanner Procurement Bureaucracy

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need a $1,600 handheld bar code scanner to finish my lab tests.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay. Apply for a capital budget variance, prepare an RFP, get three bids, form a team to evaluate the bids, then prepare a purchase order.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Never mind. I'll just learn how to read bar codes by sight.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Quitter.

situation: Dilbert asks his boss for a $1,600 handheld bar code scanner so he can finish his lab tests. The boss responds with a long chain of bureaucratic steps required to buy it. Dilbert gives up and says he'll learn to read bar codes by sight, and the boss calls him a quitter.
punchline: The purchasing process is so burdensome that doing the impossible, reading bar codes by eye, seems easier, yet the boss still mocks Dilbert for giving up.
summary: A modest equipment request is buried under so many approval steps that the employee abandons it, only to be scolded for not persevering.

file: 2007/2007-12-01_not enough recources_project_look lame_fixed capacity_dedicated higher priorities_donated blood_hurricane victims.gif
title: Say No Without Looking Lame

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Never tell anyone we don't have enough resources to do a project. It makes us look lame.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Instead, say we have a fixed capacity that is already dedicated to higher priorities. That makes whoever asked us for help look lame.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Can I keep telling people I donated all of my blood to hurricane victims?

situation: The Boss coaches his team on how to decline project requests, first warning against admitting a lack of resources. He then offers a replacement line that implies the requester's work is low priority. Wally asks if he can keep using his own excuse about donating all his blood to hurricane victims.
punchline: Wally's blood-donation excuse is a flimsy, dishonest brush-off, and he sees it as just as acceptable as the boss's dishonest 'higher priorities' line, which exposes how manipulative that advice is.
summary: A manager teaches his staff a spin-heavy way to refuse work requests, and Wally cheerfully asks whether his own flimsy alibi qualifies.

title: Earn Engineering Degree Instead of Raise

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't understand anything you do, so I assume it's all useless.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe you could go to M.I.T. and get a degree in engineering so you would understand what I do.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Would that be easier than not giving you a raise?

setting: Boss's office, meeting across a desk
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that he assumes Dilbert's work is useless because he doesn't understand it. Dilbert suggests the Boss go to M.I.T. and earn an engineering degree to understand his work, then asks whether that would be easier than simply not giving Dilbert a raise.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically implies that the Boss would have to do enormous effort to justify denying a raise, when the Boss is in fact the one making the unreasonable decision to withhold it.
summary: An uncomprehending boss dismisses an engineer's work as worthless, and the engineer sarcastically points out how absurd the boss's reasoning is when it comes to denying him a raise.

file: 2007/2007-12-31_hate holidays_day before holoday_stop working_cheapens work_year round_mean spirited_bitter worker_hyprocrit.gif
title: Tourist Calls Out Year-Round Slacker

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I hate it when people stop working just because it's the day before a holiday.

transcript.speaker: Off-panel
transcript.text: Ha! Ha! Ha!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It cheapens the lack of work that I cultivate year-round.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I saw the funniest video clip!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Tourist!

setting: Office break area where coworkers stand around holding coffee mugs
situation: Wally complains that people stop working the day before a holiday, saying it cheapens the lack of work he cultivates all year. A coworker then walks up and cheerfully mentions a funny video clip he saw. Wally immediately accuses him of being a 'tourist', meaning someone who only slacks off occasionally.
punchline: Wally is such a dedicated year-round slacker that he looks down on coworkers who only goof off on holidays, treating avoiding work as a serious craft.
summary: A chronic loafer sneers at part-time slackers who only stop working when a holiday arrives, as if idleness were a discipline they haven't earned.

file: 2007/2007-12-19_disciuss company politics_career monefield_project_new strategic direction_upcoming reorganization_plan to criticize_something good happens.gif
title: Boss's Plan: Criticize Until Something Good

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm not allowed to discuss the company politics that form a career minefield around your project.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And I can't tell you the company's new strategic direction, or anything about our upcoming reorg.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My plan is to criticize you until something good happens.

situation: Dilbert stands silently in front of the Boss's desk while the Boss explains everything he is not permitted to share about office politics, company strategy and an upcoming reorganization. With no useful information to offer, the Boss announces that his management approach is simply to criticize Dilbert until a good result appears.
punchline: The Boss has no real guidance, so his entire management strategy is to berate his employee and hope success eventually results.
summary: A manager who claims to be barred from sharing any useful information reveals that his only plan is to keep faulting his subordinate until luck intervenes.

title: Boss Avoids Details, Seeks Award

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's time for some generic management.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did you talk to what's-his-name about the thing?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Um... Yes.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: There should be some sort of award for avoiding minutiae.

situation: The Boss announces in a thought bubble that it's time for some generic management. He then asks a seated employee whether she talked to 'what's-his-name' about 'the thing', and she hesitantly says yes. Pleased with himself, he muses that there should be an award for avoiding minutiae.
punchline: The Boss thinks his total vagueness, which names neither person nor task, is an admirable skill, when in reality he is just being lazy and uninformed.
summary: A manager proudly congratulates himself on dodging every specific detail while giving hopelessly vague instructions to a staffer.

title: Truth Costs Less Than Lies

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert consults

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Do you want me to lie to you for $400 per hour or give you the truth for $200?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll take truth.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Okay. The problem is that having you try to manage engineers is like having an earthworm try to juggle.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: How's my premium pricing option sound to you now?

setting: Office meeting where Dogbert consults for the Boss
situation: Dogbert, working as a consultant, offers the Boss a choice between paying $400 an hour for lies or $200 for the truth. The Boss picks the cheaper truth, and Dogbert bluntly tells him he is hopelessly unsuited to managing engineers. Stung, the Boss hears Dogbert ask if the premium pricing option sounds better now.
punchline: The honest answer was so insulting that the Boss would now gladly pay double for flattering lies, which proves Dogbert's premium pricing scheme works.
summary: A consultant gives his client a brutal assessment of his abilities, then points out that the pricier flattery package suddenly looks appealing.

file: 2007/2007-10-20_security consultant_suspicious behavior_beat him_death_trash can_recycle bins_ask question_medical.gif
title: Dogbert's Security Advice: Beat Suspicious People

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Security Consultant

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Be on the lookout for any suspicious behavior.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If you see a guy do something that you wouldn't do, beat him to death with a trash can.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can we use recycle bins?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I wouldn't have asked that question.

setting: Conference room during a security briefing
situation: Dogbert, acting as a security consultant, briefs the Boss and a coworker on spotting suspicious behavior. He defines suspicious as anything you wouldn't do and advises beating that person to death with a trash can. The Boss asks whether a recycle bin would also work, and a coworker thinks to himself that he wouldn't have asked that.
punchline: The Boss's only concern about Dogbert's absurdly violent advice is whether a recycle bin is an acceptable weapon, which makes him exactly the kind of person his coworker finds suspicious.
summary: A consultant's extreme security tips are met with a manager's eco-friendly follow-up, leaving a colleague privately wary of him.

file: 2007/2007-12-17_dead horse_interview_offcie_meeting_chair_not answering_few hours_secretary_cancel other meetinsg_take time_business.gif
title: Interviewing a Dead Horse

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You have good experience as a dead horse, but can you take a beating?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So, you think you can ignore my questions, do you?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Cancel all of my meetings. This could take a few more hours.

situation: The Boss is interviewing a job candidate who is a horse, and he reads from a resume while asking questions. The horse never answers, and the Boss grows angry at being ignored. He then tells his secretary to cancel all his meetings because the interview will take several more hours.
punchline: The Boss takes the horse's silence as insolence and decides to keep beating a dead horse, literally, for hours, ignoring that the horse is simply dead.
summary: A manager grills a lifeless horse in a job interview and, offended by its silence, clears his schedule to continue.

title: Two Monitors Instead of Raise

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My pay is below market. Can I have a 20% raise?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, but I'll let you use two flat screen monitors in your cubicle so it feels like you're an evil genius in a secret lair.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Bu-wa-haha!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Who got a second monitor?

setting: The Boss's office, then the office hallway outside
situation: Dilbert asks his boss for a 20% raise because his pay is below market. The boss refuses but offers him a second flat screen monitor so he can feel like an evil genius in a secret lair. Dilbert's evil laughter is heard from his cubicle, and coworkers in the hall wonder who got a second monitor.
punchline: The boss tries to substitute a cheap perk for a real raise, and the plan works so well that Dilbert is cackling happily and his coworkers are now envious of the monitor.
summary: A request for better pay is brushed aside with the offer of extra screen space that makes a cubicle feel like a villain's hideout.

title: Sadist Hired to Thin Herd

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired a sadist.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll be using her to thin the herd.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Herd?

transcript.speaker: Sadist
transcript.text: That one looks slow.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They all look like that.

situation: The Boss introduces a grinning new hire he describes as a sadist, explaining that she will be used to cull the workforce. Dilbert, seated at his computer, asks what herd he means. The sadist points at Dilbert and remarks that he looks slow, and the Boss says they all look that way.
punchline: The Boss plans to use a sadist to cull employees, and his remark that everyone looks slow shows he sees the whole staff as livestock ready for culling.
summary: A manager brings in a gleeful tormentor to cull his staff, and she immediately marks the nearest employee as a weak animal.

title: Mordac's Scream-Based Biometric Scanner

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: I am Mordac, the Preventer of Information Services, and I bring you my newest biometric scanner.

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: Instead of a password, I put this on your head and squeeze until you scream in a way that only you can scream.

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: No, that's not you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: GAAA! GAAA! GAAA!

situation: Mordac, head of Information Services, visits Dilbert to introduce a new biometric scanner. Instead of a password, it is a vise-like device clamped onto the user's head and squeezed until the user screams in a unique way. In the last panel he is squeezing Dilbert's head while Dilbert screams, and Mordac rejects the scream as not matching.
punchline: The 'biometric security' is just torture, and Mordac's rejection of Dilbert's scream shows he is more interested in inflicting pain than in the system working.
summary: A sadistic IT security chief clamps a head-squeezing gadget onto an employee to authenticate him by his screams.

file: 2007/2007-09-30_carpet fishing_devised a game_computer_string_randomly picks location_hooked fish marlin_salmon_killing time_technology.gif
title: Carpet Fishing Sport Invented at Desk

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What are you doing?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Carpet fishing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's a sport I invented.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I divided the carpet in my cubicle into a numbered grid.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then I wrote a computer program that randomly picks a carpet location and a type of fish about once an hour.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If it picks the carpet location where I happen to be dangling this string, it means I hooked a fish.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: (Dilbert hums with musical notes while Alice looks on.)

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yesterday I caught a marlin.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Did you come here for some reason other than to spoil the salmon run?

situation: Alice asks Dilbert what he is doing, and he explains an elaborate game he invented: dangling a string over a numbered grid on his carpet while a program he wrote randomly picks a spot and a fish type once an hour. Alice listens through the explanation and Dilbert's cheerful humming, then asks pointedly if she interrupted his game.
punchline: Alice sarcastically implies her visit is merely ruining his imaginary fishing, pointing out how absurdly he has taken the game's make-believe rules seriously.
summary: A bored engineer turns his cubicle floor into a pretend fishing lake and a coworker's patience runs out when she interrupts the make-believe angling.

file: 2007/2007-10-11_unqualified crony_quality control group_value loyalty_great leader_extra disloyal.gif
title: Loyalty Over Competence, Disloyal Dilbert

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired an unqualified crony to run our quality control group.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I value loyalty over competence. That's the sign of a great leader.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you see any problem with that?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It makes you look extra disloyal?

setting: Conference room, with an exterior shot of an office building
situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces that he hired an unqualified crony to run the quality control group, then boasts that valuing loyalty over competence marks a great leader. When he asks whether anyone sees a problem, Dilbert points out that the decision makes the Boss look disloyal.
punchline: By putting a loyal but unqualified friend in charge of quality, the Boss betrays the company and its customers, so his own act of cronyism makes him disloyal.
summary: A manager brags about rewarding a buddy with a key job, and is told his favoritism undermines the very loyalty he claims to prize.

title: Sadist Fails to Insult Wally

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Sadist vs. Wally

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You are worthless and overpaid!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Thank you.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: He's immune to my sadism.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: So, what's it like being underpaid?

situation: Alice, in her sadist role, hurls an insult at Wally, calling him worthless and overpaid. Wally, holding his coffee mug, calmly thanks her as though it were a compliment. Frustrated that her cruelty has no effect, Alice turns the tables and asks what it's like being underpaid.
punchline: Wally is so proud of being a lazy, overpaid slacker that insults register as praise, leaving Alice's sadism powerless and her only retort an accidental admission about her own pay.
summary: A cruel coworker's attempt to wound a lazy colleague backfires when he accepts her insult as a compliment and she ends up complaining about her own pay.

file: 2007/2007-10-24_therapy session_no longer care_human interaction_too sahllow_predciatable_outdoor actvities.gif
title: Therapist Predictable, Says Internet Addict

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm addicted to the Internet.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I no longer care for direct human interaction. It's too shallow and predictable.

transcript.speaker: Therapist
transcript.text: Maybe you should try some outdoor activities.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I saw that coming.

situation: Dilbert lies on a couch and tells his therapist he is addicted to the Internet. He explains that he has stopped caring for face-to-face human interaction because it is too shallow and predictable. The therapist responds with the stock suggestion to try outdoor activities, and Dilbert says he saw it coming.
punchline: The therapist's cliched advice proves Dilbert's point that direct human interaction is shallow and predictable, since he anticipated her exact response.
summary: A man who prefers the web to people gets his complaint about predictable humans confirmed by his counselor's stock advice.

file: 2007/2007-12-20_order from boss_reptilian brain_not apparent_move cubicle_closer to department.gif
title: Reptilian Brain Cubicle Move

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, I want you to move to a cubicle closer to the rest of the department.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Is there a reason that isn't apparent, or is this coming from the reptilian part of your brain?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How would I know?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That's a surprisingly good point.

situation: The Boss tells Alice to relocate to a cubicle nearer the rest of the department. Alice asks whether there is a hidden rational reason or whether the order comes from his primitive reptilian brain. The Boss replies that he cannot know, and Alice concedes it is a surprisingly good point.
punchline: The Boss can't tell whether his own decisions are rational or instinctive, and Alice sarcastically admits that his answer is accidentally logical.
summary: An employee questions whether her manager's seating order has any real logic, and his admission of self-ignorance leaves her grudgingly impressed.

title: Decisions Made By Those With Time

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why does it seem as if most of the decisions in my workplace are made by drunken lemurs?

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: Decisions are made by people who have time, not people who have talent.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why are talented people so busy?

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: They're fixing the problems made by people who have time.

setting: Outdoors by a garbage can near a grassy roadside
situation: Dilbert complains to a garbage man that workplace decisions seem to be made by drunken lemurs. The garbage man explains that decisions are made by whoever has free time, not by the talented. When Dilbert asks why talented people are so busy, he is told they are cleaning up the messes made by those with time.
punchline: Talented people are too busy fixing the problems caused by idle people's bad decisions to ever be the ones making decisions, creating a self-perpetuating cycle of incompetence.
summary: A sanitation worker gives Dilbert a bleak explanation of why bad choices keep winning out over good judgment at work.

title: Window Cubicle Envy Turns Hostile

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Alice, did you hear I'm getting a cubicle by the window?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Although I wouldn't want that cubicle because of the glare, the fact that you want it makes me hate you for getting it.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: We're like a family here.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I hope it collapses on your head!

situation: A coworker carrying a box of belongings tells Alice he is getting a cubicle by the window. Alice calmly explains that she doesn't even want it, but resents him for wanting it. As he thinks about how the office is like a family, she angrily wishes the cubicle would collapse on him.
punchline: Alice's petty, irrational jealousy shows the office 'family' is really full of resentment, contradicting the coworker's warm thought bubble.
summary: A newly promoted coworker's good news about a prime cubicle spot prompts Alice to admit she envies him and then to wish him physical harm.

file: 2007/2007-11-15_flash_java script_website_fast guy in tights_movie about coffee_code words_remember_technology.gif
title: Boss Mangles Flash and JavaScript

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then we program the web site using a fast guy in tights and a movie about coffee.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Correct me if I'm wrong.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We use Flash and Java-script.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I said, "IF"!!!

situation: At a meeting, the Boss describes how the company builds its web site, substituting a fast guy in tights and a movie about coffee for the real technologies. He invites correction, and Dilbert supplies the right answer: Flash and JavaScript. The Boss then angrily snaps that he only said 'if'.
punchline: The Boss asks to be corrected only hypothetically, so when he is actually proven wrong he lashes out, revealing he never wanted real correction and doesn't understand the technology he is describing.
summary: A manager garbles the names of web technologies, then gets furious when an employee takes his request for corrections literally.

title: Dilbert Proves Date's Point Perfectly

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: You treat every conversation like it's a contest where you have to be the one who is right!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It only seems that way because everything you say is wrong.

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: See? There it is!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm pretty sure that was you again.

situation: Dilbert is on a date at a restaurant, and his date accuses him of treating every conversation as a contest he must win. Dilbert responds that it only seems that way because everything she says is wrong. She points out that he just did exactly what she described, and he replies that she was the one who did it.
punchline: Dilbert's defence of himself is itself an example of needing to be right, and he even denies it when she calls him on it.
summary: A man defends himself against the charge of always needing to win arguments by insisting he wins them only because his date is always mistaken.

file: 2007/2007-10-22_security consulatant_without id_badge_strip search_confiscate wallet_lock him janitors closet_extreme_living on mop water.gif
title: Security Consultant Recommends Extreme Measures

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the security consultant

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If you see someone without an ID badge...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: ...strip search him, confiscate his wallet, and lock him in the janitor's closet until he starves!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That seems a bit extreme.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You're about one minute away from living on mop water.

situation: Dogbert, working as a security consultant, stands on a stool addressing employees and explains what to do when you see someone without an ID badge. His advice escalates to strip searching, robbing, and starving the person in a closet. The Boss objects that this is extreme, and Dogbert threatens him with the same fate.
punchline: Dogbert responds to a mild objection by threatening the Boss with the very punishment he just described, showing that security consultants (and Dogbert) answer criticism with intimidation.
summary: A consultant's absurdly brutal badge-checking policy gets a timid complaint from management, which earns the complainer a threat of imprisonment and starvation.

file: 2007/2007-11-18_career day_classroom_guest speaker_dilbert_engineering_tells all_explaining things_to idiots_make decisions_misinterpreting_massic=ve problems_rumors overwhelm_assign blame_unpopular.gif
title: Dilbert's Honest Career Day Talk

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Career Day

transcript.speaker: Teacher
transcript.text: Class, today Dilbert will tell us what a career in engineering is all about.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My job involves explaining things to idiots.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then the idiots make decisions based on misinterpreting what I said.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then it is my job to try to fix the massive problems caused by the bad decisions.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Eventually, rumors overwhelm facts, and I give up.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In the final phase, I assign blame to an unpopular coworker.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So whatever you do in life, don't be unpopular.

transcript.speaker: Teacher
transcript.text: Don't listen to him!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Said the unpopular teacher.

situation: Dilbert is a guest speaker at a school career day and describes engineering as a cycle of explaining things to idiots, who then misinterpret him and make bad decisions. He fixes the resulting problems until rumors overwhelm facts, and then he blames an unpopular coworker. He advises the students not to be unpopular, and the teacher objects.
punchline: The teacher's protest is dismissed with the observation that he is the unpopular coworker, which illustrates exactly how blame gets assigned to the unpopular.
summary: A cynical engineer gives schoolchildren a bleak tour of his profession, ending with advice that proves itself at the teacher's expense.

title: Asking Permission to Give Advice

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Do you mind if I give you some advice?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Not at all.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you mind if I roll my eyes, sigh deeply, and dismiss your advice as if it came from the village idiot?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I might mind.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well then, let me give you some advice. . .

situation: A coworker (Asok, standing) asks Dilbert, who is seated at his computer, if he can offer some advice. Dilbert agrees, then asks whether the coworker would mind if he rolls his eyes, sighs, and dismisses the advice as coming from an idiot. When the coworker says he might mind, Dilbert says he will give him some advice instead.
punchline: Dilbert turns the tables by pre-announcing how rudely he will treat the advice, so the coworker objects and Dilbert gets to be the one dispensing advice (and implicitly lecturing him on how to take it).
summary: A polite offer of guidance is met with a sarcastic question about contemptuous dismissal, which flips who ends up doing the advising.

file: 2007/2007-12-09_cost estimate_user requirements_estimate_go over budget_fired_number_ten million dollars_know cost_input.gif
title: Boss Demands Estimate Without Requirements

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need a cost estimate on your project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have no idea. I haven't even gathered the user requirements.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't worry. I won't hold you to the estimate.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes you will. You will put it in the plan, forget we had this conversation, and fire me when I go over budget.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Give me a number or I'll fire you right now.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, it will cost ten million dollars.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's too high.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If you already know the cost, why are you asking me?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So you'll feel like you had input.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is input supposed to feel this bad?

setting: Office, in front of Dilbert's cubicle
situation: The Boss demands a cost estimate for Dilbert's project even though Dilbert hasn't gathered any requirements. Dilbert predicts the estimate will be turned into a binding budget, so the Boss threatens to fire him unless he names a number. Dilbert says ten million dollars, the Boss calls it too high, and it emerges the Boss already had a figure in mind.
punchline: The Boss already has a number in mind and only asks for estimates so employees feel consulted, which makes the 'input' feel like pure humiliation.
summary: A manager extracts a made-up budget figure from an engineer, then rejects it because he had already decided the answer.

title: Calculated Risk of Everyone Being Late

transcript.speaker: Meeting Leader
transcript.text: And Wally, did you finish your project tasks for today?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No. I took a calculated risk that other people would not finish their tasks either, making my lateness totally irrelevant.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Um...

transcript.speaker: Meeting Leader
transcript.text: That is the worst...

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I need another week.

setting: Conference room during a project status meeting
situation: During a project meeting, the leader asks Wally whether he completed his tasks for the day. Wally admits he didn't, explaining he gambled that others would also be late so his delay wouldn't matter. The leader reacts with dismay, and another attendee sheepishly admits he needs another week, proving Wally's gamble correct.
punchline: Wally's cynical bet that everyone else would be behind schedule pays off, since a colleague immediately confirms he needs more time too.
summary: A slacking employee justifies his unfinished work by betting his teammates were behind as well, and one of them promptly proves him right.

file: 2007/2007-10-04_vacation time_off next week_cures eyou_so much work_die! relieve stress_unsupportive.gif
title: Vacation Reminder Followed By Death Curse

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Remember to use all of your vacation time before year end.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I'm off next week.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What! I curse you for taking time off when we have so much work to do! Die, die, die!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Anyway, the point is that vacations help relieve your stress.

situation: At a meeting, the boss reminds everyone to use up their vacation time before the year ends. When an employee says he is taking next week off, the boss erupts in fury and curses him for leaving when there is so much work. The boss then calmly resumes his point that vacations relieve stress.
punchline: The boss encourages vacations in theory but reacts with rage when someone actually takes one, then pretends nothing happened and cites stress relief, showing his hypocrisy.
summary: A manager urges staff to take their leave, then screams abuse at the first person who announces a holiday before calmly carrying on as if nothing happened.

title: Shrinking Cubicle, Sneaky Spoilage

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My new cubicle is too small.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: It looks fine to me.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: It only seems small because you were so spoiled before.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I didn't feel spoiled.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Apparently it sneaks up on you.

situation: Dilbert complains to Catbert that his new cubicle is too small. Catbert replies that it only feels small because Dilbert was spoiled by his previous, larger cubicle. In the last panel, a colleague (apparently Wally, mostly hidden behind his cubicle wall) says he didn't feel spoiled, and Dilbert notes that spoilage sneaks up on you.
punchline: Management-style rationalization says a downgrade is only a problem because you were previously comfortable, and Dilbert wryly concedes that being spoiled is something you only recognize after it's taken away.
summary: A downsized workspace is dismissed as a complaint by someone who simply got too comfortable with a roomier one.

title: Everything Included, Except Everything Else

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: That price quote includes everything!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What about taxes, shipping, cables, carts, software, memory upgrades, maintenance and insurance?

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Has anyone ever called you needy?

setting: Sales meeting at a desk or conference table
