situation: A vendor salesman insists his price quote covers everything. Dilbert, reading the quote, lists a long series of costs that are not actually included, such as taxes, shipping, software and maintenance. The salesman deflects by calling Dilbert needy instead of answering.
punchline: When confronted with the many hidden extra costs, the salesman avoids the issue and insults the customer for asking for what a complete quote should obviously include.
summary: A vendor claims his quote is all-inclusive, but when the customer points out a pile of missing charges, he responds by questioning the customer's personality.

file: 2007/2007-12-11_dead for week_managed reincarnation_own clone_shapeshifting skills_snicker bar_cable guy_waited at house_equivalent.gif
title: Wildly Unequal Tales of Hardship

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I was dead for a week, but I managed to reincarnate into my own clone and use my shapeshifting skills to look less like a Snickers bar.

transcript.speaker: Coworker in green sweater
transcript.text: I once waited four hours for a cable TV guy to show up at my house.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Those stories are not equivalent.

transcript.speaker: Coworker in green sweater
transcript.text: It's subjective.

situation: A man in a white shirt and tie describes a bizarre ordeal involving death, reincarnation into his own clone, and shapeshifting away from looking like a candy bar. His coworker in a green sweater responds by claiming her own hardship was waiting four hours for the cable guy. He objects that the stories are not comparable, and she dismisses him by saying it is subjective.
punchline: Waiting for the cable guy is treated as just as awful as dying and being reincarnated, because the coworker refuses to admit that her complaint is trivial by comparison.
summary: One worker's supernatural misadventure is matched by another's cable-installer wait, and she insists the two ordeals are equally bad.

file: 2007/2007-12-24_presentation_useful parts_open to suggestions_unqualified_their own jobs_software_recycled paper_engineering.gif
title: Suggestions From the Unqualified Audience

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This concludes the useful part of my presentation.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now let's open the floor to suggestions from people who are unqualified to do their own jobs, much less mine.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes, you with the forehead.

transcript.speaker: Audience Member
transcript.text: Can you make the software out of recycled paper?

situation: Dilbert finishes his presentation, standing beside a slide showing a device. He then invites questions by insulting the audience's competence. When he calls on someone, the audience member asks whether the software can be made out of recycled paper, proving his point.
punchline: Dilbert's insult about the audience being unqualified is immediately confirmed by a nonsensical question, since software is not a physical material that can be made from paper.
summary: After a blunt presentation, an engineer invites feedback from colleagues he considers incompetent, and the first question proves him right.

file: 2007/2007-10-29_suggestions_marble sized brain_twice as smooth_root cause_mating for generations.gif
title: Dilbert Insults Suggestion Box Reader

transcript.speaker: Man with paper
transcript.text: Why didn't you use any of my suggestions?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My theory is that your brain is the size of a marble, and twice as smooth.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The root cause probably involves slow learners mating for many generations.

situation: A coworker holding a sheet of paper asks Dilbert why none of his suggestions were used. Dilbert answers by insulting the man's intelligence, first claiming his brain is marble-sized and smooth, then speculating that his ancestors were slow learners who bred together over generations.
punchline: Dilbert bluntly explains why the suggestions were ignored by mocking the man's intelligence in the guise of a formal root cause analysis.
summary: Asked why his ideas were ignored, Dilbert responds with a pseudo-scientific takedown of the man's brainpower and ancestry.

file: 2007/2007-09-25_donate_campaign_drill for oil_opppenets lawn_bureau of alcohol tobacco  firearms_politics.gif
title: Campaign Donations Buy Political Favors

transcript.speaker: Politician
transcript.text: Donate to my campaign, and I'll let you drill for oil in my opponent's lawn.

transcript.speaker: Politician
transcript.text: And I'll appoint you to run the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is that as fun as it sounds?

transcript.speaker: Politician
transcript.text: Not for your neighbors.

setting: Office or meeting room with a desk
situation: A politician seeking campaign donations tries to entice Dilbert with absurd rewards: the right to drill for oil on his opponent's lawn and an appointment to head the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms. Dilbert asks whether the job is as fun as it sounds, and the politician answers that it is not fun for his neighbors.
punchline: The politician's reply implies that a private citizen running a federal agency over alcohol, tobacco and firearms would cause trouble for everyone nearby, mocking how political appointments are traded for donations without regard to competence or consequences.
summary: A candidate openly offers a donor ridiculous perks and a powerful agency post in exchange for money, and a deadpan reply reveals the risk to everyone around.
keywords: bureau of alcohol tobacco and firearms

file: 2007/2007-12-05_intern_test pilot_new moon_shuttle prototype_wiser_monkey on first flight.gif
title: Interns Before Monkeys on Moon Shuttle

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, I need an intern to test-pilot our new moon shuttle prototype.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Wouldn't it be wiser to send a monkey on the first flight?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're thinking of the second flight.

situation: The Boss tells Asok, the intern, that he needs a volunteer to test-pilot the company's new moon shuttle prototype. Asok suggests that a monkey should be sent on the first flight instead. The Boss replies that Asok is thinking of the second flight, implying the intern goes first.
punchline: The Boss reveals that the intern is considered more expendable than a monkey, so the monkey only gets sent after the dangerous first test.
summary: A manager volunteers his youngest employee for a risky rocket trial and casually explains that animals come only after the human guinea pig.

file: 2007/2007-10-19_increased pordcutivity_watched funny videos_morning until dusk_halfway done.gif
title: Boosting Productivity With YouTube Videos

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: This week I increased my productivity by improving my morale.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I watched funny YouTube videos from morning until dusk.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's all you did?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Don't worry. I'm almost halfway done.

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: At a meeting table, Wally reports that he increased his productivity by improving his morale, which he did by watching funny YouTube videos all day. The Boss asks if that's all he did, and Wally casually replies, holding a coffee mug, that he is only about halfway done.
punchline: Wally treats goofing off online as a legitimate morale-boosting work project and cheerfully implies he plans to spend even more time watching videos.
summary: A slacking employee justifies a week of online video binging as a morale initiative and promises there is plenty more to come.

file: 2007/2007-10-14_write code_faster_high level of effciciency_recognized_rewarded_works for you_finish all projects_one hour.gif
title: Efficiency Punished With Impossible Expectations

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I found a clever way to write my application code in one hour!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Normally this sort of thing would take weeks.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I assume my high level of efficiency will be recognized and rewarded.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Let me know how that works out for you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You did all of that in one hour?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes, I did.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: From now on, I expect you to finish all of your projects in one hour.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Otherwise I'll assume you're ripping off the company.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You could have warned me.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That's not how experience works.

setting: Office cubicles and the Boss's office
situation: Dilbert proudly tells Alice he found a clever way to write his application code in one hour, expecting recognition. Alice sarcastically invites him to report back, and when he tells the Boss, the Boss demands that all future projects be done in one hour or he'll assume Dilbert is ripping off the company. Dilbert complains he wasn't warned, and Alice points out that's not how experience works.
punchline: Dilbert's efficiency is punished rather than rewarded, as the Boss turns a one-time shortcut into an impossible permanent expectation, and Alice notes that experience teaches lessons only after the fact.
summary: A worker who speeds through a task in record time learns the hard way that doing so only raises his boss's demands.

file: 2007/2007-12-13_mordac_preventer of information services_network changes_on vacation_3 weeks_russian submarine_arctic circle_blank screen_coincidence.gif
title: Mordac's Untested Network Changes Vacation Alibi

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Mordac, the Preventer of Information Services

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: I made some changes to the network that I alone understand.

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: I didn't have time to test it, but if there is a problem, I'll be on vacation for three weeks in a Russian submarine below the Arctic Circle.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My screen just went blank.

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: Let's chalk that up to coincidence.

situation: Mordac, the head of IT, tells the Boss he has made untested changes to the network that only he understands. He announces he will be unreachable on a three-week vacation on a submarine in case anything goes wrong. The Boss's screen immediately goes blank, and Mordac dismisses it as coincidence.
punchline: Mordac deliberately makes himself unreachable before the inevitable failure from his untested changes, and then dismisses the immediate outage as coincidence rather than taking responsibility.
summary: An IT enforcer rolls out risky network changes and arranges to be unreachable beneath the polar ice just before the system fails.

title: Worse Design, Vague Requirements, Blame

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I changed the product design.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's worse than the old design.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You asked me to come up with a new design.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I meant a new design that's better than the old design.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Great. You could have told me that before I did all of this work.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: How do you think this makes me feel?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: No one would blame me for hating you.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm the only sane person in this company.

situation: A coworker proudly tells Dilbert he changed the product design, and Dilbert says it's worse than the old one. The coworker points out that he was only asked for a new design, and Dilbert admits he meant a better one. The coworker then blames Dilbert for his wasted effort, says he's justified in hating him, and walks off thinking he's the only sane person at the company.
punchline: The coworker met the literal requirement and then flips the blame onto Dilbert for the vague request, concluding he alone is sane when he arguably chose to deliver a worse design.
summary: A worker delivers a redesign that is worse than the original, then insists the fault lies with whoever gave him such unclear instructions.

file: 2007/2007-12-12_coffe pot_coffee stand_offcie_yell_order coffee_quality of life_taste better.gif
title: Coffee Hoarder Scolds, Boss Retaliates

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Don't you dare take another cup of coffee.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: The more you drink, the more often I have to order coffee. You are destroying my quality of life!

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: GAAA!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If this doesn't make the coffee taste better, I don't know what will.

setting: Office cubicle area and coffee station
situation: A cubicle worker, who is in charge of ordering the office coffee, yells at the Boss not to take another cup because his drinking forces her to reorder more often. Stung by the scolding, the Boss goes to the coffee machine, apparently intending to do something nasty to the coffee.
punchline: The Boss responds to the complaint by implying he will spoil the coffee (likely by spitting in it), taking petty revenge on the person who scolded him.
summary: After being berated for drinking too much of the office coffee, the boss pours himself a cup while hinting at a grubby bit of payback.

file: 2007/2007-09-15_vp of marketing_spray paint the oadkill_dishonesty_isn't mortal_won't work.gif
title: Marketing VP Embraces Dishonesty

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert, the VP of Marketing

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's my job to spraypaint the roadkill.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll use a process the experts call "dishonesty."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My motto is "If it isn't immoral, it probably won't work."

setting: Office, across a desk from The Boss
situation: Dogbert, introduced as the VP of Marketing, explains his role to The Boss, who sits listening. He describes marketing as making a dead, worthless product look appealing, and says his method is dishonesty. He closes by stating a motto that effective marketing has to be immoral.
punchline: Dogbert cynically admits that marketing succeeds only through deception, so any ethical approach is doomed to fail.
summary: Dogbert, in his role as a marketing executive, cheerfully lays out a philosophy that deceit is the secret ingredient of selling anything.

title: Crazy, Liar, or Watched Through Monitor

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's Tech Support

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No one else has ever reported that problem.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That means you are either crazy or a liar.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: It's a little of both, but how did you know?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I can see you through your computer.

setting: Dogbert's tech support call center desk, plus the customer's workstation
situation: Dogbert, working a tech support phone line with a headset, tells a caller that nobody else has reported their problem and concludes that the caller must be crazy or lying. The caller sheepishly admits it's a bit of both and asks how Dogbert knew. Dogbert reveals he can see the caller through the computer.
punchline: Dogbert's tech support not only insults customers but also casually admits to spying on them through their own computer, turning a rude diagnosis into a privacy violation.
summary: A support agent dismisses a customer's unique problem as madness or dishonesty, then casually reveals he has been watching the customer through their machine.

file: 2007/2007-12-30_impressive resume_promoted_management_money and pretige_doing less work_opportunity_abuse subordinates_fluent managerese_love interviewing.gif
title: Alice Interviews for Management, Honestly

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: Alice, your résumé is impressive.

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me why you want to be promoted to management.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Well, obviously there's the money and prestige.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm also attracted by the prospect of doing much less work.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: The opportunity to abuse subordinates is a big plus.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: And I speak fluent managerese. Watch this...

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Fuh fuh fuh fuh fuh.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you really want that job?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: No, but I love interviewing!

setting: A management job interview in an office, with a short exterior shot of a building
situation: Alice interviews for a management promotion and cheerfully admits she wants it for the money, the prestige, the lighter workload and the chance to abuse subordinates. She then demonstrates her 'fluent managerese' by pointing and spouting nonsense syllables, while the interviewer stays expressionless. Afterward Dilbert asks if she really wanted the job, and she says she just enjoys interviewing.
punchline: Alice's brutally honest and nonsensical interview answers show how little management actually requires, and she never even wanted the job, since she just enjoys the interview game.
summary: A candidate gleefully admits every cynical motive for becoming a manager, babbles gibberish as proof of her management jargon skills, and reveals she was only there for fun.

title: Scheduling Sick Days in Advance

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: From now on, all sick days must be scheduled in advance.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That's ridiculous. How are we supposed to know when we're going to be sick?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I hired a guy who never washes his hands to help you with scheduling.

transcript.speaker: Filthy man
transcript.text: Tomorrow.

situation: Catbert, acting as evil HR director, announces that all sick days must be scheduled in advance. When Alice objects that nobody can predict illness, Catbert reveals he has hired an unhygienic man, surrounded by flies, to help with the scheduling. The man grimly predicts that she will be sick tomorrow.
punchline: Catbert's solution to unpredictable sickness is to make it predictable by deliberately exposing employees to a filthy man who will give them germs.
summary: The malevolent HR cat answers a complaint about predicting illness by bringing in a grimy germ-spreader to guarantee when everyone gets sick.

title: Cloned Asok Is Part Snickers

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your prototype killed Asok. That means it is your job to clone him and hope he reincarnates into the clone.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol used his DNA container for a snack jar, so be careful.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Why do I feel nuts?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're part Snickers bar.

setting: Boss's office, then a lab or hospital room
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that his prototype killed Asok, so Dilbert must clone him and hope Asok's soul moves into the clone. The Boss warns that Carol used Asok's DNA container as a snack jar. The clone wakes up in bed, feeling nuts, and Dilbert explains he is part Snickers bar.
punchline: Because the DNA sample was contaminated by snack food, the clone of Asok ends up part candy bar, which explains why he feels nuts.
summary: After a prototype accident claims a coworker, a cloning attempt goes comically wrong thanks to a contaminated DNA jar.

title: Wino's Spittle of Conclusions

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Did you look at my PowerPoint presentation?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes, it's a confused jumble of useless information with a wino's spittle of unsupported conclusions.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Wino's spittle?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You heard me.

situation: A coworker stands by Dilbert's cubicle and asks whether he reviewed his PowerPoint presentation. Dilbert, without looking away from his computer, gives a brutally vivid critique of its content. When the coworker repeats the odd phrase back in disbelief, Dilbert refuses to soften or retract it.
punchline: Dilbert's feedback is not only harsh but absurdly specific and bizarre, and he proudly stands by his strange insult instead of apologizing.
summary: A colleague seeks feedback on his slide deck and receives an unexpectedly colorful and unapologetic tongue-lashing from Dilbert.

file: 2007/2007-09-12_security card_appreciate_front pocket_thrust at door sensor_door opener.gif
title: Boss Doesn't Understand Security Card

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: People are complaining about how you use your security card.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We'd appreciate it if you didn't keep it in your front pocket and thrust it at the door sensor.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I didn't know the security card was why the door opened.

setting: Office, near a desk and a door
situation: Catbert, the human resources cat, tells the Boss that coworkers are complaining about the way he thrusts his front pocket at the door sensor to get in. In the last panel the Boss, holding a coffee mug, thinks to himself that he never realized the security card was what made the door open.
punchline: The Boss has been using his security card for years without understanding how it works, and the awkward way he used it gave himself away as completely clueless.
summary: The office's HR cat scolds a clueless executive for an embarrassing door-entry habit, only to discover he doesn't even know what makes the door unlock.

file: 2007/2007-10-13_targeted for elimination_rumor campaign_convince eevryone_dishonest incompetenet_wasn't hugged enough.gif
title: Rumor Campaign Because Of Missing Hugs

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Hello, Keith. You're the next coworker I have targeted for elimination.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I'll be using a rumor campaign to convince everyone you are dishonest and incompetent.

transcript.speaker: Keith
transcript.text: Why???

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Do I need a reason?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We think she wasn't hugged enough.

situation: Tina, standing at the head of the table, announces to a coworker named Keith that she has chosen him as her next target for elimination. She says she will spread rumors that he is dishonest and incompetent, and when he asks why, she says she doesn't need a reason. Dilbert, seated nearby, offers the coworkers' theory that she was not hugged enough.
punchline: Tina openly admits to a malicious office-politics campaign with no justification, and Dilbert dismisses her behavior with a pop-psychology explanation, implying she is simply a hostile person who was emotionally neglected.
summary: A coworker cheerfully announces her plan to smear a colleague's reputation for no reason, and the team blames her upbringing.

file: 2007/2007-11-24_cansisate_resume_spelling errors_hire a moron_poor perfromance_bigger reaise_interview skills_crazy good_manipulate_job interview.gif
title: Candidate Sells Boss on Hiring Him

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your résumé is riddled with spelling errors. Why should we hire a moron?

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: My poor performance would make you look good in comparison. You'll get a bigger raise if I work here.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What do you think of him?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, his interview skills are crazy good.

situation: Dilbert, acting as interviewer, points out that a job candidate's résumé is full of spelling errors and asks why they should hire a moron. The candidate replies that his poor performance will make the interviewer look good and earn him a bigger raise. Afterward the Boss asks Dilbert for his opinion, and Dilbert says the candidate's interview skills are crazy good.
punchline: The candidate is so incompetent that he is hired on the strength of his interviewing skill alone, because he cleverly appeals to the interviewer's self-interest in a bigger raise.
summary: An applicant turns a damning critique of his sloppy résumé into a winning pitch by promising to make his future colleagues look better.

title: Chain of Command Question Relay

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Where do you think you're going?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need to ask our VP of Sales a question.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Whoa! Whoa! Whoa!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You can't speak directly with a vice president.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You need to talk to your boss, who talks to his boss, who talks to someone who is friends with the VP of Sales, who then talks to him.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wouldn't that virtually guarantee that the wrong question gets asked?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's better to have the right person ask the wrong question than the wrong person ask the right question.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you have a minute?

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: Talk to my secretary.

setting: Office hallway and an executive's office
situation: Dilbert heads off to ask the VP of Sales a question, but Wally stops him and explains that employees must pass the question up a long chain of bosses and acquaintances. Dilbert points out that this ensures the wrong question gets asked, and Wally defends the hierarchy. When Dilbert tries speaking to an executive directly anyway, he is told to talk to the secretary.
punchline: The rigid chain-of-command is so absurd that even the executives refuse direct contact, deflecting Dilbert to a secretary, which shows the bureaucracy protects status rather than getting answers.
summary: A coworker insists that questions for a senior executive must be relayed through layers of intermediaries, and the executive himself proves the point by brushing off a direct approach.

file: 2007/2007-11-28_tech writer_stack of papers_speed of writing_breakthrough_realize accuracy_optional_micromanage_errors.gif
title: Fast Writing, Optional Accuracy

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Tina the Tech Writer

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: As you requested, I increased the speed of my writing.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: My breakthrough was realizing that accuracy and clarity are optional!

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Would you like to micromanage me by reading it all and pointing out the errors?

situation: Tina the tech writer delivers a huge stack of documentation to the Boss, saying she sped up her writing as he requested. She explains that her trick was to stop caring about accuracy and clarity. She then sarcastically offers him the chance to micromanage her by reading everything and finding the errors.
punchline: The Boss demanded faster output without regard for quality, so Tina gave him a mountain of error-filled pages and dares him to do the checking, which he would normally dismiss as micromanagement.
summary: Told to write faster, a technical writer drops a towering heap of sloppy pages on her boss and challenges him to proofread it himself.

title: Shopping Cures Being Wrong

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I'm always wrong about everything. What can I do to fix that?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I recommend shopping. The customer is always right.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Shopping makes me smart?!!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You aren't shopping yet.

situation: Ratbert tells Dogbert he is always wrong about everything and asks how to fix it. Dogbert, seated in his purple chair, advises him to go shopping because the customer is always right. When Ratbert excitedly asks if shopping makes him smart, Dogbert points out he isn't shopping yet.
punchline: Dogbert twists the saying 'the customer is always right' into a trick, implying Ratbert only becomes right while buying something and remains wrong the moment he isn't, which also mocks his gullibility.
summary: A gullible Ratbert seeks a cure for constant error and Dogbert sends him shopping, then deflates his hopes with a dry reminder.

title: Weaponizing Uncoolness Against Goatees

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's wrong with your face?

transcript.speaker: Balding Coworker
transcript.text: It's a goatee.

transcript.speaker: Balding Coworker
transcript.text: I hate goatees, so I am using my powers of extreme uncoolness to make them go away.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That could work.

transcript.speaker: Man with Goatee
transcript.text: GAAA!!!

setting: Office break room by the coffee maker, then an office hallway
situation: Dilbert asks a bald coworker with glasses about the goatee on his face. The coworker says he hates goatees and is wearing one himself so his extreme uncoolness will make the style go away. When another man with a goatee sees them, he recoils in horror, suggesting the plan might work.
punchline: The coworker deliberately adopts a goatee so that his own uncoolness will make the trend repellent to everyone else, and a stylish goatee-wearer's panicked reaction hints that it's working.
summary: A nerdy coworker grows a goatee on purpose, hoping his lack of cool will poison the look for everyone else.

title: Grim Reaper Co-Pilot Pushes Button

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't worry, Asok. The prototype is perfectly safe.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I found you a co-pilot. He's a bit grim, but he works for free.

transcript.speaker: Grim Reaper
transcript.text: Hey, I wonder what this button does.

setting: A launch area next to a prototype spacecraft, then in space inside the cockpit
situation: The Boss reassures a nervous Asok that an experimental spacecraft prototype is perfectly safe, then introduces a free co-pilot who is the Grim Reaper. In the final panel Asok and the Reaper are in orbit above Earth, and the Reaper idly wonders what a button does.
punchline: Choosing a co-pilot just because he is free, even though he is Death himself, makes the claim that the prototype is safe absurd, and the Reaper's casual curiosity about the button implies Asok is about to die.
summary: A manager sends an engineer into space in an experimental craft with Death as a cost-free co-pilot, who then offers to press a mystery button.

file: 2007/2007-09-14_new vp of marketing_improve revenues_ridiculous lie_gullible moron_he believed it_touche.gif
title: Gullible Moron Believed the Marketing Lie

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our new VP of Marketing promises to improve our revenues by ten billion percent!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That is a ridiculous lie that only a gullible moron would believe.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oh yeah? How do you explain the fact that he believed it?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Touché.

situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces that the new VP of Marketing has promised to raise revenues by ten billion percent. Alice calls it a ridiculous lie that only a gullible moron would believe. The Boss retorts that the person who believed it is the VP's own boss, and Alice concedes.
punchline: Alice's insult backfires because the only person who believed the absurd promise was the Boss himself, which proves her point about gullible morons and makes her concede with 'Touché'.
summary: A boss repeats a wildly impossible revenue promise, and the employee who mocks anyone who'd believe it is promptly reminded that he does.

file: 2007/2007-11-06_marginally useful things_ageeing_say it a certain way_tone_beat up_ripped shirt_anger_repesct_high strung_co worker.gif
title: Dilbert Beaten Up Over Tone

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: You should check with Ted to see if he knows about this sort of thing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll add that to my list of marginally useful things that other people have suggested I do.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Apparently, agreeing isn't enough. You also need to say it a certain way.

situation: Carol, a co-worker with big hair, suggests Dilbert ask Ted for help. Dilbert replies that he'll add it to his list of marginally useful suggestions from others. In the final panel he appears at home bandaged, bruised and with a torn shirt, observing that agreeing isn't enough and the way you say it matters.
punchline: Dilbert's sarcastic way of agreeing with Carol apparently provoked a violent reaction, leaving him beaten up and teaching him that tone matters as much as words.
summary: A sarcastic brush-off of a coworker's advice leaves Dilbert battered and bruised, with a lesson about delivery.

title: Wally's Unverifiable Overtime Excuse

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, it's ten o'clock. You're supposed to start at eight.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That's because I plan to work for two unverifiable hours after you leave tonight.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My alleged loyalty to this company is second to none.

situation: Wally strolls in carrying his briefcase two hours after his official start time, and the Boss confronts him about being late. Wally calmly claims he will make up the time by working two hours after the Boss goes home, hours no one can check. He caps it off by boasting about his loyalty to the company.
punchline: Wally justifies arriving late by promising overtime that nobody can verify, and the word 'alleged' reveals his loyalty is as unprovable as the hours he claims to work.
summary: A late-arriving employee shrugs off his tardiness by pledging phantom overtime that conveniently happens when no one is watching.

file: 2007/2007-11-11_favor_comments_article_go away_wait util tomorrow_hope_worthless_extra work_worsen results_ignoring needs.gif
title: Wally's Honest Refusal to Review

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Wally, can I get your comments on my article by tomorrow?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Sure.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You say, "Sure," but we both know it's a lie.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You just want me to go away.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You plan to wait until tomorrow and make an excuse.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Then you'll hope I'll give up.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Yes, but remember, my comments are always worthless. They would cause you extra work and worsen the result.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: So if I give you nothing, everyone wins.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: In that case, thank you for ignoring my needs.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's the least I could do.

situation: Alice asks Wally to review her article by tomorrow. Wally says "sure," and Alice correctly predicts his whole plan to stall and make excuses. Wally cheerfully confirms it, arguing that his feedback would be worthless anyway, so doing nothing benefits everyone.
punchline: Wally turns his laziness into a favor, claiming that ignoring Alice's request is actually the most helpful thing he can do, and Alice sarcastically thanks him for it.
summary: A coworker who sees right through a slacker's empty promise is told that his neglect is really a kindness.

file: 2007/2007-12-16_highest raise_exceed expectations_thought possible_goals higher_incompetent_setting goals_maximum achievement_choices.gif
title: Dilbert Corners Boss on Raise

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't give you the highest raise because you didn't exceed expectations.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If you thought it was possible for me to exceed my expectations, you would have set the goals higher.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So there are only two possibilities here.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Either you are incompetent at setting goals. . .

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or I attained the maximum possible achievement and I deserve the maximum raise.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Which is it?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can I hear those two choices again?

setting: The Boss's office during a performance review
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he can't give him the highest raise because Dilbert didn't exceed expectations. Dilbert replies with a logical trap: either the Boss is bad at setting goals, or Dilbert hit the maximum achievement and deserves the top raise. After a silent beat, the Boss asks to hear the two choices again.
punchline: The Boss cannot work out how to answer Dilbert's either/or argument, so he stalls by asking to hear it again, implying he can't follow the logic or accept either option.
summary: An employee uses airtight logic to argue for a bigger raise, leaving his manager too befuddled to respond.

file: 2007/2007-11-20_borrow pen_need pen_order pen_order pens_parasitic arrangement_supplies_stingy_selfish_dysfunctional offcie_office supplies_fill out form.gif
title: Can't Order Pens Without a Pen

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can I order some pens?

transcript.speaker: Supply Clerk
transcript.text: No. It's impossible.

transcript.speaker: Supply Clerk
transcript.text: You need a pen to fill out the pen request form. And if you have a pen, you're not allowed to order one.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe I could borrow your pen.

transcript.speaker: Supply Clerk
transcript.text: That sounds like some sort of parasitic arrangement.

situation: Dilbert asks a supply clerk at her desk if he can order some pens. She explains a circular rule: you need a pen to fill out the pen request form, but anyone who already has a pen isn't allowed to order one. When Dilbert suggests borrowing her pen, she rejects the idea as a parasitic arrangement.
punchline: The pen request process is a catch-22, and the clerk refuses even the obvious workaround, treating a simple favor as improper.
summary: A bureaucratic supply clerk traps a coworker in a paradox where getting a pen requires already having one.

file: 2007/2007-09-16_contract changes_last month_negotiate_not authorized_hope to wear you down.gif
title: Negotiating By Wearing Down Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You didn't make any of the contract changes we agreed on last month.

transcript.speaker: Negotiator
transcript.text: That's how I negotiate.

transcript.speaker: Negotiator
transcript.text: I'm not authorized to make any changes to the contract.

transcript.speaker: Negotiator
transcript.text: And the executives who have that power will think I'm not doing my job if I ask them to do it.

transcript.speaker: Negotiator
transcript.text: So I agree to everything you ask, then I don't put any of it in the contract.

transcript.speaker: Negotiator
transcript.text: Over the course of several months, I hope to wear you down and make you sign the contract as is.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can you at least change section three the way I asked?

transcript.speaker: Negotiator
transcript.text: Sure. No problem.

transcript.speaker: Negotiator
transcript.text: I'll see you in a month.

setting: A conference room or office where Dilbert meets a contract negotiator
situation: Dilbert complains that the other party never put the agreed changes into the contract. The negotiator openly admits he has no authority to change anything and that he deliberately agrees to every request without acting on it, hoping to exhaust Dilbert into signing the original contract. When Dilbert asks for just one small change, the negotiator cheerfully agrees and says he'll see him in a month, implying nothing will happen.
punchline: The negotiator's cheerful 'Sure, no problem' shows his strategy is working perfectly: he promises everything, delivers nothing, and is so open about it that Dilbert is already giving up and asking for scraps.
summary: A contract negotiator candidly reveals that he nods along to every demand without changing a word, planning to outlast the other side until they give in.

title: Org Chart Versus Carol's Appendix

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, did you update the org chart yet?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: No. I kept waiting for it to become more important than my personal problems, but it just never happened.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How about right now?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Ouch! I think that's my appendix!

situation: The Boss asks his assistant Carol whether she has updated the org chart. She sarcastically replies that she was waiting for it to matter more than her personal problems. When the Boss asks if it's more important now, she suddenly clutches her side and claims her appendix is acting up.
punchline: Carol's sarcasm about her priorities is met with the Boss's literal-minded question, so she has to fake a medical emergency to keep dodging the task.
summary: A boss's assistant mocks his demand for an updated chart, then escapes his follow-up by feigning sudden abdominal pain.

file: 2007/2007-12-07_ask the intern_died_moon shuttle_sample of dna_jar_reincarnate to clone_jar missing_needed for candy.gif
title: Asok's DNA Jar Becomes Candy Jar

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I am sad to report that Asok the intern died during a test of our moon shuttle prototype.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Before he left, he put a sample of his DNA in a jar. His plan is to reincarnate into his own clone.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Where's the jar with Asok's DNA?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I needed a second candy jar.

setting: Office meeting room and a coworker's cubicle
situation: The Boss announces to staff that Asok the intern died while testing a moon shuttle prototype. He explains that Asok left a DNA sample in a jar so he could reincarnate as his own clone. The Boss then goes to a coworker's desk looking for the jar, and the coworker admits to using it as a second candy jar.
punchline: Asok's only chance at coming back to life has been lost because a coworker casually repurposed his DNA sample as a candy jar, showing how little the company values its interns.
summary: A manager mourns an intern killed in a risky experiment, only to learn the cloning sample meant to revive him is now holding sweets.

file: 2007/2007-11-25_boss_worker_office_wrong path_precise verbal explanation_embarrassment of undoing_good plan_progress_mistreatment of workers_corrupt policices_bad boss.gif
title: Boss Delegates Task Designed to Fail

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll give you just enough information to send you down the wrong path.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Later, after you do it wrong, I'll treat you like you're some sort of idiot.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then I'll put you through the embarrassment of undoing everything you did.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This might not sound like a good plan to you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But it takes the task off of my plate and puts it on yours.

transcript.text: That's called progress!

situation: The Boss cheerfully explains to Dilbert his entire plan for handing off a task: give incomplete instructions, blame Dilbert for the inevitable mistake, then make him redo the work. He admits it may not sound good but says it moves the task from his plate to Dilbert's. In the last panel Dilbert, outside, tells a garbage man he helped make progress and is wished better luck tomorrow.
punchline: The Boss redefines progress as simply offloading work onto a subordinate, and the garbage man's sympathetic reply shows how little Dilbert's 'progress' is worth.
summary: A manager openly lays out a scheme to dump his work on an employee through vague instructions and blame, and calls the result achievement.

title: Testing the Customer Is Always Right

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I'd like to buy some snow tires for a refrigerator.

transcript.speaker: Store Clerk
transcript.text: This is a lingerie store. Get lost before I stomp on your tail.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I think I debunked the theory that the customer is always right.

setting: A lingerie store, then a living room with a purple chair
situation: Ratbert walks into a lingerie store and asks the saleswoman for snow tires for a refrigerator. She tells him it's a lingerie store and threatens to stomp on his tail. Afterward, Ratbert limps home with a bandaged tail and tells Dogbert his experiment disproved the idea that the customer is always right.
punchline: Ratbert deliberately made an absurd request as a test of customer service, and his injured tail proves that the customer is not always right.
summary: A tiny experimenter makes a ridiculous purchase request at the wrong shop and reports the painful results of his research.

title: Dogbert Rents Scientists and Journalists

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Rent-a-Weasel

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I need three bitter and unsuccessful scientists and a hundred lazy journalists.

transcript.speaker: Weasel
transcript.text: Very good.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you know toddlers thrive on pollution?

setting: Rent-a-Weasel office, then Dilbert's living room
situation: Dogbert visits a Rent-a-Weasel agency and orders three bitter, unsuccessful scientists and a hundred lazy journalists from a weasel at a desk. Back at home, Dilbert reads a newspaper and announces to Dogbert that toddlers thrive on pollution.
punchline: Dogbert hired fake experts and lazy reporters to plant a ridiculous claim, and the newspaper story that Dilbert believes shows how easily manufactured research and uncritical journalism can pass off nonsense as fact.
summary: After Dogbert hires a crew of failed scientists and lazy reporters, Dilbert gullibly reads a news item claiming pollution is good for toddlers.

title: Two Monitors and Negotiation Gap

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Why does Dilbert get two computer monitors while I only get one?!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, according to researchers, it's because men tend to negotiate and women don't.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: So, what happens now?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If I had to guess, I'd say more complain-ing

situation: Alice confronts the boss, demanding to know why Dilbert has two computer monitors while she has only one. The boss casually cites research that men negotiate for perks and women don't. When Alice asks what happens next, he predicts she will just complain more rather than get a second monitor.
punchline: The boss admits resources go to those who negotiate, yet he expects Alice's pushback to be dismissed as mere complaining, so nothing will change for her.
summary: An employee protests unequal equipment and her manager shrugs it off with a study about negotiating habits, then predicts she will only grumble.

file: 2007/2007-12-10_death_reincarnation_snicker part_half man_half snack_studied guided reincarnation_shape shifting_indian institute_technology_medical.gif
title: Asok Reincarnated as Half-Snickers Clone

transcript.text: Asok died in a work-related accident. His disaster recovery plan was to reincarnate into his own clone.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You are his clone, but your DNA got mixed up with a Snickers bar. You are doomed to walk the Earth as half man, half snack.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Rrrrr

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Phew! It is lucky I studied guided reincarnation and advanced shape-shifting at the Indian Institute of Technology.

setting: A hospital room with a patient in bed
situation: Dilbert, dressed as a doctor, sits beside a hospital bed and explains that Asok died in a work accident and has been reincarnated as his own clone. The clone's DNA got mixed with a Snickers bar, so he appears as a candy bar creature. Asok then shape-shifts back into his normal form and says his schooling saved him.
punchline: Asok's absurdly specialized education at the Indian Institute of Technology conveniently includes guided reincarnation and shape-shifting, so even a candy-bar DNA mix-up is just another solvable problem.
summary: A doctor delivers news of a bizarre cloning mishap to a patient who turns out to have the exact mystical training needed to fix it.

file: 2007/2007-12-18_dead horse_meeting room_cahir_beating_good work_havnet beaten long enough_introduce.gif
title: Beating a Dead Horse Literally

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired a dead horse. He doesn't look like much, but if you beat him long enough, he does good work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Have you seen him do good work?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I haven't beaten him long enough.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Introduce yourself to the others!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Whap!

situation: The Boss tells his team he has hired a dead horse, claiming that if you beat it long enough it does good work. When Dilbert asks if he has actually seen it work, the Boss admits he hasn't beaten it long enough yet. He then starts hitting the horse and tells it to introduce itself to the others.
punchline: The Boss takes the idiom 'beating a dead horse' literally, believing that futile, relentless effort will eventually produce results, and he has no evidence it ever will.
summary: A manager hires an actual dead horse and keeps hitting it, convinced that enough abuse will make it productive.

file: 2007/2007-11-22_family freindly_policices_lost prodcutivity_openly hotsile_single people_not fair_impatience_contradictory remarks_hypcrisy_blatant prejudice.gif
title: Family Friendly, Hostile to Singles

transcript.text: We've decided to be more family friendly in our policies.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: To compensate for the lost productivity, we'll be openly hostile to single people.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That doesn't seem fair.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Shut up and get back to work, eunuch!

situation: Catbert, the evil human resources director, announces to a meeting that the company will adopt more family-friendly policies. He then explains that the lost productivity will be offset by being openly hostile to single people. When Dilbert objects that this is unfair, a coworker snaps at him to shut up and get back to work, calling him a eunuch.
punchline: The company treats employees without families as a disposable resource to absorb the cost of perks for parents, and when Dilbert objects, he is insulted for being single.
summary: A new benefits policy for parents is paid for by mistreating unmarried staff, and anyone who protests gets abused.
keywords: shut up and get back to work

title: Honesty Is a Brilliant Suggestion

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Explain why you charge less of your time to projects than all the other engineers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm trying something new. It's called honesty.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Stop doing that.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay. Brilliant suggestion.

situation: The Boss, sitting at his desk holding a paper, asks Dilbert why he bills fewer hours to projects than the other engineers. Dilbert explains that he is trying honesty. The Boss tells him to stop, and Dilbert agrees, calling it a brilliant suggestion.
punchline: The Boss prefers inflated timesheets to honest ones, so he orders Dilbert to stop being truthful, and Dilbert sarcastically praises the idea.
summary: A manager questions an engineer for reporting fewer hours than his colleagues, then demands he quit being truthful about it.

title: Attendance Confused With Productivity

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I don't know you. Why are you in this meeting?

transcript.speaker: Man in meeting
transcript.text: I'm creating the illusion of work by conflating the concepts of attendance and productivity.

transcript.speaker: Man in meeting (off-panel)
transcript.text: You should leave.

transcript.speaker: Another attendee (off-panel)
transcript.text: And who should I say hates teamwork?

situation: A woman at a meeting asks a man she doesn't recognize why he is there. He cheerfully admits he is only attending to create the illusion of work. She tells him to leave, and he threatens to tell people she hates teamwork.
punchline: The man openly admits that attending meetings is just a way to look busy, then shields himself from being kicked out by threatening to brand her as anti-teamwork.
summary: A stranger caught loitering in a meeting confesses he is only there to look busy, then uses the corporate cult of teamwork as leverage to stay.

file: 2007/2007-11-16_mordac_reventer_information services_complete log in_stare directly at sun_computer message.gif
title: Mordac Demands Security Over Usability

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Mordac, the Preventer of Information Services.

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: Security is more important than usability.

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: In a perfect world, no one would be able to use anything.

transcript.speaker: Computer
transcript.text: To complete the log-in procedure, stare directly at the sun.

setting: Conference room, then an office cubicle
situation: Mordac, head of information services, tells a meeting that security matters more than usability and that ideally nobody could use anything. In the last panel an employee at a computer is shown a log-in instruction demanding he stare directly at the sun.
punchline: Mordac's extreme security policies make systems so hostile that logging in requires harming yourself, showing how security taken to absurd lengths destroys usability.
summary: An IT security chief boasts that locking everything down beats usability, and the result is a login step that would blind the user.

title: Teamwork By Being Unhelpful

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: My accomplishment this week was helping Alice finish her project in a timely manner.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You didn't do anything to help me.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: Sure I did.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: Remember when I came to your cubicle to ask for some data I need for my project?

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: You said you were too busy, and shooed me away.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: If I had insisted on doing my job, you would have had less time to do yours.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: It's called teamwork.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Are we still big on that?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Must... control... fist... of... death.

setting: Conference room during a weekly status meeting
situation: At a team meeting, a bald coworker claims his weekly accomplishment was helping Alice finish her project on time. Alice insists he did nothing, but he argues that by not pestering her for the data he needed after she shooed him away, he freed up her time. Alice quietly seethes while the Boss wonders if teamwork is still a priority.
punchline: The coworker takes credit for 'helping' simply by not doing his own job and not bothering Alice, redefining laziness as teamwork, which leaves Alice fuming with violent frustration.
summary: A coworker claims credit for assisting a colleague by leaving her alone and neglecting his own work, to her barely contained rage.

file: 2007/2007-12-21_staff meeting_take an hour_skip meeting_agree to die_earlier_deadness_haunt boss_agreement.gif
title: Dying Earlier to Skip Meeting

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Your staff meeting will take an hour of my life that I will never get back.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: If you let me skip the meeting, I will agree to die an hour earlier to make up the difference.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He agreed?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Yes, and I'm going to use that extra hour of deadness to haunt him.

situation: Wally holds his coffee mug and tells the Boss that his staff meeting will steal an hour of his life. He offers to die an hour sooner if he can skip the meeting, and the Boss agrees. Wally then explains to Dilbert that he plans to use the extra hour of being dead to haunt the Boss.
punchline: Wally turns the boss's agreement into a lose-lose deal for the Boss, since the lost hour of life becomes an hour of haunting him as a ghost.
summary: Wally bargains his way out of a staff meeting with a morbid offer and then reveals the vengeful twist hidden in the deal.

title: Wally Demands Supervision to Work

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, did you get those cost estimates I asked for last week?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No, I need constant supervision.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can you do it now?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Do you have time to watch?

situation: The Boss asks Wally whether he finished the cost estimates requested a week ago. Wally calmly says he didn't because he needs constant supervision. The Boss eagerly asks if he can do it now, and Wally, sipping coffee, asks whether the Boss has time to stand and watch him work.
punchline: Wally turns his laziness into a management problem, claiming he can only work while being watched, and the Boss's willingness to oblige would force him to waste his own time supervising.
summary: An employee dodges an overdue task by insisting he only works when someone babysits him, and his boss falls right into the trap.

file: 2007/2007-09-26_high priority tasks_launched_abyss of total nothingness_never talk about you.gif
title: Dilbert's Tasks Rot in Miasma

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Today I completed my high priority tasks and launched them into the miasma.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There they will rot from neglect while I draw closer to the abyss of eternal nothingness.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I have an idea: Let's never talk about you.

situation: Dilbert gloomily announces that he finished his high priority tasks and sent them off into the miasma, where they will sit neglected while he approaches eternal nothingness. Ratbert, standing on the desk, listens to the bleak monologue and suggests they never talk about Dilbert again.
punchline: Dilbert's melodramatic despair about his work and existence is so tiresome that Ratbert proposes simply never discussing him, a deadpan brush-off of his self-pity.
summary: After a dreary speech about his finished work vanishing into neglect and his own approaching oblivion, Dilbert is coldly shut down by a small pet who wants to avoid the subject entirely.

title: Insulting Your Way Through Introductions

transcript.speaker: New Employee
transcript.text: At my old job, we did everything better than we do it here.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: They sound like a great company.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It's no wonder they fired you.

transcript.speaker: New Employee
transcript.text: They didn't fire me. I quit to come work here.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: So, your point is that you're a moron?

setting: Conference room at a meeting table
situation: At a meeting, a new employee complains that everything was done better at his previous company. Alice sarcastically assumes he must have been fired from such a great place, and he protests that he chose to quit and join this company. Alice then points out that this makes him a moron.
punchline: By insisting he voluntarily left a superior company for this inferior one, the new hire unwittingly proves Alice's point that he made a foolish decision.
summary: A newcomer's boasting about his former employer backfires when a coworker turns his own claim into an insult.

file: 2007/2007-10-18_make cahnges_history suggests_infinyte loop_furious ball_wild about font_no hope finsihing.gif
title: Endless Revisions and the Font

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Make these changes and run it by me again.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: History suggests I have entered an infinite loop of making changes with no hope of finishing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My life is a furious ball of nothing.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And I'm not wild about the font.

situation: The Boss hands Dilbert a document and tells him to make changes and bring it back for another review. Dilbert realizes he is stuck in an endless cycle of revisions and laments the pointlessness of his work. The Boss, reading the latest version, responds with yet another trivial complaint about the font.
punchline: Dilbert's despair over his futile revision loop is met with the Boss's petty new criticism about the font, proving the loop will never end.
summary: A worker trapped in a never-ending cycle of revisions gets a fresh nitpick just as he voices his despair.

file: 2007/2007-12-02_coworkers_cubicles_question_busy_promise of speed_five seconds_name calling_no time_disrespect_no help.gif
title: Five Seconds Means Five Seconds

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Do you have a minute?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: This will just take a second.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No it won't.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It's real quick.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Never is.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You have my word that it will take no longer than five seconds.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Go.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Oh, good. So, I was walking by and I thought maybe I should stop and ask you something because...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Time's up.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Jerk.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Liar.

situation: A coworker keeps asking Dilbert for just a minute, then a second, then promises her question will take no more than five seconds. Dilbert finally agrees but starts the clock, and cuts her off when five seconds have passed before she gets to her question. They part trading insults.
punchline: Dilbert takes her promise of a five-second interruption literally and enforces it, exposing that people who promise quick questions never actually keep them short.
summary: A pushy coworker's pledge of a five-second question is held against her when Dilbert cuts her off the instant the time runs out.

file: 2007/2007-09-17_vp of marketing_describe prodcut_marketing language_overheat_hottest prodcut_know carcinigens_appreciate life!.gif

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: All the parts are known carcinogens.

situation: Dogbert, as VP of Marketing, asks an engineer to describe a product in technical terms so he can translate it into marketing language. The engineer reveals that the product overheats and that all its parts are known carcinogens, and Dogbert cheerfully writes a positive slogan for each flaw.
punchline: Marketing turns serious product dangers into upbeat slogans, showing how spin can disguise harmful defects as selling points.
summary: A marketing executive happily rebrands a product's fire and cancer hazards as enticing advertising catchphrases.

title: Status Report on Status Report

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When will I get your project status report?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're asking for a status report on the status of the status report?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Right. When can I get that?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's starting to look like infinity.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert when his project status report will be ready. Dilbert points out that the Boss is now asking for a status report about the status report, and the Boss agrees and asks when he can have that. Dilbert replies that the answer is starting to look like infinity, since each report spawns another one.
punchline: Reporting on reports creates an endless recursive loop, so the delivery date for the status of the status report heads toward infinity.
summary: A manager's demand for reports about reports sends Dilbert's workload into a never-ending recursion.

file: 2007/2007-11-23_family friendly policy_implemented_children_parents_needs of family_school_sick_rugby game_denta;appoitments_responsibility of parent_surprised_family_education_medical.gif
title: Family Friendly Policy Backfires on Boss

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Three of my kids have bronchitis, two have dental appointments, one is in a school play, and one has a rugby game.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: In all likelihood, you will never see me again.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We didn't think this through.

situation: An employee approaches the boss's desk to use the company's new family friendly policy. She lists the many obligations of her very large family, including illnesses, dental appointments, a school play and a rugby game. She concludes she will probably never come to work again, and the boss realizes the policy was a mistake.
punchline: The company introduced a family friendly policy without considering that an employee with a huge family could use it to justify being absent essentially forever.
summary: A worker with a houseful of kids invokes the company's new family-leave perk so thoroughly that management realizes it has handed out an unlimited excuse to stay away.

title: Wally Accidentally Admits Faked Loyalty

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Wally, your choice of words leads us to think you are only pretending to be loyal to the company.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Sorry. I'll try to appear more loyal in the future.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You did it again.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Don't be silly. I couldn't be more loyal.

situation: Catbert, the evil human resources director, tells Wally that his wording suggests he is only pretending to be loyal to the company. Wally apologizes and promises to appear more loyal in the future, which is itself an admission that his loyalty is an act. Catbert points out he did it again, and Wally insists he couldn't be more loyal.
punchline: Wally's promise to 'appear' more loyal gives away that his loyalty is fake, and his insistence that he couldn't be more loyal makes the slip even more obvious.
summary: Wally tries to reassure the HR cat about his devotion to the firm but keeps incriminating himself with every attempt.

file: 2007/2007-12-23_management retreat_golfing_swimming_drinking_getting massages_count printer papaer_meaningless work assigned_dead body_sports.gif
title: Boss's Retreat, Employee's Dead Body

transcript.text: I'm off to the management retreat.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I won't be reachable because I'll be busy golfing, swimming, drinking, and getting massages.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: And attending meetings?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't see how we'll have any time for that.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: While I'm gone, I have a few tasks for you to do.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Open all the packages of printer paper and make sure they have the right number of sheets.

transcript.text: Then crawl into the heating ducts and see if you can find what died in there.

punchline: Alice's deadpan implication that she killed her last boss and stashed him in the ducts is met with the Boss's complete indifference, suggesting she may be next and he doesn't care.
summary: A boss leaves for a pampering retreat after assigning absurd busywork, then shrugs off the discovery that his subordinate's predecessor is decomposing in the vents.

title: Meaningless Jargon Meets Unverifiable Claim

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What have you done lately to enhance our strategy into the next adjacency?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't know what that means, so I'm going to say, "Everything."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He's lucky there's no way to verify that claim.

situation: The Boss stands at Dilbert's cubicle and asks what he has done to enhance strategy into the next adjacency. Dilbert admits to himself that he has no idea what that means, so he answers "everything." The Boss walks away, thinking that Dilbert is lucky his claim can't be verified.
punchline: The Boss's buzzword question is so vague that Dilbert's blanket answer can't be checked, and the Boss admits as much in his own thoughts, showing that neither of them knows what the jargon means.
summary: A manager's incomprehensible buzzword question gets an equally empty catch-all answer that nobody can disprove.

file: 2007/2007-10-07_mandatory meeting_health and well being_theme of meeting_healthy employees are unprodcutive_exercsing_eating fruit_work hard and die_feel sick_right on schedule.gif

transcript.text: Doesn't that send a message that work is more important than health?

transcript.text: I hope so. That's the theme of the meeting.

transcript.text: Healthy employees are unproductive.

summary: A manager holds an early-morning health seminar whose hidden message is that fit workers are a nuisance and worn-out ones are ideal.

title: Promoting Incompetence Through Lack of Training

transcript.text: Bruce, you're totally incompetent at your job, so I'm moving you to another job.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm hoping your lack of training for your new job will make your incompetence seem normal.

situation: The Boss tells an employee named Bruce that he is totally incompetent and is being moved to a different job. He explains that Bruce's lack of training for the new role should make his incompetence blend in as normal. In the last panel the Boss, holding a coffee mug beside Catbert, adds that knowing when to give up is half of the job.
punchline: The Boss's plan for dealing with an incompetent employee is to reassign him somewhere he is untrained so that failure looks normal, and he casually admits that giving up is a core management skill.
summary: Rather than fire a hopeless worker, a manager shuffles him to an unfamiliar role where his failures will go unnoticed.

transcript.text: No, I think you're misinterpreting it.

transcript.text: I wrote it!!!

situation: A coworker holds a document and claims it says a backup server is overkill. Dilbert calmly corrects him, saying it says the opposite and that he wrote it that very morning. The coworker insists Dilbert is misinterpreting it, and Dilbert shouts in frustration that he is the author.
punchline: The coworker is so confident in his own reading that he tells the document's author he misunderstands what he himself wrote.
summary: A man argues with the author of a memo over what the memo means, even after learning who wrote it.

title: Boss Ignores Rebellion, Promises Monitoring
