transcript.text: But I promise to monitor the situation.

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss that his unqualified crony is provoking a staff rebellion. The Boss calmly dismisses the concern as exaggerated. In the last panel, an angry mob has thrown the Boss onto his desk and is pitchforking him, yet he promises to keep monitoring the situation.
punchline: The Boss insists the problem is overblown and promises passive 'monitoring' even as the rebellious staff literally attack him with a pitchfork.
summary: Faced with a warning about employee unrest, a complacent manager downplays it while an angry mob physically assaults him.

title: Paid By The Page, Hairball Moved

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Tina the Tech Writer

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I decided to base your salary on the number of pages you write.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Fine. I'll give you a high volume of low quality work.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sometimes the best you can do is move the hairball to another pocket.

setting: Office cubicle and the Boss's office
situation: The Boss announces that Tina the tech writer's salary will now be based on how many pages she writes. Tina responds that she will simply produce lots of low-quality pages. The Boss then reflects to Catbert, who is sitting on his desk, that sometimes the best you can do is move the hairball to another pocket.
punchline: The Boss knowingly creates a perverse incentive that rewards quantity over quality, and shrugs off the predictable bad result by admitting he's only shuffling his problems around rather than solving them.
summary: A manager ties a writer's pay to page count, gets exactly the junk output that incentive invites, and philosophically accepts it as merely relocating a problem.

file: 2007/2007-10-28_empty brain_stress_word knowledge_past the filters_mantra_lindsay lohan_britney spears_paris hilton.gif
title: Emptying Your Brain With Celebrity Mantra

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: My brain is empty.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: It feels great!

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Stress is just another word for knowledge.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Wait a minute. How do I know that?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Gaa!!! Something got past the filters!

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Must... do... mantra...

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Lindsay Lohan... Britney Spears... Paris Hilton... Ommmmm.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Are you all good now?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Have we met?

situation: Ratbert walks beside Dogbert and proudly announces that his brain is empty and it feels great. When he accidentally spouts a bit of real insight, he panics that knowledge has slipped past his mental filters and chants celebrity names as a mantra to purge it. Afterward he is so thoroughly blank that he no longer recognizes Dogbert.
punchline: Chanting tabloid celebrity names erases even his memory of his friend, implying that mindless pop-culture noise is the surest way to a truly empty head.
summary: A cheerful rat who has cleared his mind fights off a stray thought by reciting gossip-magazine stars until he forgets everything, including his companion.

title: Cheering For Busywork Toner Labels

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm trying to develop a good attitude about my job.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Every morning I tell myself I am invigorated by busywork.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, I need you to relabel the toner cartridges.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Woo-hoo!

situation: Wally, holding a coffee mug, explains to a coworker that he is trying to improve his attitude by telling himself each morning that he is invigorated by busywork. The Boss then walks up and assigns Asok the tedious task of relabeling toner cartridges. Asok cheerfully responds with enthusiasm.
punchline: Asok sincerely cheers at a mindless busywork assignment, showing he has taken the self-deluding positive attitude Wally describes to an absurd extreme.
summary: A coworker's forced optimism about menial tasks is put into practice when the boss hands Asok a dull chore and he celebrates it.

title: Discrediting New Hires Before They Complain

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The new guy is a huge weasel. Don't believe anything he says.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: You say that about all the new hires so they won't seem credible when they complain about you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll stop doing it when it stops working.

situation: The Boss, seated in a chair behind his desk, warns an employee holding a coffee mug that the new guy is a weasel who can't be trusted. The employee points out that the Boss says this about every new hire to undermine their credibility in advance. The Boss cheerfully admits it and says he'll keep doing it as long as it works.
punchline: The Boss openly admits to a manipulative tactic of smearing new hires before they can complain about him, and refuses to stop because it is effective.
summary: A manager pre-emptively trashes every newcomer's reputation so their grievances will be ignored, and shamelessly vows to continue until the trick fails.

file: 2007/2007-10-30_credible scientist_products harm enbviornment_cats doubt on data_eat wrong food_hope you die.gif
title: Dogbert's Climate Doubt Consulting Advice

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert consults

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Every credible scientist on Earth says your products harm the environment.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I recommend paying weasels to write articles casting doubt on the data.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Then eat the wrong kinds of foods and hope you die before the Earth does.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're making me hungry!

setting: The Boss's office, with Dogbert consulting across the desk
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, tells the Boss that every credible scientist says his company's products harm the environment. He advises paying weasels to write articles casting doubt on the data, then suggests the Boss eat unhealthy food and hope to die before the Earth does. The oblivious Boss only responds that the talk of food is making him hungry.
punchline: Dogbert's cynical plan is to deny the science and simply outlive the consequences, and the Boss misses the insult entirely, caring only that he's hungry.
summary: A consultant dog proposes buying fake doubt about environmental damage and then dying early, while the clueless executive just wants lunch.

file: 2007/2007-11-12_tech support_asks customer_information_transfers call_same questions_barrier to progress_other guy.gif
title: Tech Support: Professional Roadblock Wanted

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, I need you to fill in at tech support for a few days.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You'll be the guy who asks the customer for information, then transfers the call to another person who asks exactly the same questions.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Wouldn't that make me a barrier to progress?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Only if the other guy actually helped.

situation: The Boss asks Asok to temporarily cover tech support. His job would be to collect information from the customer and then transfer the call to another person who asks the very same questions. Asok worries this makes him an obstacle, and The Boss replies that it only would if the next person were useful.
punchline: The Boss's reply implies that the second tech support person is no help either, so the entire support process is useless and Asok's role does no harm.
summary: A manager assigns a young employee to a call-transfer role in support, then admits the whole help desk is equally pointless.

file: 2007/2007-12-28_alice quits_2 weeks notice_20% raise_calls father_quitter_moron_raise instead of quit.gif
title: Alice Quits, Then Insults Dad

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, I got your two weeks' notice.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Will you stay if I give you a 20% raise?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Hey Dad, do you remember you said I should never be a quitter? You do?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Well, it turns out that you're a moron.

setting: Office break area and Alice's cubicle
situation: The Boss tells Alice he received her two weeks' notice, then immediately offers her a 20% raise to stay, and she accepts. Alice then phones her father, who had always taught her never to be a quitter, to tell him his advice was wrong.
punchline: Alice discovers that threatening to quit instantly earns her a raise, so she sarcastically tells her dad that his never-quit advice was foolish.
summary: A single resignation notice gets Alice an instant pay bump, proving to her that her father's advice about never quitting was wrong.

file: 2007/2007-09-18_public relations_marketing claims_tap water_unleaded gasoline_reanimate the dead_lousy job_job easier.gif
title: PR Head Mocks Absurd Marketing Claims

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert, VP of Marketing

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: As head of public relations, it will be my job to explain your marketing claims.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: So?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: You claim our product can turn tap water into unleaded gasoline and reanimate the dead.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Are you asking me to do a lousy job of marketing just so your job is easier?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Um. . .

setting: Dogbert's office, where he sits as VP of Marketing
situation: Dogbert, the newly titled VP of Marketing, meets with the head of public relations, who must explain his marketing claims to the public. She reads out his claims that the product turns tap water into gasoline and brings back the dead, and then accuses him of making her job harder on purpose to make his own easier.
punchline: Dogbert's outrageous, unbelievable marketing claims are absurd enough to make the PR person's job impossible, and she points out that he is effectively dumping his own work onto her, leaving him with no good answer.
summary: A public relations chief confronts the marketing VP over product promises so ridiculous that no one could defend them.

file: 2007/2007-12-14_theoretically impossible_looped back_mobs strip_to- do list_had a pencil.gif
title: Mobius Strip Excuse For Idleness

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It was theoretically impossible to work this week.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Everything I needed to do required me to do something else first, until it all looped back on itself like a Möbius strip.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe you could make a to-do list.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: As if I had a pencil.

situation: During a meeting, Wally explains that he got no work done all week because every task depended on another task in a circular loop. The Boss suggests he make a to-do list, and Wally replies that he has no pencil to write one with.
punchline: Wally's absurd excuse for doing nothing is so airtight that even the obvious fix of a to-do list is dismissed with the claim that he lacks a pencil.
summary: Wally blames a circular chain of dependencies for a week of zero productivity, then shoots down his boss's helpful suggestion with a flimsy new excuse.

title: Bug Documentary Ruins the Date

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I saw a fascinating documentary about bugs.

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: In other words, you like bugs more than you like me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes, but I didn't realize it until just now.

setting: Outdoor walking path through grassy hills
situation: Dilbert takes a walk with a woman on a date and mentions that he saw a fascinating documentary about bugs. She interprets this as him preferring bugs to her. Dilbert agrees, admitting he only just realized it himself.
punchline: Dilbert unintentionally confirms his date's accusation, revealing his obliviousness and that he really does find bugs more interesting than her.
summary: A stroll with a date goes sour when a casual remark about insects exposes where Dilbert's real interests lie.

file: 2007/2007-12-04_private moon shuttle_3 months_doom inevitable_scapegoat_blame_project_never getting finsihed.gif
title: Scapegoat Delivered for Moon Shuttle

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My company wants me to design a private moon shuttle in three months. Doom is inevitable.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What you need is a scapegoat to blame for the project never getting finished. I'll send one over.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I was almost done, and then this idiot comes along.

setting: Dilbert's home living room, then beside a moon shuttle
situation: Dilbert tells Dogbert he has been ordered to design a private moon shuttle in only three months and expects to fail. Dogbert offers to send over a scapegoat to take the blame. In the last panel, a literal goat is stuck headfirst in the shuttle, and Dilbert blames it while pretending he was nearly finished.
punchline: Dogbert takes 'scapegoat' literally and sends an actual goat, which Dilbert promptly blames for the failed project, showing how blame-shifting is planned in advance.
summary: Facing an impossible deadline, an engineer gets a farm animal delivered to take the fall for his doomed spacecraft.

title: Competing Through Fraud, Called Marketing

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We can't compete on price.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We also can't compete on quality, features or service.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That leaves fraud, which I'd like you to call marketing.

situation: The Boss addresses his team at a conference table, listing the ways the company cannot compete: price, quality, features and service. He concludes that the only option left is fraud, and instructs the team to label it as marketing. Dilbert, Alice and Wally sit and listen.
punchline: Having no real competitive advantage, the company's strategy is to deceive customers and simply rebrand the deception as marketing.
summary: A manager admits his company has nothing legitimate to offer customers and proposes dishonesty under a friendlier name.

title: Rationalizing Deadly Mistakes in Space

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our next project is building a private shuttle to the moon.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now if you make any mistakes, innocent tourists will perish in the vacuum of space.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We need to work on our rationalizations.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Is anyone really "innocent"?

situation: The Boss announces that the team will build a private moon shuttle for tourists and warns that any engineering mistakes will kill innocent passengers. Afterward, Dilbert and Wally walk away and agree they should prepare excuses in advance, with Wally questioning whether anyone is truly innocent.
punchline: Instead of focusing on safety, the engineers plan to justify potential deaths in advance, with Wally cynically casting doubt on the victims' innocence.
summary: Given a deadly responsibility, two engineers respond by rehearsing their excuses for failure rather than preparing to prevent it.

file: 2007/2007-10-15_spreading rumors_make me quit_false rumors_actual facts_poacher_endangered species.gif
title: Rumors Versus Facts, Poacher Accused

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Alice is spreading false rumors about me. She's trying to make me quit.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: At this company, we don't get all anal about the difference between false rumors and actual facts.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's not fair!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Said the alleged poacher of endangered species.

situation: Dilbert complains to Catbert, the HR head, that Alice is spreading false rumors about him to force him to quit. Catbert replies that the company doesn't distinguish between false rumors and actual facts. When Dilbert protests that this is unfair, a caption reveals he is the alleged poacher of endangered species.
punchline: The rumors about Dilbert may actually be true, and the caption exposes his hypocrisy in demanding fairness while accused of poaching endangered species.
summary: A man grumbles to the HR cat about slanderous gossip, only to have a closing caption suggest the gossip might be right on target.

title: Unproven Strategy Is Surprisingly Good

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our new strategy has never worked for anyone before.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That will give us the element of surprise.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's get started!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can I rebalance my 401(k) first?

situation: The Boss tells his team at a meeting that their new strategy has never worked for anyone before, and spins this as an advantage because it will surprise the competition. When he calls for them to get started, Dilbert asks to rebalance his retirement account first.
punchline: Dilbert's request implies he expects the doomed strategy to fail and tank the company, so he wants to protect his retirement savings before it does.
summary: A manager proudly presents a never-successful plan as a tactical advantage, prompting an employee to hurry off and safeguard his retirement money.

file: 2007/2007-10-01_six months_task_simple task_continuous cahnges_unclear communication_short work days_being lazy.gif
title: Blame Me, Not Your Management

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why did it take six months to complete this simple task?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Because of your continuous changes, your unclear communication, and your short work days.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm looking for something more along the lines of you being lazy.

setting: The Boss's office, across a desk
situation: The Boss asks Dilbert why a simple task took six months to finish. Dilbert accurately lists the boss's own faults: constant changes, unclear communication, and short work days. The Boss rejects this and says he wants an explanation that blames Dilbert for being lazy.
punchline: The boss isn't seeking the real cause of the delay; he only wants an answer that blames the employee rather than his own management failures.
summary: A manager demands to know why a project dragged on, then dismisses the honest answer because it points back at him.

file: 2007/2007-09-24_dogcart for president_decisons_based on polls_single thing_called leadership.gif
title: Dogbert Campaigns on Withholding Everything

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert for President

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: As president, I will not make decisions based on polls.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: In fact, I won't give you a single thing that you want. That's called leadership.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll never understand why that works.

transcript.speaker: Audience
transcript.text: Yay! Clap! Clap! Clap! Clap! Clap!

setting: Campaign rally with a podium and microphone in front of a silhouetted crowd
situation: Dogbert, running for president, tells a crowd he won't base decisions on polls. He then promises not to give them anything they want and calls that leadership. The crowd applauds enthusiastically while Dogbert privately wonders why this works.
punchline: Voters cheer a candidate who promises to ignore their wishes, and even the cynical Dogbert is baffled that such an openly unappealing pitch is rewarded.
summary: A candidate wins over a cheering crowd by vowing to deny them everything they desire, puzzling even himself.
